Poa asked to see at least one sample because he was responsible for submitting DepEd’s response to the COA. The envelope was opened and he was shown an acknowledgment receipt.
‘First time’ hearing of Nolasco

Poa prepared DepEd’s response to COA’s AOM covering confidential expenditures for the first three quarters of 2023. The COA had flagged the lack of documents supporting the use of P112.5 million in confidential funds. Poa submitted DepEd’s response for the first two quarters in February 2024 and for the third quarter in April.
Poa likewise testified that he first learned during the 2024 congressional hearings that the confidential funds had allegedly been transferred to a security officer.

He had previously said that only Duterte and Fajarda were privy to the use of the funds. But Fajarda testified during the House inquiry that he had turned over the funds to Col. Dennis Nolasco, then deputy chief of the Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group.

Tolosa asked whether Fajarda’s statement was the first time Poa learned of Nolasco’s involvement. Poa said it was, adding that it was also the first time he learned that Nolasco was a security officer and that Fajarda had transferred the funds to him.
Poa agreed that when he prepared DepEd’s response to the COA, he did not know about Nolasco’s role and could not have spoken with him about payments supposedly made to informants.
Meanwhile, the House prosecution panel is weighing whether to abandon the bribery article against Duterte.

Public prosecutor Joel Chua said in a press briefing that the panel was studying whether to proceed directly to the unexplained wealth article after completing its presentation on the alleged misuse of P612.5 million in confidential funds.
“We are considering dropping one article,” Chua told reporters, stressing that no final decision had been made. The panel is still weighing an option.

Chua said dropping one article could shorten the proceedings, with the prosecution hoping to finish its presentation by the first week or middle of October, the defense by November and the impeachment court potentially issuing a decision by December. — With reports from Zacarian Sarao and Keith Clores /das

articles.title: Only P80M recovered so far out of Leviste solar firm’s P24-B penalty
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The government has recovered only P80 million so far from the P24-billion penalty imposed on the solar energy company of Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste, according to the head of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The government has recovered only P80 million so far from the P24-billion penalty imposed on the solar energy company of Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste, according to the head of the Department of Energy (DOE).

Energy Secretary Sharon Garin gave the update after Akbayan party-list Rep. Chel Diokno brought the matter up during the House appropriations committee hearing on the proposed 2027 DOE budget on Wednesday.

The DOE in January this year imposed a P24-billion penalty on Leviste’s Solar Philippines Power Project Holdings Inc. (SPPHI) for failing to produce the power capacity that the company committed under the more than 30 service contracts awarded by the government during the Duterte administration.
“P80 million, Mr. Chair,” Garin said when asked by Diokno on the amount recovered so far.

Asked how the DOE plans to compel SPPHI to pay the balance, Garin said a criminal complaint had already been filed with the Department of Justice (DOJ) against the company and while a civil case has been filed with the Office of the Solicitor General.
“The purpose of these cases is also to recover the P14 billion in expired bonds, is that correct? Diokno asked, to which Garin said yes.
Also according to the secretary, SPPHI has not yet been “blacklisted” based on the terms set by a recent DOE circular on holding power generation firms accountable.

“I think a month or two months ago, we issued a new circular on GenCos’ (generation companies) accountability, which gives them [up to] ‘three strikes’ and [then] we can blacklist them,” Garin said, again in reply to a question from Diokno regarding SPPHI’s status.
“We’re working on it, she added.

In July, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla disclosed that Leviste and his mother, Sen. Loren Legarda, as well as former Energy Secretary Alfonso Cusi, are under preliminary investigation for possible plunder and graft over the uncompleted solar power projects.
The Office of the Ombudsman ordered them last week to formally reply to the complaints. /das

articles.title: Dissenting view: Bonoan removal as co-accused questioned
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — A Sandiganbayan justice was opposed to the removal of former Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan as an accused in two criminal cases involving alleged kickbacks, saying the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A Sandiganbayan justice was opposed to the removal of former Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan as an accused in two criminal cases involving alleged kickbacks, saying the Office of the Ombudsman failed to apprise the court of the details of his immunity agreement.

Associate Justice Gener Gito of the antigraft court’s Fifth Division was the lone dissenting vote in the 2-1 ruling that dropped the plunder and graft charges filed against Bonoan over an alleged P573-million kickback scheme in flood control projects last year.
The 29-page ruling was released on Tuesday and published on the court’s website on Wednesday.

“In effect, the prosecution would want the court to discharge Bonoan on the sole basis of the Resolution of the Ombudsman recommending his discharge on account of Bonoan’s desire to cooperate with the government,” Gito said in his 32-page dissenting opinion.

“But as to how Bonoan would cooperate with the government, what information Bonoan would relay to the prosecution, what his testimony would be, and in what cases his testimony would be used, the court is kept in the dark,” Gito said.
Associate Justice Zaldy Trespeses, the division chair, and Associate Justice Maryann Corpuz-Mañalac voted to grant the prosecution’s motion.

With Bonoan out, only Sen. Jinggoy Estrada and three former personnel of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH)—then assistant district engineer Denryl Caesar Cortuna and district engineers Manny Bulusan and Arturo Gonzales Jr.—stand accused in the cases.
According to the charges, they engaged in and benefited from an “intricate mechanism involving illegal budgetary insertions and project allocations” within the DPWH infrastructure portfolio for 2025.

Bonoan, 81, was arrested in June and had since been allowed to stay at the Philippine National Police General Hospital at Camp Crame. The Ombudsman later asked the court to have him discharged as a coaccused so he could turn state witness in other flood control corruption cases.

Last month, he was used for the first time as a prosecution witness in the malversation case against former Sen. Ramon “Bong” Revilla Jr. involving an alleged “ghost” flood project in Bulacan. He recalled, among others, that all incumbent senators in 2024 availed themselves of the DPWH “leadership fund” for their “priority projects.”
Vital details
In his dissenting opinion, Gito said the Ombudsman’s resolution seeking Bonoan’s discharge was “bereft of such important and vital details.”

“What the prosecution wants the court to do is simply accept its justification for discharging Bonoan from the information hook, line and sinker. The Sandiganbayan cannot do that without diluting its judicial power,” he said.
Gito recalled that, during one hearing, the court was told by Assistant State Prosecutor III Reza Casila-Derayunan that the “immunity agreement (with Bonoan) is still forthcoming.”

“The terms and conditions of the immunity agreement are vital to the court’s reasoned assessment of whether to discharge Bonoan. It must be emphasized that Section 17 of [Republic Act] No. 6770 is not carte blanche authority for the Ombudsman to grant immunity from criminal prosecution to accused already charged in court,” he said.
“Besides, if there is prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction on the part of Bonoan, why discharge him in the first place?” Gito asked.
Ombudsman’s discretion

The Fifth Division’s resolution, however, noted that “the decision to move for the discharge of an accused is part of the Ombudsman’s prosecutorial discretion in the determination of who should be used as a state witness to bolster the successful prosecution of criminal offenses.”

“Unless made in clear violation of the Rules, this determination should be given great weight as courts do not, as a rule, have a vision of the true strength of the prosecution’s evidence until after the trial is over,” it said.
Estrada’s defense counsel had opposed the prosecutor’s motion, saying it would affect the senator’s defense. Cortuna, Bulusan and Gonzales also filed their respective oppositions.

The case information earlier alleged that Estrada and Bonoan caused, facilitated, or ensured the inclusion of the questioned projects in the national budget. Later, however, it was amended to state that Estrada acted “by himself and/or through” Bonoan.
Jinggoy’s options
In a statement on Wednesday, Estrada said he respected the court resolution on Bonoan.

“(But) I wish to emphasize that there remain legal remedies available to me under our judicial system, which my legal team will carefully study and pursue at the appropriate time,” the detained senator said.
“My faith in our judicial system remains firm. I will continue to stand by the truth and pursue every lawful means available to protect my rights and clear my name and honor,” he said.
Discharge up to court
Meanwhile, the PNP General Hospital on Wednesday reported that Bonoan remained “clinically stable” and under maintenance medication, but that he no longer needed a wheelchair to move.
As to the court ruling, Lt. Col. Benaly Bayani, the hospital’s chief for internal medicine, said the release of Bonoan from the PNP hospital is still up to the Sandiganbayan.

According to a medical certificate dated May 29 and issued by Bonoan’s personal doctor, the former secretary has been diagnosed with prostate cancer, Stage 4 chronic renal disease, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, gouty arthritis, spondylolisthesis, and a spinal condition. — With reports from Isabelle Pechay and Andrea Gregorio /das

articles.title: DOH, PhilHealth chiefs worry over cuts in proposed budgets
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Steep cuts made by Malacañang in the proposed 2027 budgets of the Department of Health (DOH) and the Philippine Health Insurance Corp. (PhilHealth) may hobble hospital expansion…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Steep cuts made by Malacañang in the proposed 2027 budgets of the Department of Health (DOH) and the Philippine Health Insurance Corp. (PhilHealth) may hobble hospital expansion efforts and strain state-backed health insurance coverage, officials said on Wednesday.

The DOH requested a spending plan of P837 billion for next year, but the Department of Budget and Management slashed it by more than half to P353.8 billion in the P7.2-trillion National Expenditure Program submitted to Congress.

At a House hearing on the DOH budget, acting Health Secretary Edwin Mercado said the reduction could delay plans to expand public hospital capacity by 15,000 beds by 2028, from the current total of around 30,000 beds.

“Because of the cut in the HFEP, the target may be delayed unless we reinstate what we are asking for,” Mercado told lawmakers, referring to the department’s Health Facilities Enhancement Program, whose budget is down to P14 billion from P29 billion.
Funds earmarked for the program are geared toward improving existing health facilities and constructing new ones.
PhilHealth subsidy, too

On top of HFEP’s budget slash, the agency’s hospital operations funding also took an P11-billion cut, and its subsidy for PhilHealth saw a drastic reduction from P379 billion to P73 billion, according to Mercado.
PhilHealth president and chief executive officer Beverly Lorraine Ho said their requested budget to subsidize claims of indirect contributors is a “gap” that could dig into its finances.
Ho said the state-run health insurer expects to pay out about P240 billion in hospital claims from indirect contributors.

“This means that if we provide the same amount of benefits with the same rate of utilization next year, we are also expecting at the minimum P244 billion in payouts for indirect contributors,” she said.

Mercado said PhilHealth may find it difficult to sustain its roster of benefit packages if government subsidy falls below the request, as the insurer seeks to expand its perks to lower out-of-pocket medical costs.

“It may be that we cannot lay out or roll out the programmed benefits,” he said in Filipino. “We can still sustain it for now. But within two to three years, we may not be able to continue unless subsidies for indirect members are increased.”
‘A direct threat’
Also on Wednesday, the Alliance of Health Workers (AHW) warned that the reduction in the DOH’s spending plan posed a “direct threat to the delivery of essential health services.”
For instance, it said that slicing a huge chunk of P33.9 billion will affect the operations of 72 DOH hospitals, and another P5.4 billion will take its toll on four specialty hospitals.
These are the Philippine Heart Center, National Kidney and Transplant Institute, Lung Center of the Philippines, and Philippine Children’s Medical Center.

“Instead of strengthening the public healthcare system and providing hospitals with the resources they need to deliver quality healthcare, the government is proposing a drastic P39.3-billion combined budget cut,” AHW secretary general Cristy Donguines said in a statement.
“These cuts will further weaken an already ailing public healthcare system and put the health and lives of millions of Filipinos at risk,” she added.

AHW also noted that public hospitals are already experiencing “chronic shortages of health workers, overcrowded facilities, inadequate and aging equipment, and insufficient medicines and medical supplies.”

Reducing the budget for the hospitals, the group said, will worsen such “long-standing problems” and “compromise” the delivery of healthcare services to the “growing number of patients” that need treatment.
Surging cases
The group also noted that the country is currently facing a surge in cases of leptospirosis, other water-borne diseases, influenza-like illnesses, and dengue.
It added that many Filipinos are also dying from other illnesses such as ischemic heart disease and cerebrovascular diseases.

“At a time when Filipinos urgently need stronger and more accessible public health services, it is deeply alarming that healthcare continues to receive far less funding than infrastructure spending,” Donguines said.
She pointed to the P644-billion allocation for the Department of Public Works and Highways to cite a disparity. /das

articles.title: Marcos: Master plan vs floods kicks off now
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said on Wednesday that a flood control master plan, which had been ignored for decades, would finally be implemented. He made the remarks after…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said on Wednesday that a flood control master plan, which had been ignored for decades, would finally be implemented.

He made the remarks after conducting an inspection of the Aquino and Agana bridges in Tarlac City, which both partially collapsed because of strong river currents and continuous heavy rains spawned by the southwest monsoon, or “habagat.”
“We already have a master plan; it’s just never been executed,” Marcos said when asked about the flood control master plan.
“We’re only executing it now. We have had a master plan for decades, but nothing was done about it until now. We’re only starting it now. We’re only doing it now,” he added.

Discussions about a flood control master plan were prompted by widespread flooding in many parts of the country, particularly in Luzon, since last month after the country was hit by three successive cyclones and the enhanced habagat.
The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council has so far reported 39 fatalities, with 20 others injured and three more missing.
Around 2.7 million families, or around 9.4 million individuals, have also been displaced by the floods.
Marcos, meanwhile, said the government would allocate P300 million for the rehabilitation of the Agana and Aquino bridges.
Repair of bridges

According to him, Agana Bridge could reopen to pedestrians within one week and to light vehicles weighing 10 tons or less within two weeks. But the Aquino Bridge could take longer to reopen due to the extent of the damage it suffered.

Malacañang has repeatedly called for the implementation of long-term flood control measures, including improved waterways, drainage systems and proper land-use planning, as the government responds to increasingly intense rainfall linked to climate change.

The president also directed agencies and local governments to enforce existing laws and no-build zones, saying disaster preparedness and compliance with regulations are necessary to reduce the impact of severe weather events.
At the same time, he assured the public that the government would “continue to adapt” to changing extreme weather events brought about by climate change.

During a Senate hearing in 2024, then Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan admitted that despite the billions of pesos that had been allocated for years for flood control programs, the country still lacks an integrated flood control master plan.
A year later, Bonoan would be linked to the multibillion-peso flood control controversy, leading to the filing of plunder and graft charges against him before the Sandiganbayan in May this year.

Charged with him were Sen. Jose “Jinggoy” Estrada and Department of Public Works and Highways officials in connection with an alleged P573-million kickback scheme from 2025 budget insertions and infrastructure project allocations.
The charges against Bonoan, however, have reportedly been dropped after the Office of the Ombudsman earlier said it wanted to tap him as a state witness. — With a report from PNA /das

articles.title: P7.7B needed to fix schools hit by ‘habagat,’ cyclones
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Damage from floods and the combined effects of the southwest monsoon, or “habagat,” and recent tropical cyclones have affected over 11,000 classrooms nationwide, with the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Damage from floods and the combined effects of the southwest monsoon, or “habagat,” and recent tropical cyclones have affected over 11,000 classrooms nationwide, with the Department of Education (DepEd) saying it would need an estimated P7.783 billion for rehabilitation efforts.
The amount includes P65.036 million for immediate cleanup and clearing operations in 2,243 affected schools and P319.97 million for minor repairs in 1,487 schools.
On the other hand, P1.194 billion would be used to carry out major repairs in 669 schools, while P5.62 billion would go to the reconstruction of 490 heavily damaged school sites.
Overall, the combined effects of the weather disturbances have damaged 2,243 schools and 11,167 classrooms nationwide.
Of the affected classrooms, 6,530 classrooms sustained minor damage while 2,389 suffered major damage and 2,248 others were destroyed.

During an inspection of affected areas in Tarlac, Zambales and Pampanga on Wednesday, Education Secretary Sonny Angara briefed President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on emergency measures to ensure that classes in public schools would not be disrupted.
Most affected region
According to the latest data from the DepEd’s Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Service, Central Luzon sustained the heaviest damage, with at least 622 schools and 4,025 classrooms affected.

The DepEd estimated that the region would require P2.9 billion for response and recovery efforts. This includes P19.49 million for cleanup, P111.43 million for minor repairs, P402.5 million for major repairs and P2.37 billion for reconstruction.
“We are immediately allocating the necessary assistance for the repair of schools while ensuring the safety and well-being of our teachers and students,” Angara said.

In Tarlac City, Tarlac, the collapse of the Aquino and Agana bridges left isolated 23 of the 99 public schools under the Schools Division Office. As a result, classes were shifted to alternative delivery modes from Sept. 1 to Sept. 5.
A total of 786 damaged classrooms across 96 schools were reported, with response and recovery requirements estimated at P496.24 million.

In Pampanga, Marcos and Angara inspected the damaged Sto. Cristo Dam in Lubao town. The province sustained the most extensive damage in Central Luzon, with 250 affected schools and 1,752 damaged classrooms that would require an estimated P1.36 billion for recovery and response efforts.
Pampanga also reported damage to 5,369 learning materials, 66 sets of information technology equipment and 6,351 learner chairs.

In Zambales, the president and Angara visited Sta. Fe National High School in San Marcelino, where floodwaters and sand inundated school grounds. Six classrooms were destroyed while another six sustained minor damage.
Latest reports showed that floods damaged 21 schools and 82 classrooms across the province.
So far, a total of 1,748 classrooms in 442 schools nationwide are currently being used as temporary shelters for 13,723 displaced families.
As of Sept. 1, 367 public schools nationwide had suspended face-to-face classes due to the effects of the monsoon and tropical cyclones.
The DepEd, meanwhile, directed school administrators to use the new hazard assessment tool to prevent class disruptions caused by natural disasters.
“We are calling all school leaders, teachers and (Disaster Risk Reduction and Management) coordinators to use LIGTAS+ as part of our regular disaster preparedness,” Angara said in a statement.

Launched on Aug. 26, Project Ligtas+, which stands for Learning Institution Geohazard Tracking and Assessment for Safety, is a decision-support platform that converts raw weather and geological data into school-level safety alerts. — With a report from Sheridan Delfino /das

articles.title: Toll board orders NLEx operator to address flooding in Pampanga
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Toll Regulatory Board (TRB) has ordered the North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) Corp., which operates the expressway, to explain the widespread flooding experienced over the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Toll Regulatory Board (TRB) has ordered the North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) Corp., which operates the expressway, to explain the widespread flooding experienced over the weekend at Tulaoc Bridge near San Simon, Pampanga, that left thousands of motorists stuck in heavy traffic, some for nearly 22 hours.

In a letter shared by the Department of Transportation (DOTr) on Wednesday, the TRB directed NLEx Corp. on Aug. 31 to submit within three days a detailed explanation for the flooding, as well as proposed measures to mitigate the situation in San Simon and Tulaoc towns in the province “to further avoid its recurrence.”

In a separate letter, the TRB also instructed the expressway operator to consider reimbursing the toll paid by Class 1 vehicles that were “compelled to make a U-turn due to the flooding incidents in the affected area.”

According to the TRB, it expects NLEx Corp. to send alerts to motorists through Variable Message Signs (VMS), portable VMS and other messaging platforms to inform them that the San Simon-Pulillan segment of the expressway will be closed to traffic if the water level reaches critical level because of heavy rains.
Many parts of Luzon, particularly Zambales and Pampanga, have been inundated by floods for the past few days as a result of heavy rains brought by the enhanced southwest monsoon, or “habagat.”

“During such circumstances, NLEX Corp. is likewise directed to closely coordinate with the DOTr and TRB, to jointly ensure the timely implementation of appropriate flood mitigation measures and other necessary interventions, with the primary objective of ensuring the safety of the motoring public and minimizing traffic disruption,” the TRB said in its letter.
Two senators were among those stuck in the massive traffic jam along NLEx over the weekend.
Seven-hour trip
Sen. Robinhood Padilla said it took him seven hours to travel from his home to the San Simon exit, after leaving around 4:30 a.m. and getting out of the area at about 11:30 a.m.
“I personally passed through NLEx yesterday … It took seven hours … and that was only as far as San Simon. We didn’t even make it to Pangasinan,” he said on Tuesday.
Sen. Joel Villanueva said that Sen. Manuel “Lito” Lapid, who is from Pampanga, was also affected.
In a privilege speech, Villanueva, who is from Bulacan, called on NLEX Corp. to consider waiving or refunding toll for motorists who were inconvenienced.
He also urged the operator to create long-term solutions for the recurring flooding in the area. — With a report from Isabelle Pechay /das

articles.title: Calls mount for return of watchdogs to House budget talks
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Major voices from the business sector and civil society are calling on the House of Representatives to review its guidelines on civil society participation in the chamber’s…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Major voices from the business sector and civil society are calling on the House of Representatives to review its guidelines on civil society participation in the chamber’s budget deliberations, following concerns that watchdogs are being left out in talks on next year’s allocations.

In a joint statement, the People’s Budget Coalition (PBC), Makati Business Club (MBC) and the Roundtable for Inclusive Development (RID) urged the House appropriations committee to review the rules and elevate civil society organizations (CSO) as full-fledged participants in the process.
The new call was made after the queries earlier raised by society groups were not tackled during Monday’s hearings on the budgets of the Office of the President and the Department of Agriculture.

Last week, Nueva Ecija Rep. Mikaela Suansing, who chairs the appropriations committee, acknowledged gaps in the guidelines and directed the panel to coordinate with the Congressional Policy and Budget Research Department, which oversees CSO participation.
For ‘fair opportunity’

In a message to the Inquirer on Wednesday, PBC co-coordinator Gybel Agregado said that if the committee “is sincere in its apology for excluding civil society from the budget process, then that apology must be followed by meaningful action.”

The panel should lay down “clear, transparent rules that institutionalize CSO participation and ensure that questions submitted by civil society are given a fair opportunity to be raised during budget hearings,” Agregado added.

Last year, the House set interim guidelines on CSO engagement as part of transparency reforms in the budget process, after the chamber came under heavy criticism over alleged backdoor dealings that paved the way for so-called insertions that feed into corruption.
In their joint statement, the PBC, MBC and RID said the House should revisit the guidelines since they “were designed to be reviewed with civil society after one cycle.”
“Rules issued late in the cycle are rules that cannot be used,” they said.
“We ask that this review proceed, and that in the meantime the Committee confirm how organizations may accredit, attend, and submit inputs for the remainder of these deliberations.”
They also urged the appropriations panel to let budget watchdogs sit as participants instead of observers in the hearings.
“Observing a hearing and being able to speak in one are different things,” the groups said. Committee vice chairpersons currently lead agency budget hearings and field civil society questions.

“We ask for a designated point in agency hearings where accredited organizations may raise questions and present evidence, along with timely access to hearing schedules and agency submissions so that our contributions are prepared rather than improvised,” they added.
The groups also urged lawmakers to pass a bill placing the national budget on a blockchain system to boost transparency and check amendments during legislators’ review.
Budget documents should also be published in machine-readable format so checking each line item is more straightforward, they added.

The House last week began scrutinizing the proposed P7.2‑trillion national budget for next year, and lawmakers are holding marathon hearings into each agencies’ spending plan that is expected to run until the second week of September. The chamber aims to pass the budget bill by Oct. 9.
“At a moment when the public is demanding answers about how government resources are being planned and spent, congressional scrutiny should be strengthened, not suspended,” the groups said. /das

articles.title: DepEd: No more active-shooting ‘reenactment’ in school drills
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Education (DepEd) will no longer conduct active shooter “reenactments” during the simultaneous school safety drills to be held nationwide on Sept. 3. “There…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Education (DepEd) will no longer conduct active shooter “reenactments” during the simultaneous school safety drills to be held nationwide on Sept. 3.

“There will no longer be reenactments involving an active shooter or active attacker because, according to experts, these may cause psychological trauma to participating learners and teachers,” DepEd Undersecretary Malcolm Garma said on Wednesday at the sidelines of Kapihan sa Manila Prince Hotel press forum.
“What will trigger the drill are the … distinct alarms. [Once] they [go off, they] will signal the commencement of the drills,” Garma said.

The DepEd called off the active shooter drills originally scheduled on Aug. 25 over inclement weather and amid concerns from psychiatrist groups, which said that current evidence does not show that these simulations “reduce casualties or prevent incidents.”
‘Run-hide-fight’

According to Philippine Psychiatric Association and Philippine Society for Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, multiple studies also demonstrated that the drills, which “expose learners to hyper-realistic scenarios of violence,” may cause lasting psychological harm.
For Garma, the deferment of the nationwide drills also allowed the DepEd to include measures to strengthen post-incident response efforts and integrate the “run-hide-fight” protocol.

The “run-hide-fight” protocol is a procedure in which individuals in an active shooter situation may decide to evacuate as a first response; or hide silently as a secondary measure; or directly confront the perpetrator as a last resort.

The DepEd official said that one other measure that was introduced was to seek the consent of parents for their children’s participation in the exercise, noting that schools were currently in the end-of-term block for the first trimester.
“We will not be able to force them to make their children join,” he said. “But, of course, we would like to encourage our parents to make their children join.”
Muscle memory

The nationwide drill will kick off at a school in Bulacan province on Thursday morning, according to Garma, noting that other schools—particularly those affected by flooding amid inclement weather—may choose to hold the exercise some other time.

The school safety drills were prompted by school shootings in Tacloban City on June 22 and Zamboanga City on Aug. 18. A total of five students were killed, including the shooter in Zamboanga City, who turned the gun on himself after killing a fellow student. The two students who carried out the shooting in Tacloban City were arrested. Only one was charged, however, because the other student is only 14 years old and cannot be charged yet under the juvenile justice law.
“This will not be the first and the last,” Garma said. “We have to perfect that drill. It’s really for muscle memory.”

“Our earthquake drills are paying off. Our children already know what to do: duck-cover-and-hold. We hope that these drills to address human-induced incidents like this would also be part of the muscle memory of our learners,” he added. /das

articles.title: New youth trend: ‘Aura farming’ gets competitive
articles.summary: LIMA, Peru — Dozens of young people gathered recently on a beach in Peru’s capital to dance, pose and show off their most creative moves—all in pursuit of one thing: aura. They were taking part in a…

blocks.text: LIMA, Peru — Dozens of young people gathered recently on a beach in Peru’s capital to dance, pose and show off their most creative moves—all in pursuit of one thing: aura.
They were taking part in a so-called aura battle, a real-world spin on the internet trend known as “aura farming” that is sweeping across Latin America.

Dressed up as characters from comic books or animated films, competitors engaged in dance battles of sorts, vying for the crowd’s applause. Those with the loudest cheers and the most creative moves advanced to the next round.

One competitor dressed up as Spider-Man performed forward rolls and push-ups, as techno music played in the background. Another hopped on one leg while kicking the other forward, in a move that looked straight from a video game.
Shed off all ‘shame’

“Aura farming is about letting your essence flow in a place where people are watching you, but where there is no shame,” said Liam González, a 20-year-old film student who attended dressed up as the movie character Shrek.
Gonzalo Cornelio, 19, came dressed as former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, wearing a grey tracksuit like the one worn by the deposed leader the night he was captured by the US military.
Aura farming competitions first emerged in Brazil and spread through social media. Now, teenagers and adults are holding aura battles across Latin America.
“It’s not about being popular,” said María Paula Martínez, a professor in the arts faculty at Colombia’s Los Andes University. “It’s about showing off good vibes, and having others recognize that.”

Like video game characters who farm for points, people who go aura farming are trying to earn a reward. In this case, it’s about generating good vibes, and thus improving their “aura,” a term that, according to some spiritual traditions, refers to an energy field that surrounds people.

Fernando Lícito, a Peruvian content creator, said that in aura battles participants do not touch each other or trade insults. “They are simply farming their aura,” said Lícito, 25. “And whoever gets the crowd to make more noise wins.”
From digital to physical
Lícito said he saw a video in June of an aura farming contest in Brazil, and decided to bring the idea to Peru. So far, he has organized three aura battles there.
During the contests, some participants imitate soccer star Cristiano Ronaldo’s goal celebration, extending their arms downward and making a sound that sounds like “siuu.”

Aura battles have spread to cities across Latin America, including Mexico City, Quito and Buenos Aires, where dozens of people staged a battle in front of the Obelisk, one of the most iconic monuments in the Argentine capital.
The contests have also reached Spain, with events taking place in Madrid, Burgos and Zaragoza.
Martínez, the Colombian arts professor, said that the concept of aura farming has moved beyond the digital world into physical spaces, enabling teenagers to socialize.
Not everyone amused
But some aura battles have met some resistance.
In Lima’s Miraflores district, officials recently canceled an aura farming event, saying organizers had not obtained the permits required to hold it in a public space.

In July, the mayor of Cuiaba, a city in southwestern Brazil, denied permits for an aura tournament, arguing it was not in the public’s interest. The event was transferred to a university campus. And in Costa Rica, the ministry of education banned aura battles in public schools arguing they could create conflicts between students or disrupt learning.
In Mexico, by contrast, the education minister embraced the trend, posting a video in which he smiles and says he is “farming good education” as the country prepares for the new school year.

González, the aura farmer who dresses up as Shrek, said that this hobby gives him a way to have fun and express himself, even if his grandmother doesn’t get what he’s doing and thinks it’s silly. “We were born in a different era,” he said. /das

articles.title: Senate OKs bill barring politicians’ kin from gov’t contracts
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate on Wednesday passed, on third and final reading, a bill prohibiting families of public officials from engaging in government contracts. Senate Bill No. 1962, or the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate on Wednesday passed, on third and final reading, a bill prohibiting families of public officials from engaging in government contracts.

Senate Bill No. 1962, or the “Government Contracting and Procurement Integrity Act,” seeks to disqualify from government procurement and contracts relatives of politicians within the fourth civil degree of consanguinity and affinity.

Its main goal is to eliminate “potential avenues for corruption” and “uphold fairness, integrity, transparency, impartiality and accountability” in the bureaucracy’s procurement process and use of public funds.
Its counterpart measure, House Bill No. 7919, is pending before the committee on revision of laws.

Fourth-degree relatives include parents, children, grandparents, siblings, grandchildren, great grandparents, great aunts and uncles, great niece and nephews, great grandchildren, great great grandparents, great great aunts and uncles, great great nieces and nephews, and first cousins.

Officials include elected local and national officials, Cabinet secretaries, undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, officers and members of government-owned and -controlled corporations, and state universities and colleges, and their alternates.
The measure penalizes violators with imprisonment of up to more than three years, a fine of not less than P100,000 and perpetual disqualification from government procurement.
A public officer, on the other hand, may face charges for violation of graft and corrupt practices, similar imprisonment term and fines and perpetual disqualification from public office.

The measure was authored by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian, and Sens. Francis “Chiz” Escudero, Christopher “Bong” Go, Joel Villanueva, Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, JV Ejercito, Loren Legarda and Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan.

Go, together with former President Rodrigo Duterte, is facing a plunder complaint filed by former Sen. Antonio “Sonny” Trillanes IV with the Ombudsman over the Davao City government’s award of contracts to companies owned by Go’s family. — With a report from PNA /das

articles.title: Journalists’ code of ethics getting an AI-era reboot
articles.summary: NEW YORK — Walk into a corner of a newsroom somewhere and you can often find it affixed to a bulletin board, perhaps peeking out from behind the coffee pot: the Society of Professional Journalists’…

blocks.text: NEW YORK — Walk into a corner of a newsroom somewhere and you can often find it affixed to a bulletin board, perhaps peeking out from behind the coffee pot: the Society of Professional Journalists’ (SPJ) Code of Ethics. It’s less than a thousand words, fitting neatly on a poster.
But those words—organized around four key journalistic principles—are important enough, asserts Dan Axelrod, that they just might save our democracy.

“I’m going to just say it,” says Axelrod, chair of the SPJ ethics committee and former longtime Gannett business reporter. “This is the way to protect democracy. This is to protect society. There but for the grace of God goes a society without journalists.”

Axelrod is talking not only about the existence of the code but the need, every so often, to update it. It’s a laborious process, taking about a year and countless hours of meetings and feedback, virtual and in person.

Yet as the media landscape seems to shift daily and new technologies emerge, SPJ has decided that the time is at hand—for the first time in 12 years, and only the sixth in the code’s centurylong history.

The seriousness of the undertaking brought the committee and other media ethics experts to Indianapolis in June, after lots of virtual meetings. Seems it wasn’t the most relaxing way to spend a weekend.“
Passions definitely got heated,” Axelrod says.

“Well, there were no fistfights,” quips his colleague, Chris Roberts, vice chair of the committee and a journalism professor at the University of Alabama. He explains there was “a lot of smithing of the words.”
The result: No white smoke, but a 967-word draft code, 73 longer than the existing one.
Used and misused
But why update in the first place? The first reason—hardly a surprise—is the rapid emergence of AI.

“We were thinking about artificial intelligence and how it’s used and sometimes misused by news organizations,” Roberts says, “as they confront that new technology that saves them money, but also causes a lot of trouble if it’s not used effectively and ethically.”

Another issue concerns the very term “professional journalists.” Recent years have seen a huge increase in independent, so-called “creator journalists.” The SPJ thinks they, too, should have a code to guide them. (The code, as always, is a voluntary guide and not enforceable.)
One key goal is to address an existential crisis in the field: an increasing lack of public trust in the media.

“We’re talking about a world that does not trust us as much as they did,” Roberts says. “We’re talking about politicians and others who go out of their way to smack journalism around because it dares point out their shortcomings. Meanwhile, the business of journalism has changed so much financially, and a third of journalists don’t work for a traditional news organization.
Four key principles

“All of those things and so many more are pretty good reasons to take another look,” he says, “and remind people that there are standards that should be standards, regardless of whether you call yourself a journalist, or the type of platform for which you work.”

The SPJ, which has some 4,000 members nationwide, was founded in 1909. In 1926 it adopted its first code of ethics, then formed an ethics committee in 1948 and revised the code five times—the last in 2014.
The four, unchanging key principles: “Seek Truth and Report It.” “Minimize Harm.” “Act Independently.” “Be Accountable and Transparent.”

But much else has evolved. A report accompanying the draft notes that traditional newsroom jobs are dwindling as the industry contracts. Simultaneously, it says, there’s been a marked growth in citizen journalists, freelancers, online influencers and pundits.
The report cites a Pew study that shows fully one-third of journalists were freelance or self-employed in 2023.

It also cites the shrinking presence of news outlets serving as watchdogs, as well as “people, organizations and private investors without journalism backgrounds, who are buying or opening news properties, affecting news coverage, influencing editorial decisions and pushing personal agendas.”
The SPJ says the rapid rise in use of generative AI and other new technology—in news, as elsewhere—raises ethical questions.

So a new line says: “Remember that speed, technology or medium do not excuse inaccuracy or unfairness. Journalists are ethically responsible for their work, regardless of tools and technologies used.” In other words: The buck stops with the journalist, regardless of what AI might say.
“We don’t want people using the excuse of a technology to say that they couldn’t produce things ethically and transparently,” says Roberts.
What’s been replaced

But the proposed draft—to be voted on in October by the broader organization after a current feedback period—does not mention AI by name, referring only to tools and technologies, so it will remain relevant as technology changes. It also addresses other issues like verification, misinformation, crime reporting, fabricated images and more.

A notable addition—and one that generated much discussion—is this line: “Be vigilant and courageous about holding those with power accountable. Counter the unfair marginalization of those with less power.”
What’s interesting is what it replaces. The original text said: “Give voice to the voiceless.” That phrasing was seen as problematic, because it assumed that some groups lack a voice.
Notes committee member Eric Deggans: “It’s not that they don’t have a voice. It’s that too often mainstream news outlets don’t pay attention to it or don’t even know that it exists.”

“What we wanted to try to speak to,” says Deggans, NPR’s critic-at-large and a media ethics professor at Washington and Lee University, “was this idea that there are groups out there that may be marginalized from news coverage … and (journalists) should make an effort to include them when it’s relevant, particularly when it builds the accuracy of the story.”
Given the changes in the industry, one might ask another, overarching question: Does one code fit all? And will it even be acknowledged?
“We shouldn’t shy away from it,” replies current SPJ President Chris Vaccaro. “Just because the industry is changing or the idea of who a journalist is is changing.”
‘It does matter’
Vaccaro is confident that the code, which has been translated into multiple languages, will be followed by many. That newsroom bulletin board, he says, is now the entire world.

“We’re definitely not going to operate under the assumption that no one’s going to use it or nobody cares, or journalism’s changed so drastically that it doesn’t matter,” says Vaccaro. “It does matter.”

Deggans says he teaches two ethics classes, and both study the SPJ code. But besides training young journalists, the code has other key uses. “If you’re operating in a country that has had authoritarian rule for a long time or doesn’t have a long history of a free press, how do you figure out how that works? You turn to the SPJ code, right?”
Deggans wishes more working journalists would review the code.

And others, too: “I wish some people who owned journalism outlets would read the code, because too often they’re pressuring their employees to do things that are unethical, and the employee has to figure out a way to preserve their journalism ethics and also give the employer what they want.” /das

articles.title: Cassandra Wilson, Grammy-winning jazz singer, dies aged 70
articles.summary:
Mississippi-born Wilson, who worked across folk, pop, R&B and country, was once dubbed America’s best singer

Cassandra Wilson, the two-time Grammy Award-winning jazz singer, songwriter…

blocks.text: Cassandra Wilson, the two-time Grammy Award-winning jazz singer, songwriter and producer has died. She was 70.

Dubbed America’s best singer by Time magazine in 2001, Wilson was best known for her genre-bending voice, which expanded the boundaries of traditional blues-based jazz and worked effortlessly across folk, pop, R&B, country and beyond. At the heart of all her work was her idiosyncratic contralto, a soulful sound distinctly tied to her roots.
As Jon Batiste put it in a eulogy on Wednesday, Wilson sounded like the south.
She died in her native Jackson, Mississippi, on Tuesday morning, the Hinds county coroner, Jeramiah Howard, confirmed.

“It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of Cassandra Wilson, the Grammy Award-winning and legendary jazz artist. Cassandra Wilson transitioned peacefully at home, surrounded by family, close friends, and her manager,” said a statement from her manager to the jazz radio station WBGO.

Born and raised in Jackson to musician Herman B Fowlkes and teacher Mary Fowlkes, Wilson showed an early love of music listening to Motown, Miles Davis and Thelonious Monk. At six, she started piano lessons. She played clarinet in marching bands. She performed at coffeehouses and in cover bands while studying at Millsaps College and Jackson State University.
In the early 80s, she mentored under jazz greats in New Orleans before moving to New York City and joining Steve Coleman’s M-Base Collective – eventually becoming its main vocalist.
Her instantly recognizable voice earned her four Grammy nominations and two wins for best jazz vocal album. Those were in 1997 for New Moon Daughter and 2009 for Loverly.

In 2015, it was Wilson who gave a special concert at the famed Apollo Theater to commemorate the 100th birthday of the blues singer Billie Holiday, the legendary American jazz vocalist who died in New York City at age 44. That same year, Wilson released her last album, Coming Forth by Day, a homage to Holiday.
In 2022, Wilson was named a National Endowment for the Arts jazz master, one of the highest honors awarded to jazz musicians in the United States.

“She had an unmistakable vocal tone, phrasing and her approach of weaving folkloric, R+B and diasporic music together with experimental and popular genres had a major impact on me,” Batiste said in his tribute to Wilson on Instagram.

“Her Mississippi heritage was always present in everything no matter how expansive her artistry evolved,” he wrote in the caption of a clip showing them together on Brazilian TV in 2009. “She was one of the first people to take me on tour around the world, the great Cassandra Wilson.”
Jackson’s mayor, John Horhn, said the city “has lost an extraordinary native daughter, and the world has lost a singular musical voice”.

“Cassandra Wilson carried the sound, spirit and history of Mississippi with her wherever her music reached,” said the mayor’s statement, shared with WJTV. “Her work had rare depth of character and a profound understanding of how music moves people, tells stories and connects generations.”

articles.title: Protests in Spain over government's handling of Ceuta migrant crisis
articles.summary: Spanish opposition parties accuse Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of abandoning the residents of Ceuta.

blocks.text: Thousands of people have protested in cities across Spain over the government's handling of the influx of migrants to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on the north African coast.
Spanish opposition parties accuse Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of abandoning the residents of Ceuta, while the government says right-wing parties are exploiting the crisis.
On Wednesday a police report said Moroccan security forces showed "total permissiveness" during the unprecedented influx, days after Sánchez insisted Morocco was not responsible.
He has blamed trafficking gangs and online misinformation for encouraging people to cross the border. Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing.

At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July and although most have returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or scattered across the city's streets or on the beach - leading to unrest in the autonomous city in North Africa and a crisis for Sánchez.
There have been near-daily protests by locals, with demonstrators calling for the migrants to be sent back to their countries of origin or redistributed across Spain.
Wednesday's rallies were called by city councils across Spain where opposition parties - the conservative Partido Popular (PP) and the far-right Vox party - govern or have significant popularity.
Demonstrators called on Sánchez to resign.
PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo was at the rally in Madrid, where more than 50,000 people gathered, according to government figures.
"A Spanish city has been invaded, occupied and, unfortunately, this happened with the knowledge of the Government of Spain," he said.
Vox leader Santiago Abascal meanwhile said Sánchez was "at the service, like a lackey, of the Moroccan regime".

articles.title: Cebu City calls off classes as haze persists in parts of Visayas
articles.summary: CEBU CITY — Mayor Nestor Archival announced a two-day suspension of in-person classes as haze from wildfires in the Kalimantan and Sumatra regions of Indonesia — some 2,000 kilometers away —…

blocks.text: CEBU CITY — Mayor Nestor Archival announced a two-day suspension of in-person classes as haze from wildfires in the Kalimantan and Sumatra regions of Indonesia — some 2,000 kilometers away — persisted.
Archival ordered the cancellation of classes at 2 p.m. on Wednesday, with the suspension taking effect through Thursday.
He urged schools to implement modular distance learning, asynchronous classes or other appropriate flexible learning modalities, pursuant to Department of Education (DepEd) policies.
Archival also asked businesses and the private sector to ensure employee safety by encouraging telecommuting or work-from-home arrangements for nonessential, office-based personnel.

“The Cebu City government will continue to monitor the situation and issue further advisories as conditions develop. Please remain vigilant, take the necessary precautions, and protect one another,” he said.
As of 11 a.m. Wednesday, the air quality index (AQI) in Metro Cebu was 208, placing it in the “acutely unhealthy” category.
The Environmental Management Bureau (EMB) of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) in Central Visayas measured the AQI at 173 on Tuesday.
Under the EMB scale, an AQI of 201-300 is classified as “acutely unhealthy,” the second-highest category, next to “emergency,” with an AQI of 301-500.

The bureau advised the public, particularly those with existing respiratory conditions, to stay indoors. Others were urged to wear face masks, stay hydrated and take other precautions to reduce their exposure to polluted air.
Asthma surge
Despite the worsening air quality, the Department of Health (DOH) in Central Visayas said no hospital admissions related to the haze had been reported as of Wednesday.

Still, rural health units (RHUs) have been advised to prepare for a possible increase in consultations involving health problems linked to the haze, said Dr. Van Philip Baton, chief of the Local Health Support Division of the regional DOH.
“We’re anticipating a possible increase in asthma (cases), so we may see this in our RHU and private clinics,” he said.

Smoke from fires in Kalimantan was being carried toward the Philippines by the “habagat,” or southwest monsoon, said Arthur Niño Calupig, air quality monitoring specialist at EMB Central Visayas, adding that the haze could persist for several more days if the fires continue to burn and prevailing wind patterns remain unchanged.
In nearby Bohol province, the air quality was also in the “acutely unhealthy” category on Wednesday, prompting many residents to wear face masks while outdoors.

In Mindanao, air quality in South Cotabato province worsened at certain hours since Tuesday, with fine particle pollution reaching “emergency” and “very unhealthy” levels, according to the EMB in the SOCCSKSARGEN (South Cotabato, Cotabato, Sultan Kudarat, Sarangani and General Santos) region.
Based on the EMB’s special air quality monitoring, the AQI in Koronadal City reached 312.8 at 6 p.m. Tuesday, placing it under the “emergency” category.
Air quality improved after midnight, with readings returning to the “fair” category during the early hours of Wednesday.

In Zamboanga City, the EMB recorded poor air quality in parts of the city on Wednesday. As of noon, the AQI in Barangay Talisayan was 159, placing it in the “very unhealthy” category. But in Barangay Tumaga, the reading was “good” at 48.
In Northern Mindanao, the EMB reported a steady spike in fine particulate matter between Aug. 30 and Sept. 1 across key urban centers.
Iligan City recorded the most alarming spike, with its AQI surging past the 200 threshold into the “acutely unhealthy” category, registering 203 on Aug. 31 and 209 on Sept. 1.

In Cagayan de Oro City, conditions deteriorated from “fair” (78 on Aug. 30 and 96 on Aug. 31) to “unhealthy for sensitive groups” on Sept. 1, after the AQI reached 105. — With reports from Leo Udtohan, Leah Agonoy, Cong Corrales and Holly Bacay /das

articles.title: Trump floats renaming Strait of Hormuz as ‘Trump Strait’
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, United States — US President Donald Trump on Wednesday suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz as “Trump Strait” despite ongoing clashes with Iran — then hours later…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, United States — US President Donald Trump on Wednesday suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz as “Trump Strait” despite ongoing clashes with Iran — then hours later implied he wasn’t serious.
Trump has made a series of geographical name changes to international bodies of water in his second term, at least partly with the aim of trolling other countries.
The latest suggestion came as Trump insisted the US had full control of the crucial waterway, even as fresh clashes raged there with Iran.

“Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!” Trump said on his Truth Social network.
The White House later posted a map of the Gulf on social media with his suggested name, adding: “It’s got a nice ring to it.”
Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly threatened to claim sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, even posting a map showing the waterway as a “new US territory.”
Trump, however, later played down the idea of rebranding the Strait of Hormuz.
“It was just thrown out there,” Trump said with a chuckle after an AFP reporter asked him in the Oval Office if he was serious about renaming it.
But a number of the 80-year-old Republican’s previous suggestions have been dismissed as being humorous before they ended up happening for real.
Last week Trump signed an order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” amid a trade war with neighboring Canada, just days after apparently raising the idea in jest.
Iran war grinds on
Trump also renamed the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” on his first day back in the White House in January 2025. Neither Mexico nor Canada have accepted the changes.

He has also gone on a spree of renaming things after himself, including the Kennedy arts center in Washington, while the US Treasury meanwhile on Wednesday issued $1 coins featuring Trump’s face to mark the 250th anniversary of US independence.
The Iran war remains a deadly serious issue, with no sign of ending more than six months after the initial US-Israeli assault.
Fighting has flared again after weeks of calm, with US forces launching fresh strikes near the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday in response to what Trump said were new minelaying efforts by Iran.
Iran said one of the US strikes killed four people at a wedding, branding it a “war crime”, and launched a wave of retaliatory strikes at US bases in Jordan, the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Iraq.

At home, Trump has presided over a steep rise in US fuel costs as a result of the war and his Republican Party looks likely to lose at least partial control of Congress in the November midterm elections.
Iran has effectively shut down the choke point, through which a fifth of the world’s oil passes, in retaliation for the war Trump started along with Israel in late February.
Trump said on Wednesday that the United States was ready to attack Iran again — while adding that the renewed campaign would not last “too long.”
“It was a very heavy attack last night, and we’re prepared to do another one any time we want,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. /das

articles.title: Benguet vegetable traders lose due to NLEx gridlock
articles.summary: BAGUIO CITY — Benguet farmers and vegetable truckers raced against the clock to sell mountain-grown produce that can spoil within a day, after monsoon floods along major highways turned the usual…

blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY — Benguet farmers and vegetable truckers raced against the clock to sell mountain-grown produce that can spoil within a day, after monsoon floods along major highways turned the usual five-hour trip to Metro Manila into an ordeal of road gridlock lasting up to 12 hours.

The delays along the North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) forced Benguet traders to miss their schedules at Divisoria wholesale market in Manila, with some losing buyers from Mindoro provinces and Bicol region who already left by the time the trucks arrived in the past days.

Lorna Menzi, adviser of the League of Associations at the La Trinidad Vegetable Trading Area Inc., said traders told her they were unable to sell all their vegetables, mostly cabbage, because of the delays.
“The continuous rains already hasten spoilage of vegetables. Getting stuck for hours on the road worsens risk of spoilage,” Menzi said.
The losses came as the vegetable supply at the La Trinidad trading post began to decline because travel through Benguet mountain roads were also hampered by continuing monsoon rains and landslides.
The prolonged delay meant Benguet traders missed the 5 p.m. to 6 p.m. selling window in Divisoria.
The problem continued on the return trip to Benguet, with truckers also missing the 5 a.m. to 7 a.m. buying window at the La Trinidad vegetable trading post.

Rudy Bulawan, president of the Benguet Truckers and Traders Association, said each 10-wheel truck carries about 20,000 kilos of assorted vegetables, all of which must be disposed of immediately because of their highly perishable nature.
These trucks could pass through floodwaters that reached roughly the height of their wheels. But smaller vehicles that could not cross became stranded, preventing the trucks from moving.

The disruption was already affecting deliveries scheduled on Wednesday. Bulawan said only about 15 of the usual 25 trucks left for Divisoria as orders declined. Truckers had to combine orders to save on fuel expenses.
Vegetable traders have yet to release official reports of their losses but they often impose a P5 per kilo markup on produce sold in Divisoria, Bulawan said.
But with 10 truck trips called off, this means lost sales for some 200,000 kilos of vegetables. At P5 markup, that translates to P1 million in lost income for traders.
Situation eases

But President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Wednesday said traffic slowdown due to floods along the northbound section of NLEx in San Simon, Pampanga, has now eased, with motorists taking 45 minutes to drive past the flooded section.
He visited Pampanga, Tarlac and Zambales provinces to inspect damage from the recent floods and heavy rains.

Mr. Marcos said pumping out floodwaters on the southbound lane of NLEx in San Simon has not been efficient as the Tulaoc section of the Pampanga River continued to overflow. He saw the need to build a temporary catchment of floodwaters on this side of NLEx.

Earlier in Tarlac City, the president inspected the construction of a bailey bridge to restore access after the Aug. 29 collapse of the 136-meter Agana Bridge following heavy rains and strong current in Tarlac River.

Together with Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon, Marcos directed the Department of Public Works and Highways to fast track the construction of the alternate bridge and said the government would provide P300 million worth of assistance to the Tarlac City government for its rehabilitation.

In Zambales province, Marcos visited the residents of Barangay Santa Fe in San Marcelino town who have been living in isolation since Aug. 9, after a bridge linking their community was swept away by the swollen waters of the Santa Fe River.
A temporary wooden bridge was built to restore access to the isolated community just in time for the President’s visit.

Aeta resident Melissa Cabalic Hugatan, 43, said this was not the first time that they faced isolation because of flooding. Their dike and bridge have repeatedly been damaged whenever heavy rains cause the river to overflow.

The latest disruption cut off the northern portion of the village from the rest of the community. The situation was worsened by lahar from Mt. Pinatubo that inundated portions of the village after the river overtopped and breached a dike.
With the bridge gone, residents struggled to bring food and other necessities into the community. While there are variety stores in the area, Hugatan said many had also run out of goods to sell.
Pangasinan calamity

In Pangasinan, the provincial board, during an online session on Monday morning, declared the province under a state of calamity because weeks of monsoon rain and other weather disturbances affected more than 370,000 families (about 1.2 million people).

Flooding, the recent storms and heavy rains left significant damage, with initial estimates placing losses to infrastructure at P232.5 million, crops at P649.23 million, and livestock at P2.11 million.

As of Wednesday, 15 Pangasinan towns and two cities have barangays that are still underwater, with roads in the towns of Mangatarem and Calasiao and Dagupan City still not passable to light vehicles, according to Pia Navata Flores, spokesperson for the Pangasinan Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office.

Other towns with still flooded communities are Agno, Mabini, Aguilar, Binmaley, Bugallon, Lingayen, Malasiqui, Sta. Barbara, San Jacinto, and Basista, as well as San Carlos City. — With reports from Madelle Calayag and Tonette Orejas /das

articles.title: Andy Burnham targets migrant crisis ahead of Macron’s visit to No 10
articles.summary:
PM will aim to centre talks with French president on key foreign policy issues such as Iran, smuggling gangs and EU relations

Andy Burnham will begin the process of courting European leaders…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham will begin the process of courting European leaders when he welcomes Emmanuel Macron as the first foreign head of state to visit him in Downing Street.

The prime minister will meet the French president at No 10 on Thursday as he looks to make inroads on a number of foreign policy objectives, including curbing irregular migration and sealing a new deal with the EU.

The meeting marks one of Burnham’s first forays into foreign policy, having previously promised to remain mostly focused on domestic issues, and comes weeks before a crunch EU summit that could shape much of his future economic strategy.
Burnham said in a statement on Wednesday: “The progress we have seen this summer [in bringing down the number of small boat crossings] shows what can be achieved when the UK and France work together.

“But I am clear that we cannot be complacent. Smuggling gangs are constantly adapting their tactics, and the UK and France need to respond quickly and stay one step ahead of the criminals facilitating the dangerous crossings.

“The small boats crisis is a shared European challenge, and no country can solve it alone. Working with France and our international partners, we will restore order and control to our borders and prevent smugglers exploiting vulnerable migrants.”

While Burnham has talked almost exclusively about domestic issues such as the cost of living since becoming prime minister, he is quickly finding himself having to deal with international crises as well.

Last month he met the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to help celebrate the country’s independence day, when he announced he would declassify sensitive military information to allow Ukraine to build more cruise missiles.
On Thursday he will discuss migration, EU relations, Ukraine and the war in Iran with Macron.
The two leaders will announce additional resources for French police to help stop small boats being launched from the country’s north coast and larger “mega-dinghies” departing from the west.

Downing Street said on Wednesday that the number of French officers dealing with small boat crossings in northern France would soon rise to nearly 1,050 officers – up by roughly a quarter in four months.

The teams will include a specialist 75-person team to seize equipment and arrest smugglers on land. A separate intelligence unit will be expanded from 18 to 30, while another 45 officers will be deployed to the west coast.
Irregular migration has fallen down the political agenda in recent weeks thanks to a drop in the number of small boat crossings.

This week, Burnham said the drop in numbers to a seven-year low was a result of efforts by his predecessor Keir Starmer to tackle smuggling gangs – though experts say external factors such as an improvement in Syria’s security situation have also played a role.
The prime minister will also use the meeting to press Macron to support his efforts to renegotiate Britain’s treaty with the EU.
Brussels postponed a planned summit from July to allow the new prime minister time to review tentative agreements made by Starmer, with a new one expected in early November.

European countries have been pushing hard for Britain to agree a new youth mobility scheme and to allow their students to pay home fees at British universities – both concessions that Starmer was ready to make, according to recent reports.

However, Burnham may take a tougher line on the number of young people he is willing to admit as part of the scheme, having promised to pass all government policies through a “Makerfield test” to measure them against the views of his constituents.
In return, Britain wants new agreements to ease trade in electricity and agricultural products, which officials hope will give a timely boost to the UK economy.
The prime minister told the Guardian last year he wanted the UK to rejoin the EU, but has since said this would not be something he would actively pursue as prime minister.

articles.title: Malta: Businessman acquitted of journalist's murder
articles.summary: Yorgen Fenech was suspected to have masterminded the murder of investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia, whose family continue to demand justice for her killing.

image.caption: Yorgen Fenech was acquitted from involvement in the murder of Daphne Caruana GaliziaImage: Darrin Zammit Lupi/REUTERS

blocks.text: A Maltese businessman was acquitted after being accused of being behind the murder of investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.
Yorgen Fenech, 44, was accused of commissioning the car bomb killing of Caruana Galizia in 2017 in a case that sent waves across Europe.
Caruana Galizia, who was 53 years old at the time of her murder, was driving near her home when the bomb detonated.
Caruana Galizia's journalistic investigations included extensive information about suspected corruption in politics and business in Malta. She faced about 40 libel suits at the time of her murder.
Life in prison avoided

Fenech, who would have faced up to life in prison had he been found guilty, was cleared of both complicity for murder and criminal association to commit murder with a jury margin of 8-1. He denied the allegations that he had wanted the journalist dead due to an investigation about him being about to be published.

blocks.caption: A bomb detonated as Daphne Caruana Galizia was driving her car  [FILE: October 16, 2017]Image: Rene Rossignaud/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fenech did not comment after leaving the courtroom, with a crowd of people waiting outside the court shouting insults in his direction.
Family's demand for justice continues
Caruana Galizia's family responded to the acquittal by saying that the institutional failures that led to the murder "remain unaddressed and unreformed."
"Lasting justice means no person should ever face the same risks again. Our country failed to protect Daphne's life. It owes it to her to prevent other lives being lost."

blocks.caption: The journalist's murder triggered protests in Malta [FILE: November 29, 2019]Image: Rene Rossignaud/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Daphne Caruana Galizia's sons were in the courtroom when the verdict was read out.
Five people were convicted in connection to the murder, with three of them being found guilty of carrying it out.
All five are currently in jail.

articles.title: Clippers docked five first-round draft picks and fined $30m over Kawhi Leonard scandal
articles.summary:
• Team circumvented salary cap rules to sign star

  • Owner Steve Ballmer lands one-year ban

The NBA has handed down one of the biggest punishments in the history…

blocks.text: The NBA has handed down one of the biggest punishments in the history of the league to the Los Angeles Clippers after finding that the franchise circumvented salary cap rules when it courted Kawhi Leonard as a free agent.
The league has stripped the team of five first-round draft picks, giving the team no natural pick in the draft from 2029 through 2033.

The NBA also fined the Clippers $30m, and suspended owner Steve Ballmer from all league and team activities for a year. In addition, the league issued suspensions without pay to president of basketball operations Lawrence Frank (six months) and president of business operations Gillian Zucker (one year) for their involvement in the scheme.
Leonard was also fined $700,000. Leonard is due to make $50m in salary this season, while Ballmer, the former CEO of Microsoft, has an estimated wealth of $152.7bn, according to Forbes.

“The NBA’s collectively bargained system for determining player compensation is a fundamental component of the basketball competition that the league oversees for the benefit of the teams and players and ultimately the fans,” NBA commissioner Adam Silver said in a statement. “I am deeply disappointed by the flagrant violations of our rules and by the Clippers’ institutional and leadership failures that led to this misconduct. The severity of the penalties reflects the seriousness of the violations.”

In a statement through his agent, Leonard said he took “full responsibility for lapses in judgment by people within my inner circle and regret the distraction this situation has caused the fans and my family. I entered into my contract with the Clippers as well as the agreements in question in good faith, fully committed to fulfilling my obligations and with no knowledge of any intent on anyone’s part to circumvent the salary cap.”
New York law firm Wachtell Lipton conducted the NBA’s investigation into the matter after reporting by journalist Pablo Torre last year.

Torre, citing legal documents, claimed Ballmer employed Leonard for a non-existent role in one of his companies to circumvent the NBA salary cap, which punishes teams for spending too much on player salaries.

Torre claims that Ballmer partially funded a now defunct tree-planting company called Aspiration. That company then allegedly entered into a $28m agreement with KL2 Aspire, LLC, a company owned by Leonard.

Torre says he could find no evidence that Leonard had ever performed any work for Aspiration, and there was a clause in the contract between KL2 Aspire and Aspiration effectively allowed Leonard to be paid even if he did no work. Another clause said the deal would be voided if Leonard left the Clippers. One former employee of Aspiration told Torre he had heard the deal with Leonard had been set up to “circumvent the salary cap.”
after newsletter promotion

Wachtell Lipton’s report concluded that the Clippers broke NBA rules after “initiating off-court income opportunities between Mr Leonard and four companies doing business with the team: Aspiration Partners, Boingo Wireless, Daktronics, and Lockton Insurance; facilitating endorsement agreements between these companies and Mr Leonard; inducing the companies to enter into these agreements by offering them business from the team; paying personal expenses on behalf of Mr Leonard and his representatives; and failing to report improper solicitations for off-court income opportunities made on Mr Leonard’s behalf through his then-business manager, Dennis Robertson.”

Leonard is one of the best players of his generation. The 35-year-old is a two-time NBA champion, seven-time All-Star and was twice the league’s defensive player of the year. He started his career with the San Antonio Spurs before spells at the Toronto Raptors and Clippers.
Leonard led the Clippers to the Western Conference finals in the 2020-21 season but they have failed to get beyond the first-round of the playoffs since and missed the postseason entirely in 2025-26.

articles.title: Australia news live: Jim Chalmers weighs in on One Nation WA byelection win; $2m for Indigenous racism online register
articles.summary:
Treasurer says he acknowledges concerns about inflation, cost of living and real wages were on voters’ minds. Follow the day’s news live.

  • Get our

blocks.text: Chalmers weighs in on One Nation WA byelection win

blocks.caption: Achol Arok

blocks.text: Achol Arok
Jim Chalmers says he has reflected on the key takeaways after One Nation candidate Luke Herdegen secured 57%of the vote after preferences at the Secret Harbour byelection.
Speaking on ABC’s 7.30, Chalmers said he acknowledged that concerns about inflation, the cost of living and real wages were on voters’ minds before the poll.

double quotation markI have thought very deeply about the legitimate concerns and anxieties and frustrations that people have. About how the economy works, or doesn’t work for people. That’s the thing I’m most focused on. It’s the whole reason for our efforts to get inflation down, to make the economy more productive.
Chalmers added he believes the “faultline in our politics” is now changing.

double quotation markIt’s not necessarily between the centre left and the far right, it’s not necessarily the old distinctions. The distinction in our politics right now is a Labor government working to address the very real concerns that people have, versus the Liberals and Nationals and One Nation who just want to prey on that, and pick on that.
Key events

items: 8m agoAustralia pledges $3m additional aid
9m ago$2m for Indigenous racism register
9m agoChalmers weighs in on One Nation WA byelection win
9m agoChalmers defends house prices forecast
24m agoWelcome

blocks.text: Australia pledges $3m additional aid
Australia will deploy a team of specialist drone operators to help the search and rescue effort in the deadly Nepal-Tibet floods.
Operators, including those from Fire and Rescue New South Wales and the Queensland fire department, will head to the disaster-struck region in the coming days.
It comes as the Albanese government has announced a further $3m in aid, bringing its total figure pledged to $11m.
The number of Australians unaccounted for remains at 38.
It comes as a Raaf plane arrived yesterday with humanitaian aid.
As of Thursday, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Agency reported 1,204 confirmed deaths and 4,216 missing persons (including 583 foreigners).
$2m for Indigenous racism register
An online register of racism and discrimination against First Nations people is receiving up to $2m in Commonwealth funding to help inform anti-racism action, AAP reports.
The federal government has announced the funding before the final report by a parliamentary inquiry into racism, hate and violence directed at Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.
The minister for Indigenous Australians, Malarndirri McCarthy, said the parliamentary inquiry had heard confronting stories from Indigenous people about the hurt and harm they had experienced.
