double quotation markWhile we await the committee’s final report, we are not waiting to act. This investment will strengthen the important work of Call It Out and support efforts to collate rigorous data.
Callitout.com.au is a culturally safe, trauma-informed website that collects data for analysis by the Jumbunna Institute to help raise awareness and drive systematic change.
Chalmers defends house prices forecast

Jim Chalmers has defended Treasury’s forecast on the impact of the government’s recent tax changes on housing, after the Commonwealth Bank predicted prices could fall by almost 10% across capital cities.
Treasury modelling said the changes would reduce house price growth by just 2% over the next couple of years.
Speaking on ABC’s 7.30, the treasurer said the new data did not fairly challenge the government’s forecast.

double quotation markThat Commonwealth Bank forecast that you reference in your question has house prices recovering next year, and so it’s a really important reminder that we need to compare ‘like with like’. The assumptions in the budget are over the next couple of years, not the first couple of months since the budget … and the Commonwealth Bank says they expect house price growth as soon as next year.
Chalmers pointed to several factors unrelated to the recent tax changes that he said would contribute to the dip in prices.

double quotation markThere is softness in the housing market, prices have come off a bit, auction clearance rates have come off a bit, but that was beginning before the budget, and that’s because, as a number of experts have pointed out, one of the big influences is interest rates. We have very substantial advantages in the face of some serious economic challenges. Productivity is one of them. Inflation is another. Extreme global volatility, turbocharged by a war on the other side of the world.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Nick Visser with the main action.
Let’s begin.

articles.title: Uber shuts operations in Nigeria and Uganda with immediate effect
articles.summary: Nigeria - Africa's most populous country - is proving a tough market for ride-hailing services.

blocks.text: Over the last year, Uber has also pulled out of Ivory Coast and Tanzania. The latest announcement means Egypt, Ghana, Kenya and South Africa are the only African countries in which the firm now operates.
"This decision is limited strictly to these two markets and does not impact our operations across the rest of the continent," Uber's statement to the BBC said.
"We remain committed to sub-Saharan Africa, where we continue to see strong growth and opportunity."

Over its 12 years operating in Nigeria, Uber had expanded its services. In the commercial hub of Lagos, it launched a boat service in 2019 in an effort to help commuters bypass the city's notorious congestion.
Lagos, one of Africa's largest and busiest cities, is infamous for its long traffic jams that cause gridlock and hamper business activity.
Other ride-hailing taxi apps have launched in the West African nation over the last decade, including international competitors such as Bolt and inDrive, as well as a number of local operators.

But the Nigerian market has become increasingly challenging for them all, with drivers staging protests and industrial action in recent years over rising operating costs, low fares and working conditions.
The removal of Nigeria's fuel subsidy after President Bola Tinubu's election in 2023 saw the cost of living rise. The subsidy had kept down the price of petroleum products low for decades.
This year, motorists have been hit again by the rise in petrol prices following the US's war with Iran.

Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper said Uber's departure would mean a major change for commuters in the capital, Kampala. But it said the void was likely to be filled by other taxi apps such as Faras, Bolt and SafeBoda.
Uber pledged to support employees and drivers affected by the decision and said its help centre would remain open for those in Nigeria and Uganda until 23 September to deal with outstanding issues.

articles.title: Watch: Jury still unable to reach unanimous decision in Lindsay Clancy case
articles.summary: For a second time in two days, jurors told the judge they could not agree on a verdict in the murder trial.

blocks.text: For a second time in two days, jurors in the trial of Lindsay Clancy told the judge they could not agree on a verdict.

Clancy is a 36-year-old Massachusetts mother and former labour and delivery nurse who is on trial for the murder of her three young children in 2023. She is accused of strangling her kids - Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months - in their Massachusetts home.

articles.title: Trump ‘happy’ about Harry and Meghan UK return: ‘I was not a fan’
articles.summary:
President praises late queen and King Charles but says duke and duchess treated royal family ‘with great disrespect’

Donald Trump has weighed in on the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s move back…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has weighed in on the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s move back to Britain, declaring: “I’m happy about it.”

“I was not a fan,” the US president told reporters during a question-and-answer session after a press conference with travel executives on Wednesday. “I had a very good relationship with the queen, really good. I got to know her very well. A really good relationship with King Charles – I knew him as Prince Charles and King Charles. I’ve known him for a long time.”
Trump, describing Charles as a “great, great guy”, said he thought Harry and Meghan “treated the royal family with great disrespect”.
“I didn’t like it,” he also said, adding, “If I were the royal family, I would not have taken them back.”

The couple moved back to the UK last week, six years after they left for the US. They had lived in California since 2020. They have yet to speak publicly about their plans, are said to be settling for an “extended period” of time amid speculation as to how long they will stay, and where they will live.

Trump has a longstanding fascination and admiration for the royal family, which he traces back to a childhood memory of watching Queen Elizabeth II’s coronation on TV in 1953 with his mother, Mary Anne Trump, who was born in Scotland. Trump adored the late queen, whom he described as a “great woman” who had “really never made a mistake” during her decades on the throne.

The king is reportedly looking forward to spending more time with the duke and duchess in a personal capacity, but Harry, 41, and Meghan, 45, will remain private individuals. They previously gave up their official royal duties.
The couple is not expected to be offered a “half-in half-out” option, after that was firmly rejected by Queen Elizabeth II.
Questions remain unanswered, including whether British taxpayers will foot the bill for the pair’s security detail after their return to the UK.

articles.title: Senate ratings down, House up in Q2 2026 --OCTA
articles.summary: Public trust and satisfaction ratings for the Senate declined in the second quarter of 2026, while ratings for the House of Representatives improved, according to the second quarter 2026 Tugon ng…

blocks.text: Published September 3, 2026 3:39am

Public trust and satisfaction ratings for the Senate declined in the second quarter of 2026, while ratings for the House of Representatives improved, according to the second quarter 2026 Tugon ng Masa Survey by OCTA Research.
The survey found that trust in the Senate fell from 44% in the first quarter to 41% in the second quarter, while distrust increased from 24% to 27%.
Satisfaction with the Senate’s performance likewise declined from 42% to 38%, while dissatisfaction rose from 27% to 32%.

Despite the declines, public opinion of the Senate remained mixed nationwide. The survey showed that 41% of adult Filipinos trusted the chamber, while 27% distrusted it and 32% were undecided, OCTA said.
On the Senate’s performance, 38% said they were satisfied, 32% dissatisfied and 30% undecided.
In contrast, trust in the House of Representatives increased from 36% in the first quarter to 38% in the second quarter, while distrust declined from 33% to 28%.
Satisfaction with the House’s performance also rose from 35% to 37%, while dissatisfaction fell from 35% to 32%.
Nationwide, 38% of adult Filipinos said they trusted the House, compared with 28% who expressed distrust and 33% who were undecided.
Meanwhile, 37% were satisfied with the House’s performance, 32% were dissatisfied and 31% were undecided.

The survey fieldwork was conducted from July 04 to 11, 2026, using face-to-face interviews of 1,200 respondents aged 18 and above. The survey has a margin of error of ±3 % at a 95% confidence level. Subnational estimates for the geographic areas covered in the survey have the following margins of error at a 95% confidence level: ±6% for Metro Manila, Balance Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao.

The survey was conducted during the leadership row and eventual leadership change in the Senate. It also coincided with the opening days of the Senate’s impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, which convened as an impeachment court on July 6, 2026.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Hilroy says sorry for leaving Newfoundland, Cape Breton off notebooks' Canadian map
articles.summary: Hilroy has apologized for leaving Newfoundland and Cape Breton off the Canadian map on its glossy notebooks, after the mistake led to backlash online.

image.caption: Hilroy’s 40-page exercise book with a copyright year of 2025, pictured in a Walmart in Fredericton on Sept. 2, 2026, shows a map of Canada that appears to be missing Newfoundland and a part of Nova Scotia. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New
Hilroy has apologized for leaving Newfoundland and Cape Breton off the Canadian map on its glossy notebooks, after the mistake led to backlash online.
The faulty books have been on shelves since last year, says company
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 02, 2026 3:30 PM EDT | Last Updated: 30 minutes ago

Hilroy's pastel-coloured paper exercise books are well known across the country for the map of Canada on their covers. But the map on Hilroy's glossy covered notebooks is missing a few parts of the country.
In a post to its Facebook page Tuesday, the company said its team has always been proud of the map, "which is exactly why getting it wrong stings."
The inaccurate map was the result of a production error, the post said. The company has stopped distributing the books and is fixing the cover artwork.
"That's our mistake, and we're sorry," it said. "To everyone who spotted it: you're right and thank you for telling us."

Hilroy's parent company, ACCO Brands, said Wednesday that the faulty books have been on shelves since last year. However, it seems customers only recently noticed the errors. The mishap has generated discussion on social media, prompting posts from Newfoundlanders and Nova Scotians expressing their dismay.
Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham posted a brief but blunt response on Facebook.
"You can leave Newfoundland off an exercise book, but you can't erase us," he wrote Wednesday. "Hilroy will never take away our identity, our history, or our place on the map."

items: More stories from Cape Breton

blocks.text: Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said the incomplete map was "unacceptable."
"I've asked the minister of education to send the makers of Hilroy scribblers a map of Nova Scotia that includes Cape Breton and Newfoundland," Houston said, also in a Facebook post.

The mistaken map also appears to be missing Haida Gwaii, an archipelago off the coast of British Columbia. An ACCO Brands spokesperson said the company is aware and addressing the omission is part of its "correction plan."

Sean Cadigan, a history professor at Memorial University in St. John's, said Newfoundland did not join Canada until 1949, and it has been left out of maps and descriptions of the country before. It can be a sensitive issue on the island, he said.
"When there are big tours and people say they're touring Canada, Canada often stops somewhere in Nova Scotia," Cadigan said in an interview Wednesday.

"I think that's just probably an old habit that often predates Newfoundland's joining Confederation," he added. "Obviously, people here want to emphasize, of course, since 1949, we're part of Canada."
Cadigan said the map was an "embarrassing mistake" for Hilroy.
"I wouldn't read it as any intent to slight," he said.

articles.title: Jurors in trial of U.S. mother who killed her children again tell judge they are deadlocked
articles.summary: Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial have said — for a second time — that they are unable to reach a verdict on whether she is criminally responsible in the killings of her three children, but…

image.caption: Lindsay Clancy watches jurors enter the courtroom last Friday. The jury Wednesday told the judge for a seconds time this week that they are deadlocked. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/Pool/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial have said — for a second time — that they are unable to reach a verdict on whether she is criminally responsible in the killings of her three children, but the judge on Wednesday told them again to keep trying.
Lindsay Clancy doesn't deny she strangled her kids, but jury deciding if she was crimnally responsible
WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children.
Clancy stared at the jury with no expression as Judge William Sullivan explained to the courtroom that jurors were at an impasse on their fifth day of deliberations.

The judge then sent them back out after giving them a standard, legally required instruction intended to prod them to keep discussing a possible verdict. He gave them similar instructions Tuesday morning the first time they said they couldn't reach a unanimous decision.

Clancy, a former labour and delivery nurse in Massachusetts, doesn't deny strangling her three children in their home in 2023. But her attorney argues that postpartum psychosis led to her actions. Prosecutors say she knew what she was doing.

items: Testimony concludes in trial of U.S. mother accused of killing her 3 children

blocks.text: Clancy's livestreamed trial has generated intense interest, with reporters and spectators packing the courtroom. The case has also sparked deep public divisions over her culpability and the issues around maternal mental health after childbirth.
What happens if there's a mistrial

Jurors have heard testimony from relatives and doctors about how Clancy's mental health declined in the months before the killings and how her treatment included several medications and a short stay in a psychiatric hospital. Medical experts hired by the prosecution and the defence reached sharply different conclusions about her psychiatric state when she killed the children.

If jurors ultimately can't agree on a verdict, the judge could declare a mistrial. Prosecutors would then have to decide whether to put Clancy on trial again, drop the charges or try to negotiate a plea deal with her lawyer.

If the jury decides Clancy was criminally responsible for her actions, it could convict her of either murder or manslaughter. If she is acquitted, a judge could still order her confined to a mental health facility if an evaluation determines that she poses a danger to the public.
Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial hears closing arguments
After court ended Tuesday, Clancy's attorney said it was a good sign that the jury kept working.
"The fact that they have not said that they're done is very, very heartening," Kevin Reddington said. "Obviously, they're working very hard."

articles.title: Apple Maps renames Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ for US users after Trump order
articles.summary:
Tech company submits to controversial Trump order to rename body of water amid US trade spat with Canada

Apple has renamed Lake Ontario to “Lake America” for US users of its Maps app, after…

blocks.text: Apple has renamed Lake Ontario to “Lake America” for US users of its Maps app, after an executive order from Donald Trump to change the name of the Great Lake amid his trade spat with Canada.

The Apple Maps app now displays the controversial new name for the lake, which sits between the border of New York state and the Canadian province of Ontario, for users in the US. Apple users outside the country will still see the Lake Ontario name.
Apple had been reportedly mulling whether to submit to Trump’s new order after receiving a personal request from the president for the tech company to change the lake’s name.

Trump officially declared the American name swap last week. He did not mention his escalating trade feud with the US’s northern neighbors in the order, but the timing suggested a retaliatory move after Canadian officials denounced Trump’s new sweeping tariffs and promised to instate tariffs of their own.

Canadian prime minister Mark Carney rejected the attempt to rename the body of water, saying in a post on social media that the lake’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.

Late last month, trade talks between Washington and Ottawa collapsed, with the US subsequently imposing a 50% tariff on several Canadian imports. Trump additionally threatened another round of 50% duties on Canadian steel, trucks, cars and auto parts to take effect in the new year. Carney retaliated with 25-50% tariffs on hundreds of US goods.

Rather than mention any of this, Trump instead said in the order that the purpose of the renaming is to honor “the policy of my Administration to recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people and the rich heritage of our history by naming great natural landmarks for our shared achievements.”

Apple’s competitor, Google, already made the change over the weekend, with Google Maps now showing the Lake America branding. Google cited Trump’s order and its practice of using names assigned by the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS).
In a blog post issued on Saturday, Google said US users will see the Lake America name while users in Canada will see Lake Ontario, and “those outside of the US and Canada will see both names.”

The digital name change is unsurprising considering Google Maps was an early adopter of the Gulf of America moniker and still currently displays the title, despite the renaming hardly being a success outside US government lingo.

On Tuesday, it was reported that MapQuest, the pioneering online mapping app, reached the No 1 spot on Apple’s App Store after openly rejecting Trump’s request to rename the lake. The app simply posted a screenshot of Lake Ontario on social media last Thursday along with the caption: “We’re not changing it.”
The act of defiance was enough to catapult the app into becoming the most in-demand navigation tool in the US.

articles.title: Maltese tycoon acquitted of orchestrating murder of renowned journalist
articles.summary: Daphne Caruana Galizia exposed corruption and money laundering schemes in Malta before she was killed by a car bomb in 2017.

blocks.text: A Maltese businessman on trial over the murder of investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia has been acquitted.
Yorgen Fenech, 44, was accused of complicity in her murder and criminal association to commit murder. He denied all the charges.

In 2022, brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio were jailed for 40 years over the killing of Caruana Galizia, who was an outspoken critic of the government and had uncovered networks of corruption in Malta and abroad.
She was killed by a car bomb in October 2017, with speculation at the time that senior establishment figures may have been involved.
Fenech was cleared of both counts by an 8-1 margin after eight hours of deliberation by the jury, the Reuters news agency reported.
His family members screamed with delight in the packed courtroom in Valletta, while Caruana Galizia's family wept, the agency said.
"Nine years after Daphne's brutal assassination, the institutional failures that enabled her murder remain unaddressed and unreformed," her family said in a statement reported by local media.
"Lasting justice means no person should ever face the same risks again. Our country failed to protect Daphne's life. It owes it to her to prevent other lives being lost."
Daphne Caruana Galizia gained international prominence for her investigations into corruption, money laundering and organised crime, which she published on her blog Running Commentary.

She was deeply involved in the 2016 Panama Papers investigation - a cache of confidential documents leaked from a Panamanian law firm. The investigation exposed offshore structures and triggered corruption allegations directed at top government officials in Malta.
Her shocking assassination prompted widespread public outrage and protests on the streets of Malta at the time. She was 53 years old.
During the trial, the jury heard that Fenech had wanted the journalist killed because she was about to reveal information about him.
One of Malta's richest men, Fenech is a well-known figure and was the owner of a company Caruana Galizia had written about months before her death.

Fenech denied the accusations, and during the trial he deflected blame towards his one-time close friend Keith Schembri, former chief of staff of then-prime minister Joseph Muscat and a target of Caruana Galizia's stories.
Muscat, who was never linked to the murder, stepped down in January 2020 due to the political fallout from the assassination.
Police told the court that Schembri had never been a suspect, and he has denied any role in the murder.
In 2025, two men - Robert Agius and Jamie Vella - were jailed for life by a Maltese judge for having supplied the bomb.

articles.title: Ethics watchdog finds Liberal MP Idlout violated conflict of interest code
articles.summary: Ottawa's ethics commissioner found Liberal MP Lori Idlout violated Parliament's conflict of interest code, but recommended against imposing any penalties against her.

image.caption: Ottawa's ethics commissioner found Nunavut MP Lori Idlout violated Parliament's conflict of interest code by expensing purchases from her own shop to the House of Commons. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Ottawa's ethics commissioner found Liberal MP Lori Idlout violated Parliament's conflict of interest code, but recommended against imposing any penalties against her.
Commissioner recommended no sanctions, said Nunavut MP made errors 'in good faith'
Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner Konrad von Finckenstein released his findings from an investigation into Idlout's purchases from her own shop that she charged to the House of Commons.
Idlout reimbursed the House, saying she submitted the items in error.
In a statement to CBC News, Idlout thanked the commissioner for the report.
"I acknowledge the commissioner's findings and take this matter seriously," she said.

"At the time, I did not consider that these purchases made for legitimate parliamentary purposes would further private interests, as I receive no income from the businesses in question," Idlout wrote.

In the report, Finckenstein said he believed Idlout's actions "were errors of judgment and made in good faith." He said Idlout did not realize that the purchases would further her own interests, adding the Nunavut MP repaid the House as soon as she learned of the errors.
"In my view, this shows a true desire to fully remedy each instance of non-compliance," Finckenstein wrote in the report. "I therefore recommended that no sanction be imposed.”

items: Floor-crossing MP Idlout expensed purchases from her own business

blocks.text: Idlout is the sole shareholder and director of Carvings Nunavut, a gallery that sells Inuit-made sculptures and artwork. Idlout claimed 13 purchases as "gifts given as a matter of protocol" since becoming MP, four of which were listed as being from Carvings Nunavut.
The commissioner found Idlout contravened the code of ethics' section prohibiting MPs from acting in any way to further their own private interests.
What did Idlout charge to the House?
The four purchases from Carvings Nunavut amounted to $1,756 and were all made in 2025.

The largest purchase of $1,380 worth of cards, tote bags, hand-crafted keychains and zipper pulls and sculptures was made in August 2025. The commissioner said they were all gifts to First Nations leaders, elders and speakers at the NDP's national caucus meeting in B.C. that September.

She also purchased a wall hanging for $150 in January 2025 that she gifted to a long-term care centre, a $150 lapel pin bought the same month and gifted to Liberal MP Greg Fergus — then speaker of the House of Commons — and a $76 purchase in June 2025, of a fridge magnet, bar of soap and tumbler cup gifted to Northern and Arctic Affairs Minister Rebecca Chartrand.
The expenses were made during Idlout's time as an NDP MP, before she crossed the floor to the Liberals in March 2026.
Nunavut MP Lori Idlout walks with Carney to Liberal caucus after crossing the floor from NDP
The same month, Conservative MP Michael Barrett wrote the ethics commissioner asking for an inquiry into Idlout's conduct under the conflict of interest code.
"Ms. Idlout has — now that she's been caught — admitted to doing what every member of Parliament knows or ought to know they can't do," Barrett said. "This speaks to very poor judgment."
"I regret my error in judgment," Idlout said in her statement to CBC News. "I have since learned from this experience and will work closely with the commissioner's guidance going forward."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
David Cummings is a reporter for CBC News.

articles.title: Gun found in French lake is analysed by 2012 Alps killings investigators
articles.summary:
British tourists reportedly discovered Luger pistol that is latest in long line of potential leads in mystery of al-Hilli deaths

Experts are examining a gun found by tourists to determine…

blocks.text: Experts are examining a gun found by tourists to determine whether it might have been used to kill a British family in the French Alps 14 years ago.

In what remains an unsolved murder case, Saad al-Hilli, 50, his wife, Ikbal, 47, and her mother, Suhaila al-Allaf, 74, were shot dead on a road near Annecy, a remote Alpine village in eastern France in September 2012.
The couple’s two young daughters, then four and seven, survived but a passing cyclist, 45-year-old Sylvain Mollier, was also killed.

The French prosecutor Marie-Céline Lawrysz confirmed that a pistol, thought to be a Luger, was uncovered on 20 August by two tourists swimming in Lake Annecy. The weapon is currently being analysed by ballistics experts in France in connection with the al-Hilli cold case.

During the initial investigation, pieces from the butt of the weapon used in the killings, a vintage Luger P06-29 pistol, were found on the ground near the British-registered BMW estate car that the family had been driving at the time of the attack. The gun was identified as a model used by the Swiss army in the 1930s, but its owner has never been traced.
In a statement, Lawrysz said a semi-automatic pistol had been found by the tourists, reported to be British, at a depth of about five feet, a few dozen metres away from the shore of Lake Annecy.
She said: “They kept the weapon for 24 hours and conducted online research to identify its type.
“They subsequently drew a link between the discovered weapon and the one believed to have been used in the Chevaline [near Annecy] killing on September 5, 2012.
“On August 21 2026, they handed the weapon over to gendarmes from the local Saint-Jorioz brigade.”
Detectives have so far ruled out the possibility of a contract killing, saying a professional killer would not have used such a vintage weapon as the Luger.
The discovery of the pistol is the latest in a long line of leads that investigators have followed in an effort to unravel the mystery that has surrounded the four deaths.

Suspects previously arrested in connection with the case include an Iraqi prisoner known as Mr S who was claimed to have said he had been offered “a large sum of money” to kill Iraqis living in the UK.

Mr al-Hilli’s brother Zaid was also arrested on suspicion of murder in 2013, but was later told he would face no further action after police found there was insufficient evidence to charge him with a crime.

In 2022, another suspect was questioned but released without charge. Two years ago, DNA analysis was ordered by detectives in France’s cold case unit on clothes belonging to the victims, as well as on the pieces of the gun and cigarette butts found at the scene. No arrests were made following the tests.

articles.title: Bayeux tapestry loan symbolises ‘entente amicale’ between France and UK, says King Charles
articles.summary:
Monarch tells Emmanuel Macron at the British Museum in London that the two nations will share a future ‘woven together’ by history and shared values

The loan of the Bayeux tapestry was the…

blocks.text: The loan of the Bayeux tapestry was the “the best possible symbol” of the “entente amicale” between France and the UK, King Charles said as he visited the famous embroidered masterpiece at the British Museum in London.
Though the tapestry recounts a conflict, “here it is today, nearly 1,000 years later, as a precious symbol of trust, at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations,” he said.

The “70 metres of memory and artistry” were a reminder “that our two nations have been bound together for almost a millennium,” added Charles, speaking at the new exhibition and accompanied by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and UK prime minister, Andy Burnham.
In a speech partly delivered in French, he said: “We have defended our values together in times of peril; we continue to do so today across the world.”

He continued: “May this tapestry – and the treasures that will travel in return – stand as symbols not only of our shared past, but our shared future: a future woven, as it should be, by Britain and France together.”
Macron, also speaking in French and English, said that the return of the tapestry “had required a little patience” , since he first spoke of it in 2018.
“Since the first British request dates back to 1931 I choose to regard eight years as something of a speed record,” he said,
He added that with the tapestry in Britain that his hopes are that the two countries can “forge a bond as close as the threads of this thousand-year-old embroidery”.

The tapestry – the woven record of the Norman conquest – has returned to the UK for the first time in almost 1,000 years, and is on loan until September 2027 as part of a special trilateral agreement between the UK, France and the museum.

Charles’s reference to entente amicale followed his use of the phrase to rebrand the famous “entente cordiale” between the two nations in his banquet speech at Windsor Castle when he hosted the Macrons in July last year.
During Wednesday’s visit he expressed his “deepest appreciation” to Macron and the French people “for the trust you have placed in the United Kingdom by agreeing to this unprecedented loan”.

He said: “It once depicted warriors crossing the Channel; yet today it forms part of a cultural exchange that will see some of the British Museum’s own precious artefacts travel to France in return, in a spirit of friendship.”

Thanking all those who made the loan possible, he added: “Anyone studying the tapestry’s scenes in detail will notice that even in the 11th century historic events rarely happened without extensive discussion, careful planning and a great deal of organisation beforehand.”

The party, which also included Queen Camilla, France’s first lady, Brigitte Macron, and Burnham’s wife, Marie-France van Heel, stopped at key moments along the 11th-century artwork to hear from curators about historic events such as the coronation of Harold Godwinson and the much-disputed depiction of his death by an arrow to the eye at the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

At his first prime minister’s questions earlier on Wednesday, Burnham said: “The loaning of the tapestry is a great example of French-British cooperation, the same cooperation that has helped us reduce summer small boat crossings to a seven-year low.”

The Labour leader also said the Bayeux Around Britain programme, which will see the digital exhibition displayed in museums, galleries and castles in all four nations, would “give communities across the UK the opportunity to learn about one of the defining stories of our past”.

articles.title: 2 more B.C. Conservative MLAs quit caucus to sit as Independents
articles.summary: Donegal Wilson, MLA for Boundary-Similkameen, and Scott McInnis, MLA for Columbia River-Revelstoke, have have quit the B.C. Conservative caucus.

image.caption: Donegal Wilson, MLA for Boundary-Similkameen, says she is stepping away from the B.C. Conservative caucus sit as an Independent. (Legislative Assembly of B.C.)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Donegal Wilson, MLA for Boundary-Similkameen, and Scott McInnis, MLA for Columbia River-Revelstoke, have have quit the B.C. Conservative caucus.
Donegal Wilson, Scott McInnis says she has lost confidence in new party leader

The Conservative Party of B.C. has lost two more MLAs as Donegal Wilson and Scott McInnis became the eighth and ninth members to quit caucus in recent weeks, both citing concerns about party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay's leadership.
"I never imagined things could go this wrong, this quickly," Wilson, MLA for Boundary-Similkameen, said in a statement.

Wilson, who was elected in 2024, said she remains a conservative in principle but added that communication within the party had broken down and she has worries about the direction under Findlay, particularly around staffing decisions.
McInnis, MLA for Columbia River-Revelstoke, said in a separate statement that he no longer supports "the direction, judgment and decisions of Kerry-Lynne Findlay's leadership."

"The party has increasingly become an exclusive private club more concerned with ideological bona fides than building the broad coalition required to serve British Columbians and form government," he said.

Wilson and McInnis follow seven other MLAs to step away from the Conservatives, the latest being Á'a:líya Warbus, MLA for Chilliwack-Cultus Lake, who on Monday also said she had lost confidence in Findlay.

items: More stories from the B.C. Interior
Can Kerry-Lynne Findlay keep B.C. Conservatives together amid caucus turmoil?

blocks.text: The B.C. Conservative caucus said in a statement that it remains focused on its work as the Official Opposition to "[hold] the NDP government accountable and restoring prosperity for the people of this province."
Findlay will run in a byelection triggered by Conservative MLA for Abbotsford-Mission Reann Gasper's decision to step down from her role to allow the Conservative leader to seek a seat.
Findlay said the criticisms by departing members of her caucus are baseless.
"What we are seeing is a co-ordinated political attack designed to sidetrack our campaign at the very moment we are taking our message directly to the people of Abbotsford-Mission," she said.

Findlay said she has spent her career in positions of significant public trust, including as a lawyer, a former Canadian Human Rights Tribunal judge, a King's Counsel, a member of the King's Privy Council for Canada and as a federal cabinet minister.
The B.C. Conservatives' chief of staff Chris Delaney also resigned Wednesday.
Findlay named Gasper as her new chief of staff. Gasper had served as deputy chief of staff after stepping down as MLA.

blocks.text: Findlay was elected as party leader in May. Since then, the party has lost key staffers and faced allegations that she attempted to induce MLAs to step down to open a seat for her in the B.C. Legislature, a claim which she has denied as a political smear.
Two ex-Conservatives, Peter Milobar and Ian Paton, say they intend to form a new party.

articles.title: Israel ‘seeking Trump’s support for plan to expel Palestinians from Gaza’
articles.summary:
Defence minister says he believes US backing could tip regional balance in favour of forced resettlement

Israel’s defence minister has said his country is seeking Donald Trump’s support to…

blocks.text: Israel’s defence minister has said his country is seeking Donald Trump’s support to approve plans to expel Palestinians from the Gaza Strip in what has widely been condemned as a potential war crime.

Israel Katz said there was “no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration” during a conference hosted by the Israeli news site Ynet and the newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth. He said the Israeli government was “organised and prepared to get them out by sea, by air, by every way possible”.

Trump discussed a US takeover of the Gaza Strip in early 2025 that would have involved removing Palestinians from the territory, but has since pulled back from the idea. A 20-point peace plan the White House drew up last year did not call for Palestinians’ deportation, an act that would be widely seen as ethnic cleansing.

blocks.caption: Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said removal of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip was ‘being discussed all the time’. Photograph: Israeli Defence Ministry/Reuters

blocks.text: Katz, however, said on Wednesday that he believed US support could tip regional opinion in favour of the forced resettlement of Palestinians from Gaza. He said Trump’s approval was crucial to convince neighbouring countries to accept Palestinian refugees.
“Every country that is willing to take them in wants American backing,” he said. “Trump has not cancelled this at the moment. He has frozen it.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request from the Guardian for comment on whether Trump was continuing to hold discussions on Israel’s proposals to forcibly depopulate the Gaza Strip.

Katz pointed in particular to Egypt, which he said had lobbied Washington to oppose the forced removal of the Palestinian population. “It has not been cancelled,” he said. “It is being discussed all the time, including now, and I think there is no other solution in the end that is in everyone’s interest.”

The remarks come during a competitive election season in Israel in which the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his rightwing allies have appealed to voters by calling for more aggressive measures against Palestinians.

Some have been openly inflammatory and cruel. The far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, posted footage on X from a women’s prison where he said he was responsible for the dire conditions in the facility.

When one prisoner told him they were not receiving medical care, showering or receiving clean clothing, Ben-Gvir said: “The good conditions in the prisons are over. This is the current situation, and I am directly responsible for everything. I am pleased with these conditions.”

Netanyahu visited an Israeli military post close to the yellow line in the Gaza Strip on Wednesday. Israel has said it would not pull back from that line until Hamas disarmed, despite calls for a phased withdrawal to facilitate a recent ceasefire with the group.

“We control the territory and are staying on this line,” Netanyahu said. “We are doing everything to achieve our goal – disarming Hamas and demilitarising Gaza. Gaza will no longer pose a threat to Israel.”

articles.title: Green party members back Zack Polanski to stand in London byelection
articles.summary:
Party leader in England and Wales seen as favourite to contest Holborn and St Pancras after Starmer’s resignation

Zack Polanski moved a step closer in his quest to become an MP on Wednesday,…

blocks.text: Zack Polanski moved a step closer in his quest to become an MP on Wednesday, with local Green party members supporting him to become the party’s candidate in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.

The party leader in England and Wales started campaigning alongside his fellow Green, Hannah Spencer, the MP for Gorton and Denton, in the Holborn area on Tuesday, and is seriously considering putting himself forward as the party’s candidate in the seat vacated by Keir Starmer on Monday.

Green party sources said local party members would have the final say on the selected candidate, but the Guardian understands local members are supportive of Polanski running, with no clear local activist with significant support expected to oppose him. It is understood nominations will open soon and candidates will be selected by the end of next week.

Lorna Jane Russell, the leader of the Greens on the local Camden council, will not stand, having previously expressed a desire to focus on her role as the leader of the opposition at Camden Town Hall and her pregnancy.

On the anniversary of his election on 2 September 2025, Polanski said the byelection would be a “referendum on ending rip-off Britain”, adding: “I am very excited for the next chapter for myself, for the Greens and for people across the country.”
Sources inside the party in London said that the rise in membership since Polanski became leader made him the favourite for the role.

“There would be a lot of excitement about him standing,” said one Green party source. “This is the kind of seat that has always had high-profile figures and I think having someone with Zack’s profile would play very well with local party members.”

The move is not without risk for Polanski, with the former prime minister’s seat traditionally considered to be safe for Labour. The Green party leader may prefer to contest a seat in Hackney, where the party has recently won the mayoralty, if a sitting MP such as Diane Abbott were to step down. In a difficult political climate in the May local elections, Labour lost seats but held on to Camden council. “This is not Gorton and Denton,” said one Labour source. “The Burnham bounce will help.”

Tulip Siddiq, the Labour MP for Hampstead and Highgate, said party members were already out campaigning and were confident they could retain the seat. “I know Camden through and through and I do believe that we can win this,” she said.

Siddiq added: “I think the Labour vote is resilient and I think Andy Burnham’s pledges on the doorstep are being gratefully received by people in Camden. Certainly I’ll be out campaigning every day and giving it my best shot.”
Labour will not run an all-women shortlist and will announce their candidate by next Wednesday, with applications closing on Friday and shortlisting expected by the start of next week.
after newsletter promotion

The frontrunner is thought to be Sagal Abdi-Wali, who came to the UK as a child refugee from Somalia and has been the leader of Camden council since May. “She’s got a compelling personal story and can reach people from all faiths and backgrounds in Camden,” said one Labour source. “She’s also been really active in the local party for a long time. Lots of people know her and like her.”

Adam Hug, the former leader of Westminster council who lost his job leading the council when the Conservatives took control of it in May’s local election, is also a mooted name. Other possible candidates are Nash Ali, the former mayor of Camden, and Rishi Madlani, a former Camden councillor.

Abdi-Wali is close to Starmer and local Labour sources said any attempts to bring in a candidate not from the area would be met with fierce criticism. “It will be interesting to see if Burnham has the same appeal in north London as Makerfield,” said one. “A lot of the policies he’s been talking about feel more geared towards the rest of the country, not really London.”

articles.title: Poa, as witness, says impeachment trial ‘fair’ despite tense exchanges
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Defense counsel Michael Poa, who took the witness stand during Wednesday’s impeachment trial, said he believed the proceedings were conducted “fairly.” During the 21st day of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Defense counsel Michael Poa, who took the witness stand during Wednesday’s impeachment trial, said he believed the proceedings were conducted “fairly.”

During the 21st day of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, Poa was summoned by the prosecution as its third hostile witness as it scrutinized Duterte’s alleged misuse of the Department of Education’s (DepEd) confidential funds.
Poa was grilled by the prosecution over his supposed knowledge — or lack thereof — about how DepEd utilized its confidential funds.

“It was okay. I also just wanted to say, also wanted to thank the prosecution, si Atty. [Benjamin] Tolosa [Jr.]. I think everything that happened today was quite fair,” said Poa during a press conference after the Wednesday proceedings.
Poa also thanked defense lead counsel Sheila Sison for “handling their side.”
Previously, Poa temporarily stepped out of his role in the defense, including as its spokesperson, after he was called to testify before the Senate impeachment court.
‘Nothing personal inside the courtroom’
Meanwhile, defense deputy spokesperson Atty. Justin Gular said during the same press conference that there was no ill will between lawyers on opposing sides of the case.
He said this after the prosecution’s direct examination became noticeably heated during an exchange between Sison and private prosecutor Tolosa.
“Nothing personal. I was there and I saw that after the trial, [Atty. Tolosa and Atty. Sison] were talking,” said Gular.

“You have to understand that outside the impeachment, beyond the impeachment, we also have many cases where we are on opposing sides or, at times, are co-counsel. It’s a relatively tight-knit community, and the legal community has always functioned under the premise of mutual respect and congeniality,” he added.

Duterte is facing the impeachment trial amid allegations of misusing confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery and grave threats. — With reports from Martina Nieyandra Calica, INQUIRER.net trainee /das

articles.title: Female film-makers still being squeezed out of industry, London film festival director says
articles.summary:
Over 40% of films in LFF programme are female-made, but only two of 21 gala films are directed by women

Female film-makers are still being squeezed out of the industry as they progress…
articles.byline: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent

blocks.text: Female film-makers are still being squeezed out of the industry as they progress beyond their debut films, the director of the London film festival has said, adding that “the dial does not seem to be moving”.

Kristy Matheson’s comments came as LFF announced its full programme for this year’s event, which runs from 7 to 19 October. Of the 251 titles, 109 (43%) are made by female film-makers, but only two of the 21 gala films are directed by women.

The figure comes as the Venice film festival faces renewed scrutiny over its lack of female directors in the competition. Maggie Gyllenhaal, the president of the Venice jury, said on Wednesday that there was a “systemic problem” preventing women from getting opportunities, including access to financing.
Speaking about LFF, Matheson said programmers had no difficulty finding strong films by women at the beginning of their careers, but numbers declined sharply thereafter.

“The statistics are not where you would want them to be,” she said. “We have no problem finding incredible films by female directors. We could make a whole Sutherland competition [recognising directorial debut] easily and have only female directors.

“Then it really drops off. So short films, first films, you’re just seeing all of this incredible talent. Second films, it starts to drop off. This is not something new to this year. It seems the dial does not seem to be moving.”
Matheson said the disparity was particularly visible in the festival’s higher-profile sections.
“You’ll find less female film-makers in the gala section, for example,” she said. “How many female directors get to make big-budget films? How many get to make fourth films, fifth films?”

The festival will also feature screen talks with Andrew Scott, Ava DuVernay, Cynthia Erivo, Jesse Eisenberg, John Malkovich, Sofia Coppola, Brad Bird, James Gray, Mahershala Ali, Naomi Ackie and Danny Boyle.

blocks.caption: Andrew Scott in Elsinore, which will open the festival. Photograph: Anthony Dickenson/Focus Features

blocks.text: Opening and closing this year’s festival are films about theatre, creativity and the communities people build around them.

Simon Stone’s Elsinore, receiving its European premiere, will open the festival with the story of the actor Ian Charleson and stars Andrew Scott and Olivia Colman. Jesse Eisenberg’s comedy The Debut, a love letter to community theatre, will close it with its UK premiere, starring Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti.
“To make theatre is to be with others. It’s an act of community,” Matheson said.

“Elsinore and The Debut are two very different films in tone. But in both, you get a sense of what creative community means, and how nourishing and enriching that can be. What they share is this idea of transformation. They’re both films about people on the precipice of something.”

Labour emerged as another theme, Matheson said, with films showing people at work opening up bigger questions about society. Mike Leigh’s Tender Loving Care follows two flatmates working in social care, while Boots Riley’s I Love Boosters, starring Keke Palmer and Demi Moore, turns a confrontation between professional shoplifters and a ruthless fashion mogul into a story about unionising.

Other films focus more explicitly on community and “radical care”, Matheson said. All of a Sudden, set in a nursing home, uses the relationship between two women to explore friendship and what it means to belong.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Kate O’Flynn, Marion Bailey and Alice Bailey Johnson in Tender Loving Care, directed by Mike Leigh.  Photograph: International Film Festival

blocks.text: Elsewhere, the programme explores political themes. Boyle’s Ink, premiering at the Mayor of London’s Gala, revisits Rupert Murdoch’s acquisition of the Sun and its impact on British politics and western democracy. Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine returns to the eve of Pinochet’s 1973 coup in Chile, while Sergei Loznitsa’s Imperium reworks footage shot in Russia in the early 1970s into a meditation on empire.
“They’re using history to process now,” Matheson said.

The Match, a documentary about the 1986 England-Argentina World Cup quarter-final, is structured like a thriller while examining politics, colonialism and ownership. Josephine, which premiered at Sundance, uses thriller conventions to explore trauma after a violent sexual assault witnessed by a young girl.
“There are films that are not usually the subject matter of a thriller, but are using this genre to explore topics in an engaging and enticing way,” Matheson said.

blocks.caption: Boots Riley’s I Love Boosters. Photograph: Neon

blocks.text: Among the festival’s international premieres is Tony Gilroy’s Behemoth!, starring Pedro Pascal, Olivia Wilde and Will Arnett, and set in the world of classical music.
World premieres include Anthony Wonke’s British boxing biopic In the Shadows and Michael Winterbottom’s The Trip to the Northern Lights, starring Rob Brydon and Steve Coogan.

Additional galas include Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s The Beloved, Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland, Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord – winner of the Palme d’Or in Cannes in May – Taika Waititi’s adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun, and Susanna White’s adaptation of Suzie Miller’s acclaimed play Prima Facie.
There is also Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial, Jordan Firstman’s Cannes breakout Club Kid, James Gray’s Paper Tiger, and Andrew Haigh’s adaptation of Colm Tóibín’s short story A Long Winter.

articles.title: Arrest warrants issued in Mexico for duo accused in alleged condo scam
articles.summary: A Mexican court has issued arrest warrants against the man and woman accused of defrauding a Canadian couple of their retirement savings through an alleged condo-flip scheme, CBC News has learned.

image.caption: Harry Robinson, left, and Jacqueline Herrera Herrera, right, are accused of defrauding an Ontario couple out of $280,000 with a condo-flipping scheme in Mexico. (Harry Robinson/Facebook; Jacqueline Herrera Herrera/Facebook)

blocks.text: World·New
A Mexican court has issued arrest warrants against the man and woman accused of defrauding a Canadian couple of their retirement savings through an alleged condo-flip scheme, CBC News has learned.
Ontario couple put $280K into plan to flip condos in Playa del Carmen
The warrants for Harry Robinson, a British national, and Jacqueline Herrera Herrera, a Mexican national, were issued in late July by a Quintana Roo state court judge.
Both are now before a Mexican federal court seeking to toss those warrants, according to copies of court records.
The criminal case against them, which is being heard at the state level, won’t be impacted by the federal court process around the arrest warrants, however.
Robinson and Herrera are accused by the state prosecutor's office of committing fraud through deception.

The Canadian couple — Cindy Thompson and Glenn Brown, of Curve Lake, Ont. — sent $280,000 to a company co-owned by a Robinson and Herrera who promised big returns on a condo flip in Playa del Carmen that never materialized.
"It is not something that leaves your mind because you’re always worried about what’s going to happen, what’s next," said Thompson this week.
Quintana Roo is a popular vacation and investment destination for Canadians, and also home to Cancun and Tulum.
Thompson and Brown filed a criminal complaint against Robinson and Herrera earlier this year.
The case stems from late 2024 when Thompson, searching for possible real estate investments in Mexico, came across the web page for XMEX Investments which was run by Robinson.
She eventually met Robinson and Herrera in Playa del Carmen. Herrera pitched her on buying a one-bedroom condo and Thompson sent $170,000 in two installments, but never received the keys.
Robinson then convinced Thompson to move her money, with an additional $110,000 from Brown, into a deal to flip seven condos, saying via WhatApp it was looking "to be 100 per cent profit."
Thompson and Brown’s money then vanished.
A federal court judge granted a stay on Aug. 27 against the warrant seeking Herrera’s arrest, but the process to have it tossed continues, according to court records.
A hearing on Robinson’s application is scheduled for Sept. 8 in Cancun, according to court records.
Herrera has claimed in WhatsApp messages that Robinson took some of the money. Robinson filed a criminal complaint against Herrera in late 2025 alleging she stole all the money.

items: Mexican authorities probe alleged scam that wiped out Canadian couple’s retirement savings
U.S. may seek win with Mexico in wake of collapsed trade talks with Canada, says ex-negotiator

blocks.text: Neither Robinson, Herrera’s lawyer in Cancun nor the state deputy-prosecutor who is leading the case responded to a request for comment.

Herrera, through another lawyer, offered a cash settlement in early August to Thompson for about $2.3 million pesos, roughly $188,000, according to WhatsApp text and voice messages obtained by CBC News.
She then offered Thompson a commercial property in Cancun which she claimed was worth about $4 million pesos, or roughly $328,000.
Thompson rejected the offers.
"We're not going to get into any deals like that with her, ever again," said Thompson.
She says it’s been frustrating trying to understand the complex workings of the Mexican judicial system and the various moving parts associated with the case.
"I'm a little more hopeful, although today, my anxiety's through the roof," said Thompson. "It's hard not being there and not really knowing firsthand what’s going on."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jorge Barrera is a Caracas-born journalist currently based in Mexico City for CBC News. He previously worked with CBC's Investigative Unit and CBC's Indigenous Unit. Follow him on X @JorgeBarrera or email him jorge.barrera@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Maltese tycoon found not guilty of involvement in Daphne Caruana Galizia murder
articles.summary:
Yorgen Fenech cleared on both charges he faced over 2017 killing of journalist that prompted global outrage

One of Malta’s richest men has been found not guilty of involvement in the murder…

blocks.text: One of Malta’s richest men has been found not guilty of involvement in the murder of the anti-corruption journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.

The verdict, which is expected to be appealed against by the prosecution, will come as a blow not only to the victim’s family, but to the politicians and campaigners who regard the case as a landmark action in the fight to protect press freedom in Europe.

Nearly nine years after Caruana Galizia’s death, aged 53, in a car bombing in October 2017, a jury of six women and three men found Yorgen Fenech, 44, not guilty of both counts with which he had been charged: complicity in the voluntary homicide of Caruana Galizia, and association with the intention of committing a crime.

The verdict was decisive. As family members and the media watched, the forewoman announced the verdict to gasps and cheers, saying the jurors had voted to dismiss both counts by an eight to one majority.

Fenech, an influential businessman and property developer whose family owns two Hilton hotels and has a share in a power station in Malta, had been accused by prosecutors of paying €150,000 via a middle man, Melvin Theuma, to have the journalist killed. Prosecutors had asked for him to be sentenced to life in prison.

blocks.caption: A person holds up an image of Caruana Galizia at a protest in Valletta in 2019. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters

blocks.text: The murder of Caruana Galizia, who targeted Fenech and leading political figures in her reporting, triggered the most consequential political scandal in Malta’s postwar history, becoming a rallying point for anti-corruption and press freedom activism.
The fallout resulted in Joseph Muscat, the then prime minister of the EU’s smallest member state, being forced out of office along with two of his ministers and his chief of staff.

The two-month trial laid bare the extent of Fenech’s network of political contacts, and raised questions about attempts to sabotage and interfere with the police investigation. Key witnesses, and the defendant himself, claimed the prime minister’s chief of staff had repeatedly leaked sensitive information to Fenech.

Summing up the case against him, the prosecutor Anthony Vella said Fenech believed he could “buy justice”, telling the jury: “You are being asked to decide whether a man who had extensive contacts in politics and among the heads of public entities had enough power to pay for Daphne to be killed.”

The defence argued that the chain of command went higher, with suggestions from Fenech and his lawyers that the person who had ordered the killing was Muscat’s former chief of staff Keith Schembri. They said police had not done enough to investigate allegations about his involvement.
after newsletter promotion
“All roads lead to Keith, and all bridges to Keith were burned,” the defence lawyer Charles Mercieca said in his summing up.

In his testimony, Fenech told the jury: “I never ordered Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, or anyone else’s. I had no role in her murder”. He said he had merely acted as a messenger between Schembri and Theuma, and that the taxi-driver had blackmailed him.
Schembri, who gave evidence at the trial, denied all wrongdoing, saying he had no involvement in leaks and no knowledge of the murder.

articles.title: SWS: 33% of Filipinos say quality of life improved, same say it worsened
articles.summary: The Social Weather Survey (SWS) conducted from June 20 to 29, 2026, found that 33% of adult Filipinos said their quality of life had worsened over the past 12 months, classified by SWS as “losers.”…

blocks.text: Published September 3, 2026 1:47am

The Social Weather Survey (SWS) conducted from June 20 to 29, 2026, found that 33% of adult Filipinos said their quality of life had worsened over the past 12 months, classified by SWS as “losers.” Another 34% said their quality of life remained unchanged, while 33% said it had improved, classified as “gainers.”
This resulted in a net gainers score of zero, calculated by subtracting the percentage of losers from the percentage of gainers. SWS classified the score as “fair” (0 to -9).

The June 2026 score was 26 points higher than the “low” -26 recorded in March 2026, reversing three consecutive quarterly declines. The net gainers score fell from a “very high” +12 in June 2025 to “fair” -2 in September 2025 and “fair” -7 in November 2025, before dropping further to “low” -26 in March 2026.
The June 2026 net gainers score of zero was also 8 points higher than the 2025 annual score of “fair” -8 and was close to the “fair” -2 recorded in September 2025.

The Second Quarter 2026 Social Weather Survey was conducted using face-to-face interviews of 1,200 adults (18 years old and above) nationwide: 300 each in Metro Manila, Balance Luzon (or Luzon outside Metro Manila), the Visayas, and Mindanao.
The sampling error margins are ±3% for national percentages and ±6% each for Metro Manila, Balance Luzon, the Visayas, and Mindanao. The survey was non-commissioned.

The June 2026 survey found the net gainers registered lowest in Metro Manila at mediocre -13, followed by the Visayas at fair -1, Mindanao at high +3, and Balance Luzon (or Luzon outside Metro Manila) at high +4.
"The 26-point rise in the nationwide net gainers score from March to June 2026 was due to increases in all areas," SWS said.

Compared to March 2026, net gainers rose from very low to fair in urban areas, up by 27 points from -32 to -5. It rose from mediocre to high in rural areas, up by 23 points from -18 to +5, SWS also said. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Berlin's punitive measures unlikely to deter Putin: experts
articles.summary: Germany has announced punitive measures after publicly blaming Russia for an attempted airport drone attack. But a former diplomat, political and security analysts warn it will likely do little to…

image.caption: Speaking on Tuesday, President Putin called Germany's response 'another mistake, a serious one' with the Kremlin vowing to respond 'in kind' Image: Florian Gaertner/photothek/picture alliance

blocks.text: The practical impact of Germany's latest measures against Russia may be limited, according to Russian political scientist Dmitry Oreshkin, who described the response as largely symbolic.

However, Berlin's decision to publicly attribute the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4 to Moscow reflects a growing willingness to respond to Russian President Vladimir Putin and what Berlin sees as hostile actions on its territory.

"It's only a source of joy for Putin. After all, he is restoring this Iron Curtain between Russia and all the other countries. And now he's getting help from the other side as well," Oreshkin told DW. "Putin is someone who cannot be stopped by anything other than escalation and tough restrictions."
Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig

Berlin's decision to close the Russian consulate in the western city of Bonn, terminate the contract for the Russian House cultural center in Berlin and tighten entry controls for Russian citizens does not go far enough, according to Boris Bondarev, a former diplomat who worked for the Russian permanent mission to the UN Office at Geneva.

Bondarev, who resigned his post in 2022 over Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, said reducing staff and restricting diplomatic activities may complicate Russian operations in Germany, but they will not fundamentally alter Moscow's strategic calculus.

"I'm not sure this will be perceived in Russia as something that will make them think twice," he said. "Unless there are other, more coordinated steps at the EU level, they won't stop provocations. At most, they may force them to coordinate a little differently and look for more professional operatives."
Both experts agreed, however, that Germany's measures could have an effect even if they fail to deter Moscow — by setting off another cycle of reciprocal restrictions.
How will Russia respond?
Speaking on Tuesday, President Putin called Germany's response "another mistake, a serious one," with the Kremlin telling the German Press Agency that Russia would respond "in kind."

German security policy expert Wolfgang Richter said the risk of escalation has increased compared with the early years of the Russia-Ukraine war, but said the next phase of confrontation between Berlin and Moscow is likely to remain in the areas of diplomacy and culture.

"They will, for example, close the Goethe-Institut," said Richter, a colonel with Germany's military until his retirement in 2010. "I would not quite exclude that they could also escalate a little bit and do more — for example, limit the number of diplomats in the German embassy in Moscow."
Former diplomat Bondarev, however, said the Kremlin's reaction could be difficult to predict.

"Moscow officials can surprise you. They could say: 'We have all these people under surveillance anyway, so why expel them? Let them work, and we'll continue monitoring them.' It could go either way. But most likely, there will be some high-profile retaliatory steps," he said.
Sabotage fears hit Germany's power grid

The dispute over organizations such as the Goethe-Institut and the Russian House in Berlin reflects a deeper divide in how Moscow and Western governments view their role. The Goethe-Institut, founded in 1951 to promote German language and culture abroad, is seen by Moscow through the lens of its broader suspicion of Western institutions, said Oreshkin. And, he added, the Kremlin tends to assume that such organizations serve intelligence purposes because it projects its own security-service worldview onto Western structures.

"The Russian system of thinking among the security services assumes that all Western institutions are organized in exactly the same way. This symmetrical picture of the world is deeply mistaken," he said.
Oreshkin said it's unlikely the Kremlin will escalate much further than the level of diplomacy and culture.

"Launching a missile strike — that's something Putin doesn't have the guts to do. And all these acts of sabotage and subversion — supporting alternative political movements, like Alternative for Germany — they're already doing that anyway," he said. "So I don't think Putin can escalate much beyond that. He can, in fact, escalate the rhetoric, and that's what he's doing."
Real pressure point: Russia's shadow fleet

Announcing the measures on Monday, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters that the EU would continue to work on additional sanctions "in the coming weeks." That included tougher action against Russia's "shadow fleet," though he didn't provide further details.
Russian officials have repeatedly warned that attempts to detain or seize vessels linked to Russia's network of ships ​accused of circumventing fuel sanctions would be regarded as hostile acts.
NATO listens underwater to guard against Russian sabotage

Oreshkin said if Europe really wants to put pressure on the Kremlin, targeting the financial flows behind the shadow fleet would be more effective. But he pointed to a major obstacle: European governments are constrained by their own legal frameworks, which include maritime law that ensure freedom of navigation.

Security expert Richter, however, sees a broader security risk. Pressure on the shadow fleet could increase the likelihood of incidents at sea, he told DW. "And that would, of course, mean another escalation."

For Richter, the answer lies in making sure both sides understand the risks involved. "The situation has become more tense and it's high time to speak," he said. Without communication between the parties, he warned, any actions could be misinterpreted and might trigger further escalation.

articles.title: Unity at last: Is Libya's damaging power struggle at an end?
articles.summary: For over a decade, Libya has been split between two opposing governments. Elections, meant to end the rivalry and unite the country, are now scheduled within two years.

image.caption: On the road to democracy? Local elections were held in Libya in August 2025Image: Mahmud Turkia/AFP

blocks.text: There have been other attempts made in the past but this time, those involved hope it will finally work out: Thanks to mediation by the United Nations, the two opposing governments in the west and east of Libya have agreed that they will hold parliamentary and presidential elections within the next two years.
"The agreement marks an important step in advancing Libya towards national elections and ending the transitional period," the UN's Support Mission in Libya, or UNSMIL, said in a statement.

Among other things, the country's electoral commission will be restructured and, according to the UN, various points about the legal framework for the elections that had previously led to disagreements have now been resolved.
But whether all this will actually result in free and fair elections in Libya remains to be seen.
Divided for over a decade
After former Libyan dictator Moammar Gadhafi was overthrown in 2011, Libya ended up divided in two.

Since 2014, the country has been split between opposing governments located in the east and west of the country. A UN-backed administration known as the Government of National Unity is based in Tripoli in the west, and its rival, known as the House of Representatives, is based in the east, in Tobruk.
Former warlord-turned-politician Khalifa Haftar, is based in the east while Prime Minister Abdul-Hamid Dbeibah is in charge in the west.

Each is supported by a number of local militias and foreign powers, and each has tried to wrest control from the other. Up until now, attempts to hold an election that would unite the country have failed.
For Andreas Dittmann, a geographic conflict expert and professor at the University of Giessen in Hesse, central Germany, the apparent unity is a positive.
"Things could not continue the way they were," he told DW.

After years of civil war and political division, the desire of many Libyans to end the fighting permanently has only grown. Dittmann believes the attitudes of political actors have also changed in this regard.

Previously foreign actors had supported just one Libyan government, but now that has also changed and the prevailing argument seems to be that Libya can only develop further if both sides are incorporated into one administration.

This is why the UN is trying to go beyond simply arranging a date for elections. It also wants to strengthen the electoral commission and work on electoral laws. The new and united government will be responsible for establishing the conditions for a secure and trusted electoral process.
The UN has also set up what it calls "Structured Dialogues," during which consensus was sought on questions of leadership, security, the economy and reconciliation.
Past agreements didn't work out

Michael Bauer, who heads the Tunisia office of Germany's Konrad Adenauer Foundation, believes the agreement is an important, if limited, step. Its success will depend on how binding any decisions are, he argued.
After all, Bauer said, there have been plenty of political agreements in Libya in the recent past but none were really ever implemented.

Parallel to the UN process, the US is also trying to work on bringing the disparate leadership together. Massad Boulos, the Trump administration's senior adviser on Arab and Middle Eastern affairs, has been trying to bring the Dbeibah and Haftar families together.

blocks.caption: Libya is potentially a rich country due to its mineral resources and large oil reservesImage: Hussein Malla/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: In June, Haftar's son Saddam was in Washington where he met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Bauer said the American way of dealing with Libya differentiates from the UN plan. "While the UN mission has basically been very inclusive, in my opinion, the American mission is trying to bring about a kind of deal between the country's elites," he told DW.
He questions how such a deal would fit into free and fair elections in Libya.
"Elections can only be meaningful if the outcome has not already been decided beforehand," Bauer said. The same is true for any pre-election allocation of political positions.
Elites strike a deal?

UK-based think tank Chatham House has already warned that a deal like this, around ministries and resources, will only institutionalize the existing rivalry between Libya's ruling elites. With such an arrangement the rival actors would just divide the state's resources between themselves, and corruption and patronage systems would continue.
The country's division into east and west will be hard to overcome. A new united government would have to deal with preexisting power structures, rather than starting anew.

Dittmann said there is a further problem. Much of the Libyan population lives in the western areas, especially in the Tripoli region. This would see the eastern half of the country lose power if elections are held.

blocks.caption: Locals hope for economic growth and stabilityImage: Islam Alatrash/DW

blocks.text: "If there are elections, and if those elections proceed mostly according to democratic principles, then the east can really only lose," he explained.
Additionally, there are also external actors to consider. Russia has extended its positioning in the east while Turkey supports the government in the west.
Alongside all of that is also the question of what the Libyan people want and what they expect from a united government. Bauer doubts elections alone can resolve Libya's problems.
"The people have a particular interest in seeing the country's dysfunction end," he said.

Libya is rich in raw materials and energy reserves, but also plagued by problems like power outages and inadequate public services. If the state was functioning properly, it would likely curtail the power of those currently benefiting most from the country's resources and, as Bauer argued, "why would they voluntarily give up these opportunities?"

That will be the most difficult question for the next two years. The new agreement between Libya's political rivals must do more than simply establish a path toward elections. It must also create a framework in which those rivals accept the results of an election and in which public institutions function properly.
This story was originally written in German.
