articles.title: No details in AFP papers on use of DepEd secret funds – prosec
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The military certifications submitted by the Department of Education (DepEd) to the Commission on Audit (COA) showed no details on how it used its confidential funds, which it…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The military certifications submitted by the Department of Education (DepEd) to the Commission on Audit (COA) showed no details on how it used its confidential funds, which it supposedly released for the Youth Leadership Summit activities listed.

The House prosecution pointed this out in a statement issued on Wednesday, citing the testimony of former DepEd Undersecretary Michael Wesley Poa on the 21st day of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial.

According to the statement, Poa’s testimony revealed that ₱15.54 million allegedly spent on confidential-fund rewards was not supported by details in the certification issued by the Armed Forces of the Philippines.
No specifics

During Wednesday’s trial proceeding, private prosecutor Benjamin “Jay” Tolosa Jr. asked Poa whether the AFP certifications identified the rewarded informers or the particular information obtained through the alleged payments.
“No particular specific information was identified,” Poa replied.
One certification had information from DepEd, local governments, and the Philippine National Police identifying areas where Youth Leadership Summits would be conducted.
But when Tolosa asked whether the document stated that the information came from a confidential informer, Poa answered: “Not in that document.”
Poa also agreed that the certification did not state that the information was obtained by paying a reward.
“Tama po,” he said.
(“Right, sir.”)
Tolosa then asked him whether the same deficiency applied to the other AFP certifications attached to DepEd’s response.
Poa replied: “Yes.”

According to the prosecution statement, the admissions matter because Commission on Audit Joint Circular No. 2015-01 does not treat the existence of a government activity as proof that a confidential-fund reward was properly “paid.

“The circular requires rewards to informers to be approved by the head of the agency, supported by documents showing successful information-gathering or surveillance because of information supplied by an informer and directly related to a specific confidential activity,” the prosecution statement said.
The AFP certifications, however, did not identify an informer, the amount paid, the information bought, or the result directly produced by that information.
No funds transferred
The statement added that Poa also confirmed that no DepEd confidential funds were transferred to the AFP for the summits covered by the certifications.
“Yes, sir. I confirm that,” he said.

Poa’s testimony corroborated what had already been established by two previous witnesses — Army officers Col. Manaros Boransing II and Col. Magtangol Panopio —who testified that their units did not receive DepEd confidential funds for the activities listed in their certifications.

“Boransing testified that the 1st Infantry “Tabak” Division received no DepEd funding, confidential or otherwise, for the eight YLS and 53 information, education and communication activities covered by his Jan. 1, 2024 certification,” the prosecution statement said.

“The testimony does not dispute that the programs occurred. It separates the existence of legitimate military activities from the question of how DepEd’s confidential funds were spent,” it added. /atm

articles.title: Tacloban air quality ‘unhealthy for sensitive groups’
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY — Air quality in Tacloban remained generally satisfactory for coarse particles but showed elevated levels of fine particulate matter on Wednesday, as haze associated with forest fires…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY — Air quality in Tacloban remained generally satisfactory for coarse particles but showed elevated levels of fine particulate matter on Wednesday, as haze associated with forest fires in Indonesia continued to affect parts of the Philippines.

The Environmental Management Bureau Region 8 (EMB-8) reported a slight increase in particulate matter levels during the noon-to-1 p.m. monitoring period at the Tacloban Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Station on Sept. 2.
The station recorded an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 48 for PM10, or coarse particles, which falls under the “good” category. At this level, air pollution poses little or no risk to the general public.
However, PM2.5, or fine particles, registered an AQI of 108, placing air quality in the “unhealthy for sensitive groups” category.

The classification means people who are particularly sensitive to air pollution, including those with respiratory conditions such as asthma, may be more vulnerable to health effects and are advised to limit prolonged or strenuous outdoor activities.
PM2.5 is of particular concern because these fine particles can penetrate deep into the respiratory system.

The latest monitoring comes as transboundary haze from forest fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia, has reached parts of Luzon and the Visayas. Environment and health authorities have intensified monitoring as prevailing winds associated with the southwest monsoon have carried smoke and pollutants toward the Philippines.
The EMB has emphasized that air quality conditions can vary depending on wind patterns, rainfall and the movement of the haze.
EMB Region 8 said it will continue round-the-clock surveillance of air quality parameters to track changes in pollution levels and provide timely information to the public.
Residents, particularly those belonging to sensitive groups, are encouraged to stay updated on official air quality advisories and take precautions when pollution levels rise.

The latest reading underscores the importance of monitoring PM2.5 levels even when overall air quality appears acceptable, as fine particles can pose health risks at lower concentrations than larger particulate matter. /das

articles.title: Russia's hybrid attacks on Germany: When is it 'war'?
articles.summary: The German government is holding Russia responsible for an unsuccessful attack in Leipzig. Yet many feel that its response has been too mild.

image.caption: Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes like this one also take off from Leipzig, carrying military supplies for UkraineImage: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fortunately, nothing bad happened this time around. Had the attack succeeded, however, who knows what the consequences might have been: On the evening of August 4, a drone outfitted with explosives and a detonation device was discovered near Ukrainian cargo planes in the security area of Leipzig Airport. The airport serves as a hub for military aid to Ukraine.
The German government hesitated for a long time before publicly holding Russia responsible. But now the government has announced its findings.

On Tuesday, September 1, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters that the methods used in the attempted attack were consistent with those seen in other Russian hybrid operations, citing the drone's construction, various components, explosives and detonation technology. He noted that the attack had been planned with a "high degree of technical expertise and considerable organizational effort."

Back in late August, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said of the incident: "The federal government will make the perpetrators of hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for this." At the time, he did not mention Russia by name. And even now, Merz himself has not commented on the matter.

However, the price Russia will have to pay is relatively small. The Russian House cultural institute in Berlin is being shut down amid suspicions that it is serving as a cover for espionage. The Russian Consulate General in Bonn is also being closed. What's more, entry requirements for Russian citizens are set to be tightened, and Germany also plans to take tougher action against the Russian "shadow fleet." Exactly how and when remains unclear, however.
Mixed reactions to measures

For the environmentalist Green Party in the Bundestag, however, this does not go far enough. "The federal government's analysis came a bit late, and the steps it's taking aren't enough for me," said Sara Nanni, the Greens' security policy spokesperson, in an interview with DW. "I don't think anyone in Moscow is afraid or giving it a second thought right now." As an example, she said Germany should be taking tougher action against the Russian shadow fleet. This would be necessary to "stop the flow of money to the Russian war machine," she said.
Acts of sabotage linked to Russia surge in Europe

Roderich Kiesewetter, security expert with Chancellor Merz' center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is also dissatisfied. In the Handelsblatt newspaper, he called for the delivery of Taurus cruise missiles to Ukraine — and for the activation of Article 4 of the NATO Treaty, which requires allies to engage into consultations in the event of an external threat. He urged the German government to abandon "the politically convenient path of appeasement."

However, wouldn't responding more assertively, as Kiesewetter demands, risk provoking a military confrontation with Russia, especially given that Russia flatly denies responsibility for the Leipzig incident? President Vladimir Putin called the German sanctions against his country a "serious mistake" and accused Germany of fabricating evidence. The Foreign Ministry in Moscow announced that it would take countermeasures.
Foreign Minister Wadephul sees Germany as a target

Once again, the question of whether Germany is already at war with Russia is being raised — and this time with even greater urgency. But the federal government has unequivocally denied it. "We are not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," said Interior Minister Dobrindt on Tuesday, after he blamed Russia for the failed attack. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told German public broadcaster ARD that Germany is not at war but is a Russian "war target."

A year ago, in September 2025, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said — though without naming Russia: "We are not at war, but we are no longer at peace either." This came against the backdrop of increasing attacks on data networks, critical infrastructure and hybrid threats.

Security expert Sönke Marahrens from the University of Kiel offered a more nuanced answer: "No, Germany is not at war at the moment. We are facing hybrid activities by other countries, but we are not at war."

In Western countries, he noted, declarations of war are regulated by law. And in Germany, according to the constitution, the Bundestag must declare that the country is at war, and that applies only after a physical attack. "Nothing currently meets that definition," he said.
Ex-Lithuanian FM: 'We are on a trajectory of escalation'

However, Green Party lawmaker Sara Nanni fears that Russia will continue to escalate the situation. "We are not yet at war with Russia, but Russia appears to be preparing for a war not only against Ukraine but against all of Europe," she told DW, calling the incident in Leipzig an "attempted terrorist act."
Not at war with Russia

From a strictly legal standpoint, Germany is not at war with Russia. No declaration of war has been made, no recognized armed conflict exists, and no collective defense obligation has been invoked under Article 5. Furthermore, consultations among NATO members, which must take place before a collective defense obligation can be invoked, have not been scheduled under Article 4.

But things look different when it comes to hybrid warfare, which is not as precisely defined. Numerous security experts argue that Russia is already waging just such a hybrid war against Western nations. This refers to attacks on infrastructure, cyberattacks, disinformation and traditional espionage.

However, the line between hybrid war and an open act of war are blurry. Sönke Marahrens believes that Russia is using hybrid actions — such as the one in Leipzig — to advance its strategic interests in Germany, the second-most important supporter of Ukraine after the US. Had the attack at the airport been successful, it would have relieved pressure on the Russian front, Marahrens says. He went on to say that, "If Russia succeeds in convincing the German public not to support these political decisions (to support Ukraine), that would also directly reduce the pressure on the front lines."
The AfD factor and the Saxony-Anhalt election

The state elections coming up on Sunday in Saxony-Anhalt are one current example of Russian strategic interests. Many observers believe that this election is the most important in Germany in decades. The key question is whether the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — which is classified as far-right by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution — will secure an absolute majority and, for the first time, govern a German state.

The AfD opposes further military support for Ukraine and would like to normalize relations with Russia. This resonates with many in eastern Germany, where the war in Ukraine is seen as none of Germany's business and where there is a feeling that too much money has already been sent to Ukraine.
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?

This is why the federal government — composed of the conservate CDU/CSU bloc and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — is being careful about stepping up its rhetoric, as doing so could potentially help the AfD secure an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt. On the other hand, it can hardly afford to place the blame for the events in Leipzig on Russia while also responding in only a relatively mild manner.
This dilemma may also be the reason why Chancellor Friedrich Merz has so far refrained from speaking out to blame Russia.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Austria women ice hockey team fight for future generations
articles.summary: Austria are getting ready for their first Women's Ice Hockey World Championship. But preparations have been overshadowed by a dispute about conditions, pay and getting men's cast off kit. A solution…

image.caption: Austria won an IIHF Division 1 tournament in China last year to qualify for this year's World Championship in DenmarkImage: Peng Zhigang/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: When the Austrian women's national ice hockey team took to the ice in the Women's European Cup of Nations in Slovakia last month, they did so without 11 of their top players.

Captain Anna Meixner and the rest of her team were frustrated that the Austrian Ice Hockey Association (ÖEHV) still hadn't responded to a list of grievances outlined in a letter to the organization last March. Meixner stresses that the players only went public with their complaints as something of a last resort.

Among the nine complaints on their list of demands were the standard of accommodation, having to change in unheated dressing rooms in the winter and not being paid per diems during training camps and international tournaments. They also said they had to make do with hand-me-down equipment from the men's team.
"We really tried to respect the federation (ÖEHV) and we really tried to solve it from within, without outside noise," Meixner told DW in a Zoom interview on Wednesday.
"So we had been fighting for four or five months without going out to the newspapers. But when we realized that nothing had changed, we had to take the next step."

"The final straw, if you want to call it that, was a camp last February. It was the no-heater-in-the-locker-room situation," said the 32-year-old forward, who, after two seasons in North America's PWHL (Professional Women's Hockey League) with the Ottawa Charge and Vancouver Goldeneyes, is returning to her previous team, Swedish outfit Brynas, for 2026-27.

"Here were people that had been sitting on a train for 14 hours, who didn't get food when they arrived. We had to go on the ice straight away. So, I think that was when it really became clear to us that enough is enough."
Fighting for future generations
Meixner also stressed that their aim was primarily to improve things for the women's national team in the longer term.

"We have this older generation right now and we're not going to play for the national team forever. We really felt it's time to give the next generation everything that we didn't have over the last 10 to 15 years. We brought it up with the team and everybody was on board right away."

To rachet up the pressure on the ÖEHV, the players also threatened to boycott the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship in Denmark in November – a significant moment, as this is the first time Austria have qualified for the top IIHF (International Ice Hockey Federation) tournament.

blocks.caption: Austrian captain Anna Meixner (94) played most of her two seasons in the PWHL for the Ottawa ChargeImage: Justin Tang/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: "Going to the newspapers," as Meixner put it, seems to have worked. In a press release following last month's tournament in Slovakia, in which Austria came second out of the four teams, the ÖEHV said it had taken the opportunity to hold "constructive conversations" with the players.
Now, Meixner appears cautiously optimistic.
Demands starting to be met

"We have gotten some answers from the federation and we are just in the process of going over everything. But now, we're happy about the direction things seem to be moving in," said Meixner, who added that the players and federation were finally speaking on an equal footing.

"It feels like they (the ÖEHV) actually want to change something. If it stays that way, I'm sure we can figure something out and make it work. Because obviously the last thing we want to do is to miss the World Championship."
Indeed, in a letter to the team sent on August 31, the ÖEHV responded to each of their nine demands outlining specific steps that had either already been implemented or were in the works.

These include a pledge to implement "clear regulations regarding per diems/remuneration and the timely payment of bonuses and travel expenses," to provide "adequate accommodation and reliable, needs-based catering" for training camps, "adequate cabin and gym facilities" as well as "sufficient time for travel and recovery."
Battling for 'bare minimums'
It also notes that it would seek a "teamwear solution" as part of a new contract with the association's equipment provider.
While this all seems promising, Meixner still finds it frustrating that in 2026, she and her teammates have had to battle so hard for what she termed "bare minimums."

At the same time though, she said that if the players and the ÖEHV do actually manage to put aside their dispute, it will be bigger than everything she has achieved on the ice – including winning the tournament in China last year that put Austria through to a first Women's Ice Hockey Championship.

"I'm unbelievably proud of us for staying hard at it for many months. There are so many girls from other nations reaching out saying, 'you know what? It's great that you're doing that and we should do the same," she said.
"We've heard the men's team stepping up, cheering for us. I think this is bigger than hockey. Hopefully this will be a big step for Austrian women's sports and Austrian women's in general."
Unless an unforeseen hitch arises over the next few weeks, Austria will open their first-ever World Championship campaign against Czechia in Esbjerg, Denmark on November 6.
Mathias Brück contributed to this report.

articles.title: Palestinian Australian sues NSW police claiming he was punched at Herzog rally when helping prayer group
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Eyad Shadid launches civil case in district court after charges against him dropped, alleging he was ‘battered’ near Sydney’s town hall in February

  • Get…

blocks.text: A Palestinian Australian man who alleges he was punched in the face when trying to stop police from harassing Muslim men praying during an anti–Isaac Herzog protest is suing New South Wales over “a series of false accusations”.
Eyad Shadid has launched a civil case in the NSW district court, alleging he was assaulted, battered and falsely imprisoned by police near Sydney’s town hall.
The Palestine Action Group member, in his statement of claim, says NSW police committed misfeasance in public office and subjected him to a malicious prosecution.

“I attended the protest to object to our government rolling out the red carpet for Isaac Herzog, president of a state that has been found by United Nations commissioners and most major human rights organisations to be perpetrating a genocide,” Shadid told Guardian Australia.
“The right to protest in this state must mean more than words on paper and, if we must go to court to prove that, then so be it. I did not go to town hall looking for trouble. I went to be counted.”
Shadid, 26, was looking for his mother – who, like his father, is from Palestine – after they became separated during the protest on the evening of 9 February.
He found himself between a group of Muslim men praying and advancing police when, according to his statement of claim, he told officers: “Stop, they are praying.”

Const Daniel Stewart then allegedly dragged Shadid, who had travelled from Parramatta, to the ground and punched him in the face and twisted his wrist. Another officer kneeled on his head, the documents allege.
Shadid alleges that when on the ground another officer handcuffed him and he was taken into custody. He was charged with failing to comply with a police direction and resisting arrest.
In May, NSW police dropped the charges. Since then, three others charged after the protest have had their charges withdrawn. More than 20 protesters are due to face a joint trial in mid-2027.

blocks.caption: Eyad Shadid returns to Sydney’s town hall. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: Shadid alleges in court documents that Stewart failed to tell another officer deciding whether to charge him that the police line had been advancing towards people praying – and he’d requested the police stop because of that.
He claimed the omission was “deliberate” and that Stewart falsely alleged Shadid threatened him with words to the effect of: “Mate, I’d fuckin’ drop you.”
In his police statement, Stewart wrote the group of men “began” to pray as the police line moved forward and he was acting in the lawful execution of his duty when he arrested Shadid.
Shadid claims that allegation was “dishonest” and designed to make it look like the prayer was a “cynical ploy” to frustrate officers.

NSW police issued a statement three days after the protest confirming the prayer had been authorised, but claimed that message was not passed on to officers. The police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, apologised “for any offence that may have been taken” after officers dragged away those praying.
After Shadid’s charges were dropped, the police prosecutor agreed officers had not given him a move-on direction. The 26-year-old was awarded costs.

“As a consequence of the matters pleaded herein, the plaintiff was assaulted, battered, falsely imprisoned, subjected to a misfeasance in public office, and maliciously prosecuted,” his statement of claim argues.

Shadid, a social services worker, is seeking aggravated and exemplary damages, arguing there was an “oppressive abuse of police powers” and he was prosecuted for “exercising a lawful democratic right to engage in peaceful protest”.
Shadid said after he was charged his name was published in media reports and he lost business clients.

blocks.caption: Eyad Shadid’s lawyer, Nick Hanna. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: Shadid’s lawyer, Nick Hanna, said the case involved “very troubling allegations of police misconduct”.

“We claim that Mr Shadid was violently assaulted and arrested without any lawful basis and then charged and prosecuted on the basis of a series of false accusations and misleading omissions,” Hanna said.
The defence is yet to file its response to Shadid’s statement of claim. The NSW premier, Chris Minns, and NSW police declined to comment while the matter was before the court.

Minns said after the rally that police were “put in an impossible situation” after protesters attempted to defy the public assembly restriction declaration (Pard) law. He refused to apologise to the prayer group or for the police’s conduct.
In April, the state’s court of appeal found that law unconstitutional, ruling in favour of the Palestine Action Group and Blak Caucus.
Derek Jones, who became known as “white shirt guy”, said in May he intended to launch legal action in the supreme court against police regarding their conduct at the Herzog rally.
“It was completely unprovoked, unwarranted, excessive, crazy,” the 56-year-old finance worker told Guardian Australia at the time.

The February protest is the subject of a police watchdog investigation after allegations of widespread police brutality. Footage emerged earlier this week of a separate incident in which an officer boasted about punching a protester.
The police commissioner, when asked about the video on Wednesday, said: “The language is something that I don’t condone, but I need to understand the context of it.”
Herzog was invited to Australia by the federal government after the antisemitic massacre in Bondi when 15 people were killed by two allegedly Islamic State-inspired gunmen.

articles.title: US sanctions halt TOEFL and GRE tests in Iran, disrupting study plans
articles.summary: Students in Iran can no longer take TOEFL and GRE exams after a US sanctions exemption was suspended. Applicants say the move threatens university deadlines and adds costly travel obligations.

image.caption: Until recently, some educational activities in Iran were exempt from US sanctionsImage: Pond5 Images/imago images

blocks.text: Iranian students hoping to study abroad are facing a new obstacle after TOEFL and GRE testing was suspended inside the country following changes to US sanctions regulations.

"My entire plan was built around taking this exam," a TOEFL candidate in Tehran told DW. She said she had spent months preparing applications for a PhD program, contacting professors and gathering documents despite internet disruptions and other challenges.

ETS, the US-based organization that administers both exams, announced it suspended testing in Iran after the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) froze General License G, which had allowed certain educational services to continue in Iran.
"Following OFAC's suspension of General License G, ETS has paused administration of the TOEFL and GRE tests in Iran effective immediately," the organization said in an official notice.
ETS added that Iranian nationals can still take the exams outside Iran and that it is exploring options to restore testing.

TOEFL is a US-based English-language proficiency test accepted by universities worldwide. The GRE, also administered by the same US organization, is a standardized test required by some graduate programs, particularly in the United States and Canada.
Since the Iran war began in late February, the US has increasingly expanded sanctions targeting Iranian trade and exports, contributing to broader disruptions throughout the Iranian economy.
No timeline for testing to resume
An Iranian institution that administered TOEFL exams told DW that new registrations had stopped following the latest sanctions changes.
The institution added that the suspension could be temporary, but no date had been given for exams to resume.

That uncertainty is particularly serious for students approaching university and scholarship deadlines who have spent months preparing documents, contacting professors and paying application-related costs.

The suspension follows earlier problems with IELTS (British equivalent of TOEFL) testing in Iran. An IELTS center in Tehran told DW that sanctions-related difficulties transferring money had become one of the main obstacles to continuing exams.
Some Iranian applicants had already been traveling to countries such as Turkey and Armenia to take IELTS. TOEFL and GRE candidates may now have to do the same.
Can Iran survive Trump's new sanctions?
Rising costs for applicants
Alireza, who is preparing to apply to a university in Italy, said the suspension of TOEFL had disrupted a backup plan he had arranged after IELTS testing became unavailable.

"European universities usually accept IELTS. But because IELTS has been suspended in Iran, after extensive correspondence with the university, they agreed to let [Iranian students] meet the required score through an equivalent TOEFL result," he told DW.
"But now TOEFL has also been suspended in Iran. Travelling to a neighboring country just to take the exam is very expensive, especially given Iran's current economic situation," added Alireza.
Another candidate told DW that taking the exam in Turkey or Armenia would mean paying for travel and at least one night's accommodation on top of the test fee.
For students hoping to secure scholarships or full funding, those additional expenses can be significant.

blocks.caption: Many Iranian students pursue post-graduate education abroadImage: Sigrid Gombert/Image Source/IMAGO

blocks.text: Students launch petition
Iranian TOEFL and GRE candidates have launched an online petition urging ETS to restore access to the exams.

The petition says thousands of students are losing access to tests required for university admissions, scholarships, graduate programs and other academic opportunities. Many, it says, have spent months preparing, paid exam-related costs and built their application schedules around specific test dates.
"Students should not lose years of preparation or their chance to pursue higher education because access to required examinations has suddenly been removed," the petition states.
Narges, an Iranian applicant affected by the suspension, said she had seen the petition circulating in Telegram groups used by language learners and students applying to foreign universities.
"I doubt it will have any impact," she said. "Still, I'm going to sign the petition."
Experiences of international PhD students navigating Germany
The organizers are calling on OFAC to provide a specific exemption for standardized academic testing and on ETS to restore TOEFL and GRE services in Iran as soon as legally possible.
They argue that sanctions aimed at the Iranian government should not restrict educational opportunities for ordinary citizens who have no role in state policy.
When sanctions impact education
Until recently, the General License G had provided a legal channel for certain academic exchanges and educational services despite broader US sanctions on Iran.
For many students, the suspension is the latest in a series of barriers to studying abroad.
Bahar, who is applying for PhD programs, said many Iranian students had already shifted their focus from the United Statesbecause obtaining visas had become increasingly difficult.
"American universities were our first choice because they generally offer funding for PhD programs more readily than European universities," she told DW.
Now, she said, applicants are increasingly turning to Europe and Australia, but the testing suspension has created a new hurdle.

blocks.caption: Missing a required exam can add months, or even a year, of waiting for affected applicantsImage: Rainer Unkel/Imago Images

blocks.text: "There is effectively no difference between IELTS and TOEFL for us now, because in either case, we have to leave Iran to take an English language test," Bahar said.

For students approaching admissions deadlines, postponement may not simply mean waiting a few months. It can mean missing an entire admissions cycle, losing scholarship opportunities or delaying academic plans by a year or more.

While ETS says it is examining possible ways to restore testing in Iran, there is currently no indication of when that might happen. For many applicants, the immediate choice is limited: wait without knowing when testing will return, or spend considerably more to take the same exam abroad.

articles.title: Trump ally defends Venezuela oil deal amid ‘gunpoint diplomacy’ criticism
articles.summary:
Energy secretary Chris Wright denies US seeking to ‘take’ country’s oil, saying deal is ‘transformation’ of relations

The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has denied Washington is seeking…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has denied Washington is seeking to commandeer huge quantities of Venezuelan oil, amid growing criticism of Donald Trump’s energy deal with the country’s interim leaders.
“Absolutely not,” Wright replied when asked by a CNBC journalist if the US was engaged in a “heavy-handed” attempt to “take” Venezuelan oil in violation of the South American country’s constitution.
Wright landed in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Tuesday night, four days after Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history”.

“I think we are seeing an absolutely historic transformation of both Venezuela and the relations between Venezuela and the US,” Wright said of the deal, which Trump has claimed will give the US control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil. “This is President Trump’s grand plan to replace conflict with commerce,” Wright said.

The White House says the deal will help secure US “energy dominance for the next century” as well as “purging foreign malign influence from our back yard” by excluding China and Russia from oilfields in the country with the world’s largest proven oil reserves. But there has been criticism from across the political spectrum.

The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board said Trump’s deal with Venezuela’s unelected interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, “looks less like a normal commercial transaction than it does the famous scene of US businessmen meeting with the Cuban strongman in The Godfather Part II”.

“The US government is essentially getting in bed with a foreign dictator and her favored capitalist,” the newspaper complained, in reference to Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan tycoon at the centre of the deal.

The economist Francisco Rodríguez told Democracy Now: “It’s clear that this is not a deal that any Venezuelan government would have entered into unless this country had been subject to an invasion, and unless its authorities had been held at gunpoint. So I think we’ve replaced gunboat diplomacy now for gunpoint diplomacy.”

Delcy Rodríguez was installed as interim president on 5 January, two days after the president, Nicolás Maduro, was abducted by US special forces during a predawn raid on Caracas. Trump warned Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president, she would face an even worse fate if she did not toe the US line.

Since Maduro’s capture, Rodríguez has made a series of once unthinkable concessions to US officials who their nominally socialist political movement, Chavismo, had spent years denouncing as predatory imperialists bent on stealing Venezuela’s natural resources.

On Saturday, Rodríguez claimed the oil deal had “endless” benefits and would help produce more than $209bn in revenues that could be used to improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said during a televised broadcast to the nation.

The deal has dealt a body blow to Venezuela’s political opposition who fear Trump is unlikely to push for a democratic transition or fresh presidential elections given his lucrative arrangement with Rodríguez.
“This is a game between the Trump administration and Delcy and her people,” one opposition figure lamented after the deal was unveiled.

articles.title: Pete Hegseth criticized for body-shaming Canadian cadet program members
articles.summary:
US defense secretary faced backlash for attempting to mock Canada’s armed forces amid trade war

A social media post by Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, body-shaming female members…

blocks.text: A social media post by Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, body-shaming female members of a Canadian youth development program remained online on Wednesday despite a furious backlash on both sides of the border.

On Monday night Hegseth posted on X a photograph of two people in uniform with a Canadian flag and the caption “this is real”, an apparent attempt at mocking the country’s armed forces amid the Trump administration’s trade spat with its northern neighbor.

However, the photograph was reproduced from an Instagram post by the Vernon Cadet Training Centre in British Columbia, which hosted a summer camp in July for teenagers learning adult skills on the military base.

Its subjects are not members of Canada’s front-line military, and the person whose appearance Hegseth was attempting to ridicule is likely a volunteer instructor, critics said. The girl receiving a medal is a teenager no older than 18.

The post, widely seen as part of a Trump administration “bullying campaign” over the trade war, was immediately condemned by officials in Canada and in the US. Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, called it “beneath the office” of the secretary of defense.

Responding on Tuesday to attacks on his country by US government officials, including Donald Trump’s attempt to rename Lake Ontario by executive order, Carney told reporters it was time for Washington to “start being serious” about efforts to deescalate trade tensions.
“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” he said.

David Eby, the premier of British Columbia, echoed Carney’s sentiment. “It tells you everything you need to know about the amateur-hour, distracted, bizarre leadership that Americans are being subjected to,” he said.

The civilian Army Cadet League of Canada accused Hegseth of online harassment. “Directing derogatory commentary toward youth who are actively working to better themselves and serve their communities is unacceptable,” the group said in a statement.
Adam Kinzinger, the former Republican US congressman and a military veteran, was even more outspoken in a post on X.

“Literally they’re kids. This is a cadet program and our ass hat of a Secdef is making fun of children,” he wrote. “MAGA [make America great again] males are betas who have to punch down to feel big.”
Ruben Gallego, the Democratic Arizona senator and a former marine, called the post “stupid” and “disrespectful”.

Danny O’Regan, a Canadian veteran writing on X, also criticized the post. “The Secretary of Defence is body shaming cadet groups,” he said. “This is not a military unit. They are kids looking for adventure, test themselves and align themselves with the values of service. Don’t be a Pete.”
The Pentagon, meanwhile, defended Hegseth. On Tuesday, Jacob Bliss, the defense department’s deputy press secretary, said: “The X post speaks for itself.”

The incident comes as Hegseth faces increasing pressure on several fronts. The US army chief Dan Driscoll resigned this week, reportedly after months of internal clashes with Hegseth. Democrats have accused the defense secretary of having “hollowed out” the military’s senior ranks.

On Wednesday, Iran accused the US of a “war crime” after five people were killed, including a four-year-old child, and dozens injured in a reported missile strike on a wedding at a home in the south of the country.

The ongoing Iran war has also left the US with a “beyond critical” shortage of missile interceptors, the Associated Press reported, sparking fears among Nato allies of increasing vulnerability to a potential Russian military attack.
Hegseth has previously been critical of body shapes in the US military, telling senior commanders in Virginia last year that “fat troops are tiring to look at”.
Ordering military officials to crack down on a lack of physical fitness, he said: “It’s tiring to look out at combat formations, or really any formation, and see fat troops.”

articles.title: DOH seeks P358.8-B budget for 2027, needs more for PhilHealth, hospitals
articles.summary: The Department of Health (DOH) has proposed a P358.8 billion budget for 2027, which aims to provide affordable and accessible healthcare to Filipinos. But the agency said it needs close to P200…

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 10:43pm
The Department of Health (DOH) has proposed a P358.8 billion budget for 2027, which aims to provide affordable and accessible healthcare to Filipinos.
But the agency said it needs close to P200 billion more for the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) and hospital operations.
During the House budget hearing on Wednesday, Secretary Edwin Mercado said the proposed 2027 budget is 21% lower than the P448 billion appropriated budget in 2026.
He provided a breakdown of the budget under the following Unified National Agenda for Health (UNA):

items: Health schools, workplaces, and communities (P60.5 billion)
Functional primary care system (P29.1 billion)
Quality and efficient hospitals (P207.3 billion)
Information technology transformation (P2.7 billion)
Strong institutions and health workforce (P54.2 billion)

blocks.text: Mercado said P117 billion was allotted for Personnel Services (PS), P218 billion for Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE), and P19 billion for Capital Outlay (CO)
According to Mercado, the three priority items of DOH’s 2027 proposed budget are PhilHealth, the Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP), and the operations of DOH hospitals.
To fund its planned programs, the DOH is seeking the following additional funding:

items: PhilHealth: P170 billion
HFEP: P15 billion
DOH hospital operations: P12 billion

blocks.text: Based on our projections of the actual benefit payments for indirect members ay kulang po iyong P74 billion. Ang initial projection po is P244 billion," Mercado said.
He added the additional funding for HFEP and operations of DOH hospitals, including regional hospitals, will help local government units provide for the health needs of the people. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: House backs longer VP Duterte trial days to hasten proceedings
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — House leaders and impeachment prosecutors favor proposals for longer trial days, even whole-day sessions, for Vice President Sara Z. Duterte’s impeachment case to help both…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — House leaders and impeachment prosecutors favor proposals for longer trial days, even whole-day sessions, for Vice President Sara Z. Duterte’s impeachment case to help both prosecution and defense present their evidence faster before the Senate gets busy with the 2027 national budget.
“We welcome that. We know that there’s a time element there, Deputy Speaker Francisco Paolo Ortega V at a press briefing on Wednesday, the 21st day of the trial.

Ortega, who endorsed one of the complaints that led to Duterte’s impeachment and Senate trial, acknowledged that the proposed arrangement would mean longer days but could shorten the overall proceedings.

The Senate impeachment court, as the presiding officer, Sen. Francis Escudero, said toward the end of Wednesday’s proceedings, is looking at starting whole-day proceedings at 10 a.m., potentially continuing into the evening to accommodate two or three witnesses in a day.
Escudero laid out a tentative calendar covering Oct. 1 and 2, Oct. 5 to 9, and Oct. 12 to 15 before the proceedings give way to Senate committee hearings on the proposed national budget.

The trial could resume on Nov. 9 and 16 during the period for plenary budget deliberations, with a more regular schedule returning on Nov. 23. The calendar remains subject to final agreement among the senator-judges.
According to Rep. Terry Ridon, House prosecutor and Committee on Public Accounts chair, said the prosecution is prepared for the more intensive schedule.
He estimated that the prosecution could present as many as three witnesses in a whole-day session, depending on the length of direct and cross-examinations and questioning by senator-judges.
He said he was hoping that the arrangement would speed up not the presenstation of both sides.

Former Rep. Robert Ace Barbers, House impeachment team adviser, said agreements between the two sides on stipulated facts and evidence could further cut trial time by eliminating unnecessary testimony.
One possible arrangement concerns former Department of Education (DepEd) special disbursing officer Edward Fajarda, whom the prosecution has sought as a witness.

Rep. Gerville Luistro, the lead House prosecutor and Committee on Justice chair, told the impeachment court that the prosecution was exploring whether Fajarda’s testimony could be dispensed with through stipulations with the defense, given his medical condition.
Luistro stressed that any agreement would have to preserve the prosecution’s ability to establish its charge.
According to Barbers, said such moves could bring the proceedings sooner to the point where the senator-judges can decide the impeachment charges.

The prosecution is currently presenting evidence on the first impeachment article, which accuses Duterte of misusing P612.5 million in confidential funds — P500 million at the Office of the Vice President and P112.5 million at DepEd during her tenure as education secretary. /atm

articles.title: Highlights: Day 21 of Sara Duterte impeachment trial | Sept. 2, 2026
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Day 21 of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial on Wednesday centered on the Senate impeachment court’s declaration of her own defense counsel, former…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Day 21 of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial on Wednesday centered on the Senate impeachment court’s declaration of her own defense counsel, former Education Undersecretary Michael Poa, as a hostile witness for the prosecution, with presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero granting private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa Jr. the right to ask leading questions.

Poa, who served as DepEd chief of staff from 2022 to 2024, was called to testify on the department’s disbursement of P112.5 million in confidential funds during Duterte’s tenure as education secretary.

The examination opened with immediate friction. Tolosa’s offer of testimony, which ran to 13 points, was dismissed by defense lead counsel Sheila Sison as sounding “like rhetoric aimed at providing drama” in the proceedings.
The impeachment court itself scolded Tolosa for engaging in what it called “intramurals” with the defense and wasting time after he opened by asking Poa whether he is a competent lawyer.

Prosecution spokesperson Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong and public prosecutor Rep. Joel Chua later said that Tolosa’s aggressive style reflects his background as a trial lawyer and is a deliberate strategy, not a liability.

Among the substantive admissions Poa made under examination: he confirmed that not a single peso from DepEd’s confidential funds went to the Armed Forces of the Philippines for its Youth Leadership Summits in 2023, corroborating testimony from an Army officer the previous day.

Poa also admitted that he only learned about the practice of handing over confidential funds to Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group officials during a House of Representatives hearing in October 2024, not while serving inside DepEd.

In a separate development that could reshape the trial’s remaining schedule, Chua announced the prosecution panel is considering dropping the bribery article against Duterte, similar to what prosecutors did during the impeachment trial of former Chief Justice Renato Corona.
Chua was careful to say the decision is not yet final and that the bribery case is not weak, explaining that the panel is evaluating dropping it purely for efficiency.

Lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro added that the panel may also forgo presenting the testimony of ailing former DepEd special disbursing officer Edward Fajarda, but only if the defense agrees to accept stipulations in lieu of live testimony.

On scheduling, presiding officer Escudero informed the court of a proposal to hold whole-day trial sessions in October, running from 10 a.m. into the early evening, before suspending proceedings in November to give way to deliberations on the 2027 national budget.

The Senate separately approved a resolution allowing its Committee on Finance to conduct budget hearings simultaneously with plenary sessions on Monday to Wednesday afternoons, after morning impeachment proceedings conclude. /dp

articles.title: No more realistic simulations in school safety drills, says DepEd
articles.summary: The Department of Education (DepEd) on Wednesday said that there will be no more realistic simulations in the planned school safety drills.

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 10:22pm
The Department of Education (DepEd) on Wednesday said that there will be no more realistic simulations during school safety drills, after experts warned these may have negative psychological effects.
“Ipinagbabawal po natin ang anumang simulation na parang totoong insidente. Kailangan din po ang pahintulot ng magulang bago makilahok ang mga learner,” DepEd said in a Facebook post.
(We are forbidding any simulation of realistic incidents. The parents also need to give their permission before a learner could participate.)
The DepEd said that it is collaborating with medical and mental health partners so that the drills are age-appropriate and sensitive to trauma.
“Our goal is to prepare [the students] with confidence, not fear,” the DepEd said.
The DepEd is set to implement a nationwide school safety drill on Thursday, September 3, after being postponed due to these concerns.

The school safety drills come in light of a string of school-based violence, with a school shooting in Tacloban killing four students. A few months later, a shooting in a Zamboanga high school left two students dead, including the shooter. — Jean Mangaluz/BM, GMA News

articles.title: Guinea-Bissau referendum tests democratic future
articles.summary: Following voter approval of a constitutional change that expands presidential powers, Guinea-Bissau faces renewed debate over legitimacy, civilian rule and democratic safeguards.

image.caption: Guinea-Bissau has voted in support of expanding presidential powers and trimming the country's legislatureImage: Samba Balde/AFP

blocks.text: Guinea-Bissau is facing a new political test after voters approved a referendum on a proposed charter that will give the president the power to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and government ministers, while reducing the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65..
Sunday's referendum came less than 10 months after a coup in which the military seized power and three months ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled to take place on December 6.
The transitional authorities say the constitutional reform is intended to bring stability to the impoverished West African country and prepare it for a return to civilian rule.
Victory claimed, legitimacy disputed

On Monday, the National Transitional Council claimed victory for the "Yes" camp. "The majority of those who went to vote voted yes. In conclusion, the victory of yes is guaranteed," council spokesman Alberto Pinto Pereira said.

On Tuesday, the National Electoral Commission (NEC) confirmed victory for the "Yes" side, saying it had received 70% of the vote, compared with 30% for the "No" camp, and that voter turnout exceeded 50%.

NEC chairperson Carmen Izaura Lobo described the Guinea-Bissau referendum as a success, due to the "organizational capacity, professionalism and dedication" of teams on the ground, Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported.
Lobo praised the "transparency" and "credibility" of the process.

blocks.caption: The army took power in Guinea-Bissau in November 2025 just days after a presidential electionImage: Patrick Meinhardt/AFP

blocks.text: The opposition, however, says the referendum has no legal basis because it was organized by institutions created after the military coup. It had called on voters to boycott the vote.

Domingos Simoes Pereira, leader of the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), who was detained after the military coup and later released into house arrest, rejected the referendum as legally invalid.
Speaking to DW from Portugal, he said the institutions established by the military have no democratic mandate to rewrite Guinea-Bissau's constitution.
The PAIGC and other opposition groups maintain that the vote is a continuation of the November coup.
Fernando Dias Costa, the main challenger to then-President Umaro Sissoco Embalo in the November 2025 presidential election that was annulled by the military, disputed the official turnout figures.
"Very few citizens took part in this referendum," he said, noting that the people have sent an important message that must not be ignored.
"They are not prepared to simply accept political changes that are clearly unconstitutional and have not been publicly debated."
More power for the president

The proposed constitution would move Guinea-Bissau toward a much stronger presidential system. The president would appoint and dismiss the prime minister and government ministers and would have the power to dissolve parliament.

Supporters argue that the existing political system has repeatedly led to conflicts between the president, government and parliament. They say stronger presidential authority would create greater stability.
Bubacar Ture, head of the Guinea-Bissau Human Rights League, told DW that the draft constitution would lead to "an excessive concentration of power in the person of the president."

He argues that the proposed system could make parliamentary elections less meaningful because the president would have much greater control over the government regardless of the parliamentary balance.

Ture also criticizes the way the constitution was drafted. "No one was consulted," he said. "Neither the parties nor civil-society organizations, nor traditional or religious authorities. Everything was produced in secret."
He is particularly concerned that provisions concerning constitutional oversight have been removed. In his view, this would weaken the rule of law.

Supporters and critics view the referendum through the lens of the political crisis that began in November 2025, when both former President Umaro Sissoco Embalo and opposition candidate Fernando Dias claimed victory in a disputed presidential election.
Before the results could be officially announced, the military seized power.

Embalo was briefly detained and subsequently left the country. His current whereabouts are unclear, and speculation continues over whether he retains influence over the military leadership or could seek a political comeback.
The referendum in Guinea-Bissau also reflects a broader trend across parts of Africa, where constitutional reforms have sparked debate over the concentration of presidential power.
In recent years, countries including Togo, Chad, Uganda, Zimbabwe and Guinea have seen leaders pursue constitutional changes that critics say strengthen executive authority.
What comes next in Guinea-Bissau?

Despite the "Yes" vote, opposition and civil society groups continue to challenge the legitimacy of the process. The referendum also takes place against a backdrop of longstanding political instability.
Guinea-Bissau has experienced repeated coups and attempted coups since independence, contributing to recurring periods of political instability.
The December elections are intended to mark the return to civilian rule. But opposition criticism of Sunday's referendum has raised further questions about how difficult that transition may be.
A key point of contention is whether the new constitutional order will strengthen democratic institutions or concentrate more power in the presidency.

articles.title: India rejects Hague ruling on Indus waters: What's next?
articles.summary: By rejecting an international arbitration panel's ruling, New Delhi has cast fresh doubt on the future of the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty.

image.caption: The 1960 Indus Waters Treaty governs the use of water from six rivers flowing through India and Pakistan [FILE: May 29, 2021]Image: PPI/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Indus Waters Treaty is facing a fresh dispute after India rejected a Hague-based Court of Arbitration ruling that the 1960 agreement remains in force.
Pakistan has welcomed the decision and says India remains bound by the treaty.
India's Ministry of External Affairs described the tribunal as a "so-called Court of Arbitration" that was "illegally constituted."

It said the body had been established by the World Bank in breach of the treaty and that India "categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body."
"The Court of Arbitration has no jurisdiction whatsoever to pronounce on India's sovereign decisions," the ministry said.
What to know about the treaty
The Indus Waters Treaty, brokered by the World Bank, governs the use of water from six rivers flowing through India and Pakistan.

The agreement largely gives India rights over three eastern rivers while Pakistan has rights over the western Indus, Jhelum and Chenab. India is allowed to use the western rivers for specified purposes including certain hydroelectric projects.
India, Pakistan could be ready to talk 1 year after standoff
The treaty had endured wars and prolonged periods of intense hostility between the two nuclear-armed neighbors.

But India placed the treaty in abeyance in April 2025 as part of a package of diplomatic and economic measures announced after a deadly attack in India-administered Kashmir killed 26 people, mostly tourists.
New Delhi accused Islamabad of backing the attack. Pakistan denied the charges.
High stakes for Pakistan
Millions of people in Pakistan depend on the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab rivers for drinking water, farming and daily life.
The rivers are particularly important to Punjab and Sindh provinces, whose agriculture is central to the country's food supply and rural economy.
After India's move to suspend the treaty, Pakistan approached the court in The Hague over the status of the accord.
Pakistani officials have repeatedly warned that any attempt to deny the country its share of the waters of rivers flowing across the border would be treated as an act of war.
Ajay Bisaria, a former Indian high commissioner to Pakistan, said India had challenged the treaty on both political and legal grounds.
"Politically, abeyance hands India a new point of leverage, one more lever to press Pakistan into changing its behavior on cross-border terrorism," Bisaria told DW.
He also pointed to India's earlier requests to renegotiate the treaty, citing climate change, new dam-building technology and the deterioration of relations between the two countries.
India chose to put the treaty in abeyance rather than formally abrogate it. Bisaria said the Hague ruling would not change that course.
"The tribunal will not alter this trajectory," he said. "India's course on the Indus Waters Treaty is set. The treaty will not be revived in its present form."
A 'frozen conflict': India-Pakistan tensions persist
The legal battle
Pakistan has taken the opposite view.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said the ruling "decisively rejects" India's attempt to place the treaty in abeyance and reaffirmed that it remains "fully in force and binding on both parties."
"The Award vindicates Pakistan's consistent position that a binding international treaty cannot be unilaterally suspended or set aside," Dar said in a post on X.
He added that India must comply with its obligations under the treaty and with binding decisions arising from its dispute settlement mechanisms.
Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani political scientist and defense analyst, said the ruling may be difficult to implement if India refuses to accept it.
"The arbitration court's ruling may not be implementable because the court doesn't have the force to do so," Siddiqa told DW.
But she said the decision gave Pakistan an advantage as a lower riparian state.
"It does give Pakistan a moral edge," said Siddiqa, a senior fellow in the Department of War Studies at King's College London.
She also questioned what India's rejection of the ruling could mean for its international position, particularly given that India has accepted international legal decisions in other disputes.
"This is not just an issue of pure military power but an international standing where India will not be able to justify its position to the world any longer," she said.
Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, a South Asia analyst and founder of the Mantraya think tank, said the ruling did not materially change India's position.
"The Permanent Court of Arbitration is an administrative body, not a conventional sovereign court with enforcement capabilities," D'Souza told DW.

"In this particular case, India chose not to participate in the proceedings. This allows it not to recognize the tribunal's rulings. Therefore, it has no enforceable constraint on India and nothing changes materially for New Delhi," she said.
A dispute over the rules
India and Pakistan have disagreed for years over the interpretation of the treaty, particularly over Indian hydropower projects on rivers allocated primarily to Pakistan.

Uttam Kumar Sinha, a senior fellow at the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and author of "Trial by Water," said India is now no longer merely contesting the interpretation of the treaty, but rather "contesting the authority of the treaty's dispute-settlement mechanism itself."
New Delhi maintains that the tribunal was improperly constituted and that its decisions have no legal effect on India.
Sinha describes the emerging contest as "lawfare," with Pakistan likely to use the ruling in international forums and frame the dispute around treaty obligations and international law.
India threatens to dry out Pakistan
The limits of India's leverage
The practical implications will also depend on what India does with its infrastructure on the western rivers.
D'Souza said the treaty's abeyance gave India more political and psychological leverage than an immediate ability to alter the flow of the rivers.

"To effectively stop or significantly alter the flows of the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab rivers, substantial infrastructure like dams, canals and large storage systems would be required, and such structures do not currently exist," said D'Souza.
"Furthermore, geographical and technical constraints limit India's capacity to block these rivers."
Sinha echoed this view.
"India cannot simply 'turn off' the western rivers," he said.

Large storage and diversion projects would take years or decades, require substantial investment and involve difficult construction in the mountainous Himalayan region, as well as environmental and domestic approvals.
"There is a significant gap between India's potential strategic freedom on the western rivers and its actual physical capacity to change water flows," Sinha said.

articles.title: Tumbler Ridge mass shooting victims file 30 new lawsuits against OpenAI
articles.summary:
The company says it prioritizes safety, but suits allege its ChatGPT bot induced shooter to carry out attack in Canada

OpenAI…

blocks.text: OpenAI faces 30 new lawsuits filed on behalf of victims of the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting.

The suits, filed on Wednesday, allege the company’s ChatGPT chatbot induced the shooter to carry out the attack in rural Canada in February, in which eight people were killed and dozens more wounded – most of them children.

“These were people who really endured just total hell that day,” Jay Edelson, the lead lawyer representing the plaintiffs, said in an interview. “Young kids who watched their teachers die, watched friends die and thought they were going to get shot and killed.”

These new lawsuits, filed in federal court for the northern district of California, come after Edelson filed seven initial suits in April – bringing the total number of cases against OpenAI for the Tumbler Ridge shooting to 37. All of the suits allege that the violent intentions of the shooter, identified as 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, were well-known to the senior leadership of OpenAI, which failed to report her to the authorities.

Employees on the company’s safety team had flagged the shooter’s account to executives eight months before the attack, describing her in internal messages as “a credible and specific threat of gun violence against real people”, according to court filings. OpenAI banned her account, but she was able to quickly create a new one, the suits claim.
The lawsuits accuse OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman, of negligence, aiding and abetting a mass shooting and product liability.

Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, said in a statement that he thinks about what happened at Tumbler Ridge every day and that the company works hard to create standards for reporting cases to law enforcement.

“The professionals working on these teams choose to do this incredibly difficult work because they care so deeply about keeping people safe,” Kwon said. “They come to work every day knowing that they may have to make a decision that they’ll think about for the rest of their lives.”

A groundswell of cases have been brought against OpenAI and other tech companies alleging that their chatbots exacerbate mental health crises and provoke violent acts. OpenAI has been sued in seven separate cases that blame ChatGPT for acting as a “suicide coach”. A criminal investigation and civil lawsuit, brought by the attorney general of Florida, accuses OpenAI of concealing safety risks after a mass shooting at Florida State University.

The shooting in Tumbler Ridge took place in a secondary school, shortly after Van Rootselaar killed her mother and 11-year-old brother in their family home. The new tranche of lawsuits includes cases from the family of one girl who was shot, along with the principal, teachers and students.
The attack was one of the deadliest mass shootings in Canadian history. In the aftermath, questions swirled in the small British Columbia town about how it could have happened.

Edelson singled out Chris Lehane, who is OpenAI’s head of global affairs and a former member of Bill Clinton’s administration who specialized in opposition research. He said Lehane was one of the people who received warnings from the company’s safety team but overruled repeated appeals to alert the authorities. That decision was also sanctioned by Altman, the lawsuits allege.
after newsletter promotion
“What’s clear is that OpenAI over and over has made decisions to hide how dangerous their platform is because they’re worried about regulation and public pushback,” Edelson said.

In response, OpenAI’s Kwon said: “It is absolutely false to say Chris Lehane was involved with our original referral decision … It’s also completely untrue to say that the people at the center of these challenging decisions do not prioritize safety, or that there are ‘political’ or ‘public relations’ factors at play.”

When the first seven lawsuits were filed against OpenAI in April, the company published a blog post about its “commitment to safety”. Altman also sent a letter to the Tumbler Ridge community apologizing for not notifying Canadian police about what OpenAI knew regarding the shooter’s potential threat.
“While I know words can never be enough, I believe an apology is necessary to recognize the harm and irreversible loss your community has suffered,” Altman wrote.

David Eby, the British Columbia premier, posted the letter to social media with the comment: “The apology is necessary, and yet grossly insufficient for the devastation done to the families of Tumbler Ridge.”

articles.title: Michael Poa: Impeachment proceedings were fair today
articles.summary: Defense counsel Michael Poa called the impeachment proceedings on Wednesday "fair" after he appeared as a witness and was grilled by the prosecution throughout.

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 9:22pm
Defense counsel Michael Poa called the impeachment proceedings on Wednesday "fair" after he appeared as a witness and was grilled by the prosecution throughout.
Poa took the witness stand as Vice President Sara Duterte’s former chief of staff during her stint as the secretary of the Department of Education.
In a short statement to the media after the day;s proceedings, Poa said that it was better for him to remain neutral.

“I am okay. I just wanted to thank the prosecution, si Attorney Tolosa, I think naman everything that happened today was quite fair, I would like to thank him for that,” Poa said in a mix of English and Filipino.
He also extended his thanks to the defense’s lead counsel Sheila Sison for managing their side.
Prosecution counsel Benjamin Tolosa Jr. and Sison had a heated exchange in the impeachment court on the 21st day of Duterte’s impeachment.
One of these exchanges included Tolosa calling Poa a “lawyer that knew nothing.” Sison objected, moving to strike it off the record.
Tolosa later clarified that the context would show that he meant "walang alam" in relation to the confidential fund use.

articles.title: Teachers, students file new wave of lawsuits against OpenAI over Tumbler Ridge shooting
articles.summary: New legal filings describe the horror students and teachers experienced on Feb. 10 and include new details of OpenAI's alleged negligence in preventing the shooting.

image.caption: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote a letter of apology to the community of Tumbler Ridge in April for failing to alert RCMP about the account of the Tumbler Ridge shooter. (Jason Redmond/AFP)

blocks.text: British Columbia
New legal filings describe the horror students and teachers experienced on Feb. 10 and include new details of OpenAI's alleged negligence in preventing the shooting.
30 new complaints to be filed alleging tech giant behind ChatGPT could have prevented tragedy
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 02, 2026 9:13 AM EDT | Last Updated: 8 hours ago
Lawyers representing victims and survivors of the Tumbler Ridge school shooting say they are filing 30 new lawsuits against OpenAI in U.S. federal court in California.

Edelson PC, a U.S. firm that specializes in class actions, says the new plaintiffs include educators, a principal and students, including siblings who were separated during the Feb. 10 attack in northern B.C.
The tragedy left eight victims dead, including six children, along with the 18-year-old shooter.
The lawsuits describe the horror they experienced that day and include new details of OpenAI's alleged negligence in preventing the shooting.
"The survivors — students, teachers, and parents alike — are living with physical and psychological injuries that will never fully heal," one lawsuit reads.
Teachers, students file 30 new lawsuits against OpenAI over Tumbler Ridge shooting
The new claims have been filed in California, where OpenAI is headquartered, and where seven other cases against the company have been filed by families of the shooting victims.

Edelson PC says OpenAI's safety team repeatedly asked to notify authorities about Jesse Van Rootselaar's activity on ChatGPT eight months before the tragedy, which allegedly included planning violent scenarios.

items: Unsealed documents reveal details of RCMP's response, investigation into Tumbler Ridge shooting

blocks.text: But the lawsuits allege those appeals were overruled by Chris Lehane, OpenAI's head of global affairs.
LISTEN | Lawyer representing victims says OpenAI failed Tumbler Ridge:
Daybreak South9:34 Tumbler Ridge students, educators file more lawsuits against Open AI

They claim OpenAI's leadership "ignored its own safety staff and refused to alert police," yet acted to safeguard its own offices after learning of threats to employees three months before the Tumbler Ridge shooting.
The lawsuits accuse OpenAI of "choosing profit over the lives of the children of Tumbler Ridge" as it prepares to become a publicly traded company.
OpenAI responds
Jason Kwon, chief strategy officer at OpenAI, said in a response posted on X that he thinks of the tragedy at Tumbler Ridge daily.
He said the company has teams that "work hard to define standards and processes for when to report cases to law enforcement and to apply those standards to really difficult and complex situations."

"They work continuously to identify potential warning signals of serious violence, while also protecting the privacy and security of the vast majority of the more than one billion users who use our tools responsibly."
Teardown of Tumbler Ridge school begins

Kwon said it was frustrating to see what he said were false claims made in the suits about his teams and individuals not involved in the process. Kwon said it is "absolutely false to say Chris Lehane was involved with our original referral decision, or that our investigators report to him in any way."
"It's also completely untrue to say that the people at the center of these challenging decisions do not prioritize safety, or that there are 'political' or 'public relations' factors at play."
The company previously acknowledged that it banned Van Rootselaar's account in June 2025, but said the activity did not meet the "higher threshold required" to refer it to police at the time.
Altman apology just 'crocodile tears,' lawsuit needed to hold OpenAI accountable: lawyer
CEO Sam Altman has apologized to the Tumbler Ridge community and says the company has updated its protocols.
The B.C. government is also planning legal action against OpenAI, and has since demolished the site of Tumbler Ridge Secondary School.

items: Tumbler Ridge school demolition 'new chapter' in recovery after shooting, residents say
Feds announce $4M in new funding supports for Tumbler Ridge after mass shooting

blocks.text: 12-year-old victim recovering
The first set of lawsuits filed against the tech giant included the family of Maya Gebala, a 12-year-old student who was shot in the head and survived the shooting.
In a Facebook post Monday, Cia Edmonds shared a video of her daughter that showed her relearning to speak, saying "mom" into the camera before cracking a smile.
"Tears of awe as I watch her crawl out of the rubble that her mind lives in," Edmonds wrote. "One step at a time. She shows me, more and more what miracles look like."
Lawyer wants chat logs released
Jay Edelson, CEO of Edelson PC, told CBC's Daybreak South one aim of the lawsuits is to have Van Rootselaar's chat-logs with ChatGPT released.
He said OpenAI has so far refused calls to make the logs public, a choice he believes indicates their contents may not work in the tech company's favour.
"If, in anyway, it helped them they would do that," he said.

The complainants also want to view internal OpenAI documents showing why Canadian authorities weren't alerted about Van Rootselaar's plans, according to John Rice of Rice Parsons Leoni & Elliott, Canadian co-counsel for the suits.

He said the families are seeking historic compensatory and punitive damages to penalize OpenAI, if the allegations are proven true, and "to express society's condemnation and outrage over such egregious corporate malfeasance."

Rice said they hope to prevent another AI-facilitated mass shooting by reforming major platform safety, including with mandatory law enforcement reporting for "all foreseeable and imminent acts of violence."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Matt Preprost is a reporter with CBC British Columbia based in Fort St. John. He has covered the B.C Peace region and Northern Rockies since 2013. Email him at fsj@cbc.ca
