articles.title: EU and Nato vow to step up pressure on Russia after 'new escalation' in Germany
articles.summary: Russia is accused of growing increasingly reckless after Berlin blamed Russia for a failed drone attack on Leipzig airport.

blocks.text: The heads of Nato and the European Commission have warned that Russia is growing increasingly reckless and vowed to respond to a "new normal".

"Leipzig marks a new escalation on European Union soil directly attributed to Russia," said Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, a day after Germany blamed Russia for a failed drone attack last month on Leipzig airport.

"We have to step up and that means being ready to respond to Russia's recklessness faster and better," von der Leyen said. Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said the whole alliance, which includes the US, stood "in full solidarity with Germany".
Russia has rejected German accusations that a drone carrying explosives deliberately targeted a Ukrainian cargo plane on 4 August.
The drone was defused by a robot at Leipzig/Halle airport and a second drone is thought to have collided with another cargo plane.
A third drone was reportedly found 10 days later at the airport, which is an important Nato hub and is regularly used by Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft.
It was not until Tuesday that the German government said police investigations and intelligence finding had proved that Russia was behind the incidents.
The interior minister said that the drone's configuration, components, explosives and detonator were all known from other Russian hybrid operations.

Two suspects have reportedly been identified in the Leipzig attack, including a Belarusian with a Russian passport who entered on a tourist visa, and another with Latvian and Russian passports who arrived by plane in Berlin and flew out two days before the failed attack.
Von der Leyen was clear in her statement that the Leipzig attack had involved "military-grade material carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil".
"We will not tolerate it," she said.

While she was meeting Rutte in Brussels, EU foreign ministers had gathered at Wicklow in Ireland, where France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said action could be taken on a European level against Russia's so-called "shadow fleet" of ships carrying oil and other cargo aimed at avoiding EU sanctions.
Barrot and fellow ministers from Belgium and the Netherlands said they had summoned Russian ambassadors in protest at the attack.
Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said it was obvious that Russia saw no political cost in its hybrid operations against European allies.
The Leipzig attack was part of a broader pattern of increasingly dangerous incidents, including drones and interference with critical infrastructure, von der Leyen said.

Mark Rutte added there had been increased risk to Europeans from drones and missiles crossing into countries on the Alliance's eastern flank, and there had been more "malign activities targeting our territory directly, whether it is fires set in factories producing defence equipment for Ukraine or indeed the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig".
Several acts of suspected sabotage have been reported in Germany in the past 24 hours alone, including two attacks on electricity substations, one in the east and one in the west near Cologne.

Although authorities do not yet know who was behind the incidents, North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul said an attack that targeted power lines at Bergheim in western Germany was deliberate and whoever had carried out was attacking the country as a whole.
"We are investigating two possibilities: sabotage directed by a foreign state and left-wing extremism," he said.
Police said six launching devices had been found in a field.
Von der Leyen said sanctions had already been used to deter Russia, and EU foreign ministers were discussing further ways of "cutting deeper in Russia's war chest".

The EU has already agreed to loan Ukraine €90bn (£77bn), and von der Leyen said Kyiv had asked for billions of extra euros in funding from Kyiv to help pay for PAC-3 air defence missiles. Work was already taking place on a joint Europe-Ukraine Freyja anti-ballistic missile defence project, she added.

She promised that Europe and Nato would just maintain pressure on Moscow but "we will increase it and we will not stop, not until Russia stops bombing and killing innocent children, men and children in Ukraine".

'I guess what the public should understand... is our objections and the number of our objections will always depend on the questions from the other party,' deputy defense spokesperson Justin Nicol Gular says
It took 21 trial days to have defense lead counsel Sheila Sison on the floor as the lawyer in charge of cross-examining a prosecution witness.
The public and media alike only knew about her appearance on Wednesday morning, September 2, when she announced that she would cross-examine fellow defense lawyer Michael Poa herself.

It makes sense, right? Poa is one of the defense’s major assets so he deserves a big gun like Sison. Plus, prosecution spokesperson Jay Tolosa, a seasoned litigator who has handled major cases, was the one assigned for the direct examination.

Tolosa came in hot with his presentation. He sought to establish that Poa prepared the Department of Education’s (DepEd) reply to questions on the confidential funds use, yet the former DepEd chief of staff was unaware that security personnel handled the said money.

But Sison showed dominance. She called Tolosa’s opening statement mere rhetoric. She also took offense at the prosecution’s phrase — “abogadong walang alam” (a lawyer who doesn’t know anything) — when it referred to Poa.

blocks.caption: Sheila Sison and her string of objections that rattled the prosecution

blocks.text: “When I said, ‘ang abogadong walang alam,’ what I meant was, in Congress, he repeatedly said he knew totally nothing about the use and liquidation of the confidential funds. Context is very important,” said Tolosa.

“I am certain that the counsel has in his vocabulary other terms for ‘ang abogadong walang alam.’ If that was his explanation, he could have simply said that the witness has no personal knowledge. And that would have been more respectful and more apt, if that was the intention, as he had said,” said the lead defense counsel in response.
The rough start spelled how the entire trial would go. Sison and Tolosa went on to have heated exchanges from time to time — sometimes partnered with snarky remarks.
The two clashed again when Tolosa cut off Poa when he was responding to the former’s question about rewards related to surveillance activities. Sison insisted that Poa be allowed to answer the query.

For the duration of Tolosa’s direct examination, Sison fired objections numerous times. The lead defense counsel objected to the prosecution’s use of the word “whatever” in a question. She raised different objections on several grounds, like for being misleading or argumentative. Presiding officer Chiz Escudero sustained most of these objections.

blocks.caption: Tolosa turns up the heat in the courtroom, sparks hot exchanges

blocks.text: Sison’s continued objections obviously affected Tolosa’s examination. The prosecutor, at multiple times, flipped the documents in his hand. There were moments of dead air, which presiding officer Chiz Escudero used to remind counsels about court matters.

“That is never our intention…. I hope the public understands by the end of the day, we have high respect for each other. And we are all aware that we are merely doing our job,” deputy defense spokesperson Justin Nicol Gular explained when asked about observations regarding Sison’s objections.
Point well taken. The defense was just doing its job which is to raise objections if there are matters that are objectionable.
But was Sison’s demeanor a strategy? A tactic to rattle the prosecution?

blocks.caption: Sheila Sison and her string of objections that rattled the prosecution

blocks.text: “I guess what the public should understand… is our objections and the number of our objections will always depend on the questions from the other party. [If they are] objectionable, we raise it and we respect the decision of the presiding officer to sustain it or not,” Gular explained in a mix of Filipino and English.
“So it’s not our strategy to raise voluminous objections on a certain day. It just depends on what comes and what arises during the trial,” he added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Pisay students develop management platform for school emergencies
articles.summary: Three junior high school students from Philippine Science High School-Caraga create Ligtas Skwela, an innovative online platform for tracking student safety during emergencies, winning top honors at…

blocks.text: EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT. From left to right, Ligtas Skwela project leader Kush Shekar, developer Vic Andrei Hernando, and market research head Lorenzo Pariñas prepare for their five-minute presentation at the Startup Technology Pitching competition on August 28, 2026.
Patrick James Lee C. Alfonso, DOST-STII

Three junior high school students from Philippine Science High School-Caraga create Ligtas Skwela, an innovative online platform for tracking student safety during emergencies, winning top honors at a regional tech competition

items: Three junior high school students from the Philippine Science High School-Caraga created an online platform called Ligtas Skwela to help schools track students during emergencies like fires and earthquakes.
The platform features two interfaces: Teacher Mode for reporting classroom conditions and Commander Mode for administrators to monitor classroom statuses and student whereabouts.
Ligtas Skwela won first place in a technology competition and the team plans to offer it through a subscription model, while also preparing to apply for a patent.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Three junior high school students from the Philippine Science High School-Caraga have developed an online platform designed to help schools track students during fires, earthquakes, and other emergencies within the school.
Called Ligtas Skwela, the platform is accessible online, allowing teachers and school administrators an overview of classrooms and students during an emergency.

The project won first place in the student category of the Startup Technology Pitching Competition during the Department of Science and Technology’s Regional Science, Technology, and Innovation Week in Caraga, held from August 27 to 29.
The team consists of project leader Kush Shekar, software developer Lorenzo Pariñas, and market research head Vic Andrei Hernando.
Pariñas said recent school emergencies, including the shooting at Ateneo de Zamboanga University, prompted the students to think about how schools account for students during a crisis.
“We’ve noticed that sometimes, in the system, they tend to not focus on the students and where they are in school,” Pariñas said.
Ligtas Skwela has two interfaces: Teacher Mode and Commander Mode.

Teachers can use the platform to report the condition of their classes, while Commander Mode provides administrators with information on classrooms, teachers, and their status, including whether a room is secure or whether people need medical assistance.
Instead of relying only on head counts, the system tracks students by name, allowing administrators to determine who is missing, Shekar said.

The developers said the website is functional but has so far only been tested on their campus. The current version requires an internet connection, although the team plans to develop an offline version.
They also plan to incorporate physical hardware, including buttons that could be used to conduct drills and trigger alarms.

The students envision offering Ligtas Skwela through a subscription model. Based on their current projections, it would cost P30,000 annually for a school with 1,000 students, or about P30 per student.
The team, mentored by engineer Lyndon Bermoy, was the only high school group among the nine finalists in the competition.
The students are also preparing to apply for a patent for the platform. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Police exhume body of former Czechoslovak foreign minister Jan Masaryk
articles.summary: The top diplomat was found dead on March 10, 1948, in the courtyard beneath his bathroom window, supposedly after a fall. Police said their probe aims to settle questions that have surrounded the…

image.caption: Some historians believe Jan Masaryk, seen as a pro-Western figure, may have been killed by Soviet agentsImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Czech police said Wednesday they had begun exhuming the remains of former Czechoslovak Foreign Minister Jan Masaryk in an attempt to clear up speculation surrounding his death nearly 80 years ago.
In a statement posted to X, police said they planned to examine the remains, buried at Prague's Olsany Cemetery, "using the most modern forensic methods."
"We believe that today's actions will bring us closer to clarifying the circumstances leading to the death of Jan Masaryk," the statement said.
What happened to the former top diplomat?
Masaryk was found dead on March 10, 1948, dressed only in his pajamas, in the courtyard at the Foreign Ministry beneath his bathroom window.
The mysterious circumstances surrounding his death, at the height of the Cold War, have fueled speculation for decades.
At the time, the Interior Ministry claimed that he had committed suicide. Others believed his fall may have been an accident, or that he was murdered by Soviet agents.

blocks.caption: Jan Masaryk was found in the courtyard of the Foreign Ministy, housed in Prague's Czernin PalaceImage: UPI/dpa/picture-alliance

blocks.text: Who was Jan Masaryk?
Born in Prague on September 14, 1886, Masaryk was the son of the first Czechoslovak president, Tomas Garrigue Masaryk.
He served as the country's top diplomat from 1940 to 1948, first for the government-in-exile during World War II and then for the post-war coalition government.
Following the Czechoslovak communist coup of February 1948, he stayed on as foreign minister, refusing to step down.
The case of his death has been reviewed several times since the collapse of communism in the 1989 Velvet Revolution. The country later split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

blocks.caption: Jan Masaryk served as foreign minister during World War II and in the post-war government [File photo: 12 July, 1947]Image: Josef Mucha/CTK/picture alliance

articles.title: No confidential funds in proposed 2027 OVP budget, says House Appro vice chair
articles.summary: There are no confidential funds in the proposed 2027 budget of the Office of the Vice President, House Committee on Appropriations Vice Chairperson Representative Jose Alvarez said.

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 8:10pm
There are no confidential funds in the proposed 2027 budget of the Office of the Vice President, House Committee on Appropriations Vice Chairperson Representative Jose Alvarez said Wednesday.

"Wala. Nothing, nothing. So it is up to the president kung bigyan niya ng [if he will give] confidential funds yung Office of the Vice President. That is his discretion," Alvarez said in an ambush interview after the committee deliberations this afternoon, at which the OVP asked for P785 million for next year.
Alvarez also said there was no request from the OVP for confidential funds.
The impeachment of Vice President Sara Duterte is currently tackling her use of the confidential funds allocated to the OVP and to the Department of Education when she was education secretary.
The Commission on Audit has issued notices of disallowance for the OVP confidential funds in 2022 and 2023.
Since then, the OVP has not been given any confidential fund.
Objection to parliamentary courtesy

During the deliberations of the House Committee on Appropriations on the proposed budget of the OVP today, BH Party-list Representative Robert Nazal moved to extend parliamentary courtesy to the OVP—the act of approving budget proposals without discussion, usually accorded to the President and the Vice President.

"Yesterday, this committee extended to the Office of the President a long-standing courtesy, passing its budget without interpellation in recognition of its standing as co-equal branch of government. Today, I respectfully ask the same courtesy to the Office of the Vice President," Nazal said.

"The vice president is currently facing the weight of an impeachment proceeding, a burden already heavy enough on its own. Her budget, moreover, has not grown. It remains modest and unremarkable," he added.
Several members of the committee objected to the motion, including House Deputy Minority Leader and ACT Teachers Party-list Representative Antonio Tinio.

"Nilinaw natin kahapon sa ating paliwanag na dapat ibasura na itong inter-parliamentary courtesy, lalo na pag usapin ng budget dahil nga tungkulin natin, ng lahat ng nasa gobyerno, ay maging transparent kung paano ginagamit ang pondo ng taumbayan," Tinio explained.

(We clarified yesterday about how we should junk this inter-parliamentary courtesy, especially when budgets are discussed, because it is the duty of all of us in this government to be transparent about how we use public funds.)

"Anong susunod dito? Another co-equal branch is the judiciary. Magmo-move na rin ba kayo na hindi na rin natin bubulatlatin o bubusisiin ang budget ng judiciary? Hindi naman yon nangyayari ever," he added.
(What next? Another co-equal branch is the judiciary. Are you also going to move that we do not discuss or scrutinize the judiciary's budget? That's not going to happen ever.)
He also called for an end to the said tradition.
"Kailangang itigil na po natin ang practice na ito. Anyway, I am sure handa naman na sagutin ng Office of the Vice President anumang tanong kaugnay sa kanilang budget ngayon," Tinio stated.
(We need to stop this practive. Anyway, I am sure the Office of the Vice President is ready to answer any questions we have regarding the proposed budget.)
Upon query of Alvarez, Nazal agreed to set aside his motion.
This was after OVP Chief of Staff Zuleika Lopez agreed to answer questions.
Alvarez said the OVP had written the committee two days ago to inform them that Lopez was representing the office in the budget deliberations.
Alvarez explained that it is usually the head of agency who defends the its budget proposal, but that an official with the rank of undersecretary is allowed to represent the agency.
Duterte has not attended the impeachment trial, at which staffers under her have already testified. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: EXPLAINER: How does haze affect your health?
articles.summary: Wildfires in Indonesia have burned about 200,000 hectares of land, producing thick haze that has spread to neighboring countries, including the Philippines.

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 8:07pm
Wildfires in Indonesia have burned about 200,000 hectares of land, producing thick haze that has spread to neighboring countries, including the Philippines.
Indonesia has been working to contain the fires, but the prevailing El Niño phenomenon has made firefighting efforts more difficult. Smoke has blanketed several parts of the country.
According to a GMA News Feed report, the haze was observed in several parts of Metro Manila, CALABARZON and MIMAROPA.

In the National Capital Region, the air quality was classified as “very unhealthy” and “accurately unhealthy,” according to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources–Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB).
What is haze?

Haze is an atmospheric phenomenon in which fine particulate matter accumulates in the air. This includes PM2.5, or particles measuring 2.5 micrometers or smaller in diameter—about 30 times smaller than the width of a human hair.
How is air quality measured?
Experts measure the concentration of PM2.5 in the air and use it to determine the air quality category under the Air Quality Index.
The index has six categories: green for good, yellow for moderate, orange for unhealthy for sensitive groups, red for unhealthy, purple for very unhealthy, and maroon for hazardous.
How does PM2.5 affect the body?

Unlike larger particles such as dust, PM2.5 is small enough to bypass some of the body's natural defenses and penetrate deep into the respiratory system. These particles can reach the air sacs in the lungs and cause inflammation.

When air quality reaches the purple or “very unhealthy” level, exposure can pose health risks, particularly to sensitive groups. Fine particles can cause coughing, throat irritation, wheezing and difficulty breathing.
Exposure to high levels of PM2.5 can also worsen asthma and other existing lung conditions.

The particles can also enter the bloodstream and affect other parts of the body. Prolonged or high-level exposure to PM2.5 has been linked to cardiovascular problems, including an increased risk of heart attack and stroke.
Who is most vulnerable to haze?

The DENR-EMB reminded the public to limit outdoor activities in affected areas, especially people who are more sensitive to air pollution, including children, older adults, and those with lung or heart conditions.
For those who need to go outdoors, wearing a properly fitted N95 or equivalent respirator can help reduce exposure to fine particles.
The public is also advised to stay informed about air quality conditions and follow guidance from reliable government sources.— Jean Mangaluz with research from GMA DigiLab/MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Armed men abduct Kenyan editor, employer suspects government
articles.summary: A newspaper editor in Kenya was kidnapped from a car late on Tuesday and then located near a dam far away a few hours later. The Standard paper said it suspected state involvement in an attempt to…

image.caption: Kenyan newspaper The Standard is often crticial of President William Ruto, who singled the paper out in comments online over the summerImage: James Wakibia/SOPA Images/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: An associate editor for one of Kenya's largest news outlets, The Standard, was abducted by armed men overnight and then released near a dam far from the scene around nine hours later, his employer said on Wednesday.
Alex Kiprotich was taken from a car at around 9:20 p.m. on Tuesday on a road near the city of Nakuru.

"The circumstances of Mr Kiprotich's abduction remain deeply troubling, and we will continue to press for full accountability," the government-critical outlet said in a press release after his discovery.
Late on Tuesday the Standard Group's CEO Chaacha Mwita had also said that the "abduction bears all the hallmarks of a targeted attack on a journalist for doing his job."

blocks.caption: Kirpotich (left in picture) and CEO Mwita appeared at a Nairobi press confernce on WednesdayImage: Monicah Mwangi/REUTERS

blocks.text: What do we know about the apparent abduction?
The newspaper released a video overnight of what appeared to be dashcam footage from the car Kiprotich was traveling in when he was abducted.

A white vehicle without any markings apparent in the footage came to a stop in front of the car in an area where temporary barriers created a single-lane bottleneck on the Gilgil-Nakuru highway, and put on its hazard lights.

Four men in civilian clothes and obscuring their faces — some holding firearms and others carrying what appeared to be baseball bats — emerged and converged on the car, soon taking a man back to their vehicle and driving off.
On Wednesday, Standard Group said that Kiprotich had been located near a dam more than 200 kilometers (120 miles) southeast the scene of the abduction roughly nine hours earlier.

"Mr Kiprotich was located by a Standard Group team led by the Group CEO Chaacha Mwita at around 6:30 a.m. near Masinga Dam, after being dumped by his captors in the early hours of the morning," it said.

Kiprotic was "safe, though understandably shaken by his ordeal," his employer said. Kiprotich works for newspaper The Standard, a flagship of the wider media group known for its critical coverage of President William Ruto's government.
Rights groups say activists still being abducted in Kenya
Right groups call for investigation, warn of pattern of abductions and intimidation
Police and the government in Kenya did not immediately comment on the incident.

Dozens of government critics and activists have been abducted in Kenya this year alone, according to a report released this week, with the practice becoming more common since widespread anti-government protests in 2024.
Human rights groups have accused state agencies of being responsible, with Standard Group voicing similar suspicions in this case.
Kiprotich had said in June that he narrowly escaped a previous attempt to kidnap him, which came three days after Ruto called out the Standard Group on social media.

Kenya's editors' guild said it was "shocked, outraged and deeply perturbed" by Tuesday's abduction, describing it as "a disturbing escalation in the intimidation and targeting of journalists in Kenya."
Amnesty International Kenya called for an independent investigation, saying the incident raised "serious concerns for media freedom."

articles.title: Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills five people at wedding
articles.summary:
Blast also injures 68 guests at the wedding in southern Iran, prompting fears of escalation in hostilities

Iran has accused the US of a “war crime” after a missile blast killed at least five…

blocks.text: Iran has accused the US of a “war crime” after a missile blast killed at least five people and injured 68 who were attending a wedding at a private home in a coastal city of southern Iran, as the fresh exchange of strikes prompted fears of a wider renewal of hostilities.

Iranian media said that the wedding ceremony was being held in a home in the city of Kuhestak, Hormozgan province, late on Tuesday when a US missile struck, with shrapnel and debris from the strike killing and injuring people.
Among the dead was a four-year-old child, Amir-Ali Karimi, and a 16-year-old, Mohammad Mollahi.
“It’s a terrible thing. I’m extremely worried and upset about what happened – really upset,” Ali Mollahi, the father of the bride, told Mehr News.
The deputy of the provincial government, Ahmad Nafisi, said first responders had headed immediately to the scene and transferred the wounded to the hospitals.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson called the US attack a “war crime” and said Iran “will respond to these savage crimes with firmness”.
The chief Iranian negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, said the attack had killed families with children, and called the US the “great Satan”.
“If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan and kills like Satan, it’s Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan,” Ghalibaf said in a post on X.

The US attacks on Tuesday ended a month-long uneasy truce between the US and Iran and appeared to signal a resumption of another cycle of escalation. US Central Command (Centcom) said the overnight strikes focused on Iranian military targets including air defence sites, radars and maritime assets.

Iran responded by launching drones and missiles on US bases across the Middle East, including in Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE. Iran’s military spokesperson, Lt Col Ebrahim Zolfaghari, vowed “heavier, broader, and more crushing and devestating” retaliation.

Videos of the aftermath of the strike show a caved-in roof, blown-out windows and ground riddled with debris, as well as walls pockmarked with what appeared to be holes from shrapnel. Footage from a nearby hospital showed women in wedding attire watching as injured children were being treated.

“When we arrived there, an explosion occurred. It was very intense. Bricks, stones and cement hit me in the face and head, and many others were injured,” a child who was injured at the wedding told the state-affiliated Fars news agency.
A spokesperson for Centcom, Tim Hawkins, said the US was aware of reports of civilian casualties, but the “US military never targets civilians, unlike the [Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps]”.

In February, a strike on an elementary school killed at least 156 people, including more than 120 schoolchildren. Independent investigations concluded that the US likely carried out the strike with the assistance of AI, though the US government said the incident remained under investigation.

Pictures of shrapnel collected at the site of Tuesday’s attack were published on Iranian state media, and appeared to show the internal components of US munitions. Trevor Ball, an independent weapons analyst, identified some of the remnants as belonging to the Standoff Land Attack Missile-Expanded Response (Slam-Er) missile, which is made by the US weapons company Boeing. The Slam-Er is a 1,500-pound, GPS-guided missile touted by Boeing to be “extremely accurate.”

It was unclear if the home where the wedding was being held was struck directly, or if a missile hit close to the home and debris from the strike hit the home and its occupants. CCTV footage captured at least six strikes in the area within a minute. A separate strike appeared to hit a communications tower about 150 metres away from the home.

The US has been targeting communications and radar infrastructure along Iran’s coast to try to stop its blockade on the strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint which prior to the US-Iran war was a transit point for at least 20% of the world’s oil supply.

Iran has virtually closed the strait since the start of the Iran war, frustrating the US president, Donald Trump, who is facing a midterm election with expensive gas prices and knock-on inflation across the board.
In recent weeks, the US has focused on trying to degrade Iran’s capacity to strike ships transiting the strait to reopen the waterway for traffic.

articles.title: More than 900 killed in Gaza this year despite ceasefire, Hamas-run health ministry says
articles.summary: The ministry says the total number of people killed in the Strip since 10 October is now more than 1,300, including 301 children.

blocks.text: ByEmma Pengelly and Richard Irvine-BrownBBC Verify
More than 900 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza this year despite the ceasefire, according to latest figures from the territory's Hamas-run Ministry of Health.
It brings the total number of people killed in the Strip since the 10 October ceasefire was declared to more than 1,300, including 301 children, the ministry says.

Hamas and Israel agreed to halt the war after accepting US President Donald Trump's 20-point peace plan. That plan included a suspension of "all military operations, including aerial and artillery bombardment".

Since then, BBC Verify has analysed dozens of videos which show the impact of Israeli strikes on locations including a beachside cafe, tents where displaced people have been sheltering, and a reported funeral procession in central Gaza.
Recent months have been some of the most deadly according to the figures, with more than 100 people recorded killed each month between April and August.
The health ministry attributes the deaths directly to Israeli military action, but does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.
The UN considers the figures reliable, and experts have told BBC Verify that their independent analysis is consistent with the ministry's data.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) disputes the ministry's figures. It told BBC Verify there is "no basis to assume" that all those listed were killed as a result of IDF activity.

It said it operates in "a precise manner to remove threats and protect its troops and Israeli civilians, in accordance with the agreement", and that it works to mitigate any civilian harm "to the greatest extent possible".

At the start of this year Israeli media reported that an Israeli security official acknowledged more than 70,000 people had been killed in the Gaza war, which it said included more than 20,000 combatants.
'Ceasefire in name only'

From the start of the ceasefire agreement on 10 October to the end of that month, the ministry recorded 251 deaths. Since then the deadly Israeli attacks have continued every month. The highest monthly death toll this year was recorded in July, when 152 people were killed including 21 children, according to the figures.
The IDF says five of its soldiers have been killed in combat since the ceasefire and one contractor was killed in an "operational accident".
It also says it has killed hundreds of military operatives since October.

Conflict monitoring group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (Acled), which uses official statements, media reports and social media to verify attacks, says it has recorded around 200 Israeli strikes during the ceasefire that have reportedly killed Hamas operatives or other armed "militants" in targeted strikes.
Acled said this includes commanders involved in planning the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack on Israel, which triggered the war and killed around 1,200 people with 251 taken hostage.

Hugh Lovatt, senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations think tank, said "Gaza has seen a ceasefire in name only" since last October. He said the Israeli military has continued its almost daily air and drone strikes, and "though it claims to be targeting Hamas or imminent threats, it is Gaza's civilians that have continued to bear the brunt".
This could now be a "central stumbling block" in international efforts to implement Trump's ceasefire deal, he added.
The IDF told BBC Verify it "remains committed" to the ceasefire agreement and that there have been "continued violations and threats posed by Hamas and other terror organizations" in Gaza.
Summer of deadly incidents
Warning: The following segment of this story contains graphic content which some readers might find distressing.
Multiple deadly Israeli strikes in Gaza in under 24 hours
BBC Verify has analysed dozens of videos of attacks in Gaza carried out since the ceasefire.

In one, emergency services are seen attending to people in the aftermath of a strike at a beachside cafe in Gaza City on 18 August, where six people were killed, according to the health ministry. The next day nine people, including a 13-year-old, were reportedly killed in a strike on a police headquarters in the al-Tuffah neighbourhood.
The IDF said it was targeting Hamas commanders and terrorists in the two incidents and that "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians".

One of the deadliest single incidents in July was a strike on a reported funeral procession in Nuseirat. Seven people were killed and 22 injured, according to the Al-Awda Hospital where casualties were taken. Several verified images show nine people covered in blood lying on the street. Two people appear to still be alive and are being treated by bystanders.
The IDF said it was targeting a "significant military operative" of the Palestinian Islamic Jihad group who was involved in the 7 October 2023 attacks.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Men assess scene of Israeli strike on high-rise block in Gaza City on 2 August

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied
Men assess scene of Israeli strike on high-rise block in Gaza City on 2 August

In a strike on an apartment block on the western edge of Gaza City overnight on 1 August, a pregnant woman, her husband and their young son were killed, according to local reports. Verified footage showed the body of an unborn baby in the rubble.

A man searching the ruins said he had heard a strike overnight and saw smoke coming from the building. "I broke the door and went up and I found dead bodies scattered," he said. The IDF said it had targeted an acting Hamas commander.
Child deaths 'absurd and devastating'

UN agency Unicef has also reported more than 300 children have been killed since the ceasefire. The aid organisation has been tracking all available reports of incidents affecting children in Gaza, including via UN personnel on the ground.
James Elder, Unicef global spokesperson, said the number of child deaths was "absurd and devastating".
He added that hundreds more have been injured. "A ceasefire that paints such a grim picture can only be failing children."

Unicef and other humanitarian organisations operating inside Gaza have also reported Israeli strikes on their workers since the ceasefire. This includes two water truck drivers contracted by Unicef killed in April by Israeli fire at the Mansoura water filling point in northern Gaza.

The IDF said its soldiers "identified suspects approaching" the Yellow Line area during the incident, who were later identified as UN contractors who had not "coordinated in advance". Unicef said the drivers were carrying out routine water trucking operations with "no changes in movement or procedures".
Aid Worker Security Database, whose figures have been cited by the UN and UK government, told BBC Verify it has recorded 22 aid workers killed in Gaza since 10 October 2025.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Palestinians grieve over bodies of people killed in an Israeli attack targeting a beachfront cafe in Gaza City

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Palestinians grieve over bodies of people killed in an Israeli attack targeting a beachfront cafe in Gaza City

Independent research group Airwars works to identify civilian deaths from a range of open sources including news agencies, NGOs and social media, matching names it finds to those published by the health ministry.
Director Emily Tripp told BBC Verify the ministry's data on death tolls is consistent with its own tracking and research, and that it recorded more than 60 deadly incidents in July.
"This is the highest number of fatal incidents we've seen in a month since the ceasefire," Tripp said. "Our own findings point to an increasing number of civilian harm incidents a month."

Professor Michael Spagat from Royal Holloway, University of London, is the chair of Every Casualty Counts, a charity that studies death tolls in wars. He told BBC Verify that the figures recorded by the health ministry are "testable" because it publishes names, ages and ID numbers of the dead.

He said that since April, the monthly death toll in Gaza has been roughly double what was seen in December. "July was the worst month but even August's lower toll is still high compared with the November to March period," he added.
Additional reporting Paul Brown, Benedict Garman and Lamees Altalebi

articles.title: Rosenberg: Putin's veiled threat to UK part of Russia's campaign against West
articles.summary: The Russian president wants to keep Britain guessing - and stressing - over Moscow's real intentions.

blocks.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin responded with one short sentence when asked at a press conference whether Moscow might strike military facilities in the UK in response to British arms supplies to Ukraine.
"That's a secret. A military secret."
Military secret is not a "yes". And not a "no". It leaves us hanging.
And that, I suspect, is the point.

Those two words feel like psychological pressure from the Kremlin: to keep Britain guessing - and stressing - over Moscow's intentions, as well as to encourage the UK to think twice about its staunch support for Ukraine.

It reminds me of a newspaper article I read a few days ago. Moskovsky Komsomolets had suggested that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham should be seeing Russia, not in his dreams, "but in his nightmares".
Scary language. But short on detail about what those nightmares will look like.
We cannot conclude that Russian missiles are about to be used against targets in the UK.
But look what's happening elsewhere in Europe.
Germany now says Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig airport.
Putin accused Germany of "planting the evidence". But German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described "the well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe".
Could such "operations" now be stepped up in the UK?
Yet it wasn't just Britain that received veiled threats at Putin's press conference.
So did the West in general. Putin referred to Western countries as sharks.

"If anyone tries to drag us down the food chain, to gobble us up or devour us, they might get punched in the teeth," he said. "Russia is ready to do that, despite the rapidly growing appetites and teeth of these sharks."
Increasingly Russia's president is mixing the geopolitical with the zoological. He recently spoke about killer whales "tearing polar bears apart" to justify Russia's war on Ukraine.
The press conference in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, was a fascinating window on Putin's state of mind.

For forty-five minutes he took questions from Russian journalists and came across as combative, confident of victory and energised. These days Putin appears most animated when talking about the geopolitical standoff between Russia and the West and the war in Ukraine.
Even though the war has not gone to plan. Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield and the country's economy is under considerable pressure.
"I have no doubt that the enemy will crumble," he declared. Yet the war has lasted more than four-and-a-half years and Ukraine fights on.
Officially the Kremlin still calls this a "special military operation". But even Putin now is using the word "war".
"War is a brutal and unpredictable thing," he said at the press conference.
He claimed that he remained open to negotiations to end the conflict and left no doubt with whom he'd prefer to sit down with from the US administration: Donald Trump's envoys.

"We are absolutely comfortable working with those people we know well and generally trust," Putin said. "[Jared] Kushner and [Steve] Witkoff are always welcome guests. It's a pleasure working with them."
There was no such name check for the CIA director who had made a surprise visit to Moscow last week. The Kremlin says the Russian president didn't meet John Ratcliffe during that trip.
Is Putin likely to meet Witkoff and Kushner anytime soon?
There's nothing in the diary. Not yet.
But if they do head to Moscow, President Trump's envoys will encounter a Kremlin leader who remains determined that any peace in Ukraine should be on Russia's terms.

blocks.text: Teamsters union leaders support Republicans despite members endorsing Democratic candidates
Michael Sainato
The powerful Teamsters union is backing Republican candidates in the 2026 election cycle even after members have voted to support their Democrat opponents.
The 1.3 million-strong union’s president, Sean O’Brien, angered many members and union leaders in 2024 when he became the first union president to speak at the Republican national convention (RNC).
The latest moves by the union’s leadership are further stoking tensions within the union.

“The Republicans have done nothing but take a gun to our head at every turn. And why we think that we can somehow change their behavior, I don’t understand it. It’s not a logical argument,” said John Palmer, who was elected on O’Brien’s slate in 2021 as an at-large vice-president on the Teamsters executive board, but who broke ranks in criticizing O’Brien’s RNC appearance in 2024. “I live in Texas. I’m a moderate guy, but I know when somebody’s trying to cut my throat.”

The national union declined to make an endorsement in the 2024 presidential election for the first time since 1996, claiming a majority of members supported Trump after they supported Biden in 2020, though Teamsters locals and councils representing 1 million members at the union independently endorsed Harris.
So far this election cycle, O’Brien has made two personal contributions – both to Republicans.
O’Brien donated $1,000 to the Republican US Senate campaign of Scott Brown in New Hampshire on 19 February 2026. Brown appeared on O’Brien’s podcast, Better Bad Ideas, on 25 February.

The only Teamsters’ local in New Hampshire, Teamsters Local 633, endorsed Brown’s Democratic rival Chris Pappas for the Senate race in April 2025. Teamsters Local 633 did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Trump nominates loyalist Hung Cao to be permanent navy secretary amid increased attacks on Iran
Hello and welcome to the US live politics blog.
Donald Trump has picked acting navy secretary Hung Cao to take on the job permanently amid concerns that some sailors have been stretched to the limit during his Iran war.
“I am pleased to nominate a true WARRIOR,” Trump wrote on social media, pushing the Senate “to confirm this Warfighter, ASAP.”

Cao has been serving as acting navy secretary since John Phelan departed the job unexpectedly and without explanation in late April. Unlike Phelan, who had not served in the military or had a civilian leadership role in the service, Cao spent 25 years in the navy as a special operations officer and went on to serve with Seal teams and special forces in Iraq and Afghanistan.
Cao on social media called it the “honor of a lifetime to lead the great warriors of the Navy and Marine Corps team”.

Cao’s nomination comes as some, including Democrats in Congress, believe Trump has been overtaxing the navy. The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier’s nine-month deployment to support the Iran war has included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea.

It comes as Iran launched a wave of attacks on US sites across the Middle East, with violence surging after an extensive American bombardment. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards announced attacks on US bases in Jordan, the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Iraq’s autonomous Kurdistan region, in the six-month conflict’s heaviest exchange in weeks.
Trump had warned earlier of “much harder and higher” attacks if Iran retaliated to the US strikes, which Iran’s military and state media said killed 18 people.
The renewed attacks deepen the impasse in the war, where Iran maintains a stranglehold on the strait of Hormuz oil export route with the US pressing a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
In other developments:

items: Senator Ed Markey won the Democratic primary in Massachusetts, beating back a challenge from Seth Moulton, who argued his opponent was too old to be effective at his job. Progressive lawmakers and the organization Our Revolution hailed the victory.

Democratic leaders in the US House sharply criticized two representatives for defecting and joining with Republicans in order to advance a procedural vote, describing it as a “significant breach of trust,” that requires “a serious response”.

The US House of Representative voted to censure Chuck Edwards, a Republican congressman who the ethics committee found violated rules against sexual harassment in his conduct towards two young female staffers.

The Trump administration seized on House Democrats voting against a resolution denouncing socialism, condemning the lawmakers as “sick [and] dangerous”. The resolution included language calling for the enactment of Trump’s SAVE America Act, a strict voting bill that would ban mail-in ballots and require voters to prove their citizenship.
Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, criticized Donald Trump for withholding $87m in counter-terrorism funds from the state, describing the move as a betrayal of 9/11 victims.
Donald Trump’s Department of Homeland Security has apparently taken steps to advance the president’s efforts to limit voting.

The Department of Health (DOH) on Wednesday assured the public that it has sufficient medicines to treat leptospirosis patients amid the surge in cases following the continuous torrential rain caused by the Southwest Monsoon (Habagat).
During the House budget hearing, DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado said the agency has already distributed leptospirosis medicines across the country before the start of the wet season.

“Meron po tayong download na preemptively even before the start of the rainy season, and then we have at least 3.1 million capsules still in the central warehouse, which is enough buffer for the rest of the year,” Mercado said.
(We have preemptively downloaded even before the start of the rainy season, and we still have at least 3.1 million capsules in the central warehouse, which is enough buffer for the rest of the year.)
For 2027, DOH has allocated P9.76 million to procure 4.88 million capsules of medicine to treat leptospirosis.

“For 2027, we have P9.76 million [and] we will procure 4.88m capsules, so we are prepositioning across the CHD (Center for Health Development) earlier. Again, this will be part of our early procurement,” Mercado said.

In a Balitanghali interview, Dr. Marc Steven Capungcol, chief of the DOH Health Emergency Management Bureau, said DOH hospital in Metro Manila have 77 beds available for leptospirosis patients, with active patient referrals and redistribution in place to prevent overcrowding.
Currently, there are 526 admissions and 33 pending admissions of leptospirosis patients in DOH hospitals in Metro Manila.
According to Capungcol, leptospirosis cases and deaths are 19% lower than those recorded during the same period last year.
The DOH official urged the public to immediately consult a doctor instead of waiting for symptoms of leptospirosis to worsen before seeking medical attention. —RF, GMA News

“Perhaps, you can not spend that anymore and use it on your other needs,” Garin suggested, referring to the remaining amount in the pledge.
Beltran also confirmed that the DOH had proposed P167.2 million under its 2027 budget as part of the commitment to WHO.
Garin, a former health secretary, previously questioned the deal during the committee-level deliberations for the DOH budget last year.

articles.title: US aircraft carrier docks near Thai beach resort Pattaya after record 250 days at sea
articles.summary: The USS Abraham Lincoln is docking close to Pattaya, known for its neon-lit nightlife, and for sex tourism.

blocks.text: US aircraft carrier docks near Thai beach resort Pattaya after record 250 days at sea
Watch: Why do US troops have history with this Thai city?
ByJonathan Head
South East Asia correspondentReporting fromPattaya, Thailand
After a record 250 days at sea without a port stop, the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln has docked in Thailand, giving its nearly 5,000 crew members a much-needed break.
The ship is docking close to the beach resort of Pattaya, known for its raucous nightlife and for sex tourism. For the US it also carries strong historical echoes.

When the weary sailors walk into the city's bars and restaurants, they will literally be treading in the footsteps of the hundreds of thousands of US troops who came here for R&R – rest and relaxation - during the Vietnam War.
They transformed it from a sleepy fishing village to one of the world's most famous and frenetic party towns.

Today the neon-lit alleys running down to the beach are much quieter than usual. The bars in the city's famous Walking Street still screen videos on their walls of pole-dancing women, trying to lure customers inside.
But there are not many of those customers, and most seem to be family groups from the Middle East more interested in the Turkish ice-cream vendor than the go-go bars.

The Iran War, which has affected tourism and consumer spending, has hit businesses hard here. The prospect of thousands of American sailors, with nine months of salary unspent while at sea, offers a rare opportunity to local businesses.

blocks.caption: Image caption, US personnel arriving at the Hard Rock Hotel in Pattaya on Wednesday

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
US personnel arriving at the Hard Rock Hotel in Pattaya on Wednesday
The US carrier left San Diego last November on what was supposed to be a six-month assignment in the Pacific and South China Sea.
However, the ship was diverted to the Gulf after the US and Israel began military operations against Iran in late February.

Recently some members of Congress raised concern about reports of food shortages, broken toilets and mental stress among the crew. The US Navy acknowledged that working conditions have been tough, but said the crew were sufficiently well-supported. It would not, however, comment to the BBC on the carrier docking at Pattaya, citing operational security.
Despite its close relationship with China, Thailand is a treaty ally of the US, and port visits by US Navy ships are a familiar occurrence.
But this is probably the largest number of US military personnel coming straight from a war zone to Pattaya since the fall of Saigon in 1975.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Pattaya's streets, know for their raucuous nightlife, are quieter than usual

blocks.text: Image source, BBC/Lulu Luo
Pattaya's streets, know for their raucuous nightlife, are quieter than usual

"This visit could be our best hope," said Anon Saiteer, who sells gems in a shop near Walking Street, which has put up a large sign welcoming the US sailors and marines and offering them a special discount. "We have nothing to lose – we just hope they will spend some money here."
But US and Thai officials are trying to ensure this happens without any of the salacious headlines for which Pattaya has become known.

The Thai authorities have said there are a few places where the US servicemen and women will not be allowed to go. One of them is Soi 6, which runs down to the main beach, and is known for its concentration of racy go-go bars.

While the Thai police have reminded their US visitors that prostitution is technically illegal in Thailand, there are actually thought to be 25,000 to 50,000 sex workers in the city. Many of them work in Soi 6, where they stand outside the bars imploring men to come inside.
The many cannabis shops in Pattaya are also off-limits to US crew members, along with sea-sports like paragliding and jet-skis.
"It is their decision," Mayor Poramase Ngampiches told the BBC. "The US military have done their homework."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The war in Iran is hurting local businesses

blocks.text: The war in Iran is hurting local businesses
US Naval Attache Kristopher Robinson rebuffed questions from the BBC about activities that soldiers were banned from doing.
Instead, he said the US troops would "conduct themselves in accordance with US law, US naval regulations, and the laws of Thailand".
"We're trying to give the sailors as much opportunity for rest as they can," he said.

The US Navy has organised shuttle buses from the port into Pattaya running from 5am to 2am every day the carrier is here in Thailand. Two hotels have been designated suitable for those US crew members who want to splash out on a night onshore.
The Thai authorities have deployed hundreds of police officers to keep an eye on the city's entertainment zones, and warned local businesses not to overcharge their American guests.
"The visits of US military men 50-60 years ago introduced Pattaya to the world and turned it into a tourist attraction," says Mayor Poramase.
"We have to be frank, the city has a reputation for bar girls. We understand the stereotypes. We can't stop that.
"What we can do is to show that Pattaya has changed, that we now have other things, such as sports, seminars, wellness and family-friendly activities. It's a mixture of everything."
Both countries hope that by the time the USS Abraham Lincoln begins the long journey home across the Pacific on 6 September, it will be with a refreshed and rested crew.
With additional reporting from Nongnapat Patcham.

articles.title: Barclays faces complaint over backing for power plant near world’s largest mangrove forest
articles.summary:
Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its…

blocks.text: Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.

Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.

The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.

Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.

Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.

blocks.caption: The Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and one of the last habitats of Bengal tigers, supports the livelihoods of millions of people.  Photograph: Bengal Picture Library/Alamy

blocks.text: Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.

The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.

Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.

The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.

The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.

Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.

“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”

Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.

Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

articles.title: [In the Public Square] Two months in: Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial so far
articles.summary: The impeachment can be viewed in terms popularized by a late, great constitutionalist: it is 'political justice'

blocks.text: The impeachment can be viewed in terms popularized by a late, great constitutionalist: it is 'political justice'

We’ve just completed Day 21, and Week 9, of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. Today, public prosecutor Representative Joel Chua suggested that the prosecution may be able to finish its presentation of evidence in chief by early October. That means, he said, the trial might end by December.
As people say, malayo pa, pero malayo na. Two months in, how goes the impeachment of Sara Duterte?

The impeachment can be viewed in terms popularized by the late, great constitutionalist Fr. Joaquin Bernas SJ: it is “political justice.” It’s important to listen to legal analysts, and we will continue to do so.
But it’s equally important to hear from political scientists, and in this episode of In the Public Square, Rappler columnist John Nery is joined by highly esteemed professors of political science.

Dr. Jean Franco is a professor of political science at the UP Diliman and Arjan Aguirre is assistant professor of political science on leave at the Ateneo de Manila, who is doing his PhD at the University of Pittsburgh.

articles.title: Guinea-Bissau voters approve new constitution expanding presidential powers
articles.summary:
Changes include fewer seats in parliament and new rules on presidential candidates ahead of December elections

Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution significantly expanding…

blocks.text: Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution significantly expanding presidential powers ahead of elections due in December.

According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago.
The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people.

The new constitution will reduce the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cut electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. New provisions will require presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for at least five years before the vote, which is believed to target diaspora-based politicians with significant followings.

The referendum’s outcome is expected to pave the way for December’s elections, which many hope will steady the political landscape in Guinea-Bissau, which has been through a series of politically turbulent periods since its declaration of independence from Portugal was globally recognised in 1974. Since then it has had at least 10 coup attempts, half of which have been successful.

The most recent came after last November’s disputed presidential elections. Both candidates declared themselves winners, citing electoral malpractice by the other’s camp. The military forcefully intervened, setting up a transitional ruling council headed by Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, a former military chief of general staff.
Na Man said: “What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance.”
Nelson Moreira, the second vice-president of the transitional council, said the outgoing constitution, which came into effect in 1993, had often been cited as “the cause of instability in Guinea”.

The leading opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which was barred from fielding a presidential candidate in the 2025 election, had asked its supporters to boycott the referendum, which it called a democratic farce.
“What will happen on 30 August is the continuation of the coup d’état carried out on 26 November,” its leader, Domingos Simões Pereira, had said.

articles.title: Cargo ship with 10 crew sinks off Istanbul – maritime authorities
articles.summary: ISTANBUL — A cargo ship sank in the Marmara Sea near Istanbul after colliding with a second vessel, with rescuers hunting 10 people who were on board, Turkish officials said Wednesday. The…

blocks.text: ISTANBUL — A cargo ship sank in the Marmara Sea near Istanbul after colliding with a second vessel, with rescuers hunting 10 people who were on board, Turkish officials said Wednesday.

The incident occurred before dawn when the ALSU, an empty oil tanker, collided with the Tugberk Imamoglu, a cargo ship carrying rolled steel, which sank shortly after, the transport ministry’s maritime directorate said on X.
The collision occurred 18 nautical miles off Silivri district on the western edge of Istanbul province, the governor’s office said on X.
“Due to the Tugberk İmamoglu not responding to any calls and the crew not answering their mobile phones… it is believed the dry cargo ship has sunk,” the maritime directorate said.
The ALSU’s captain had reported the collision as happening at 3:15 am (0015 GMT), with 14 search and rescue vessels dispatched to the area backed by a helicopter, it said.
“Life-saving equipment, including a lifeboat belonging to the Tugberk Imamoglu which had 10 crew members on board, has been found at sea. Unfortunately, the crew members were not inside.”
The ALSU, which was damaged in the collision, was also joining in search and rescue efforts, it said.
At the time of the collision, the Tugberk Imamoglu was carrying 4,200 tons of rolled sheet metal, it said.
The maritime directorate initially said the ALSU was carrying 3,000 tonnes of motor oil, but later said the tanker was empty in a detail confirmed by the governorate.
The incident took place three days after deadly ferry accident off Northern Cyprus in which eight Turkish nationals died with rescuers still hunting for another 20 people listed as missing. /dl

articles.title: EU summons Russian envoy over failed Leipzig drone attack
articles.summary: The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the attempted attack had "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism." She said the EU was summoning a Russian envoy, with France announcing a…

image.caption: Kallas and other EU foreign ministers are in Ireland, which currently holds the rotating EU presidencyImage: Ansgar Haase/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The European Unions's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Wednesday that she summoned Russia's envoy in Brussels over the alleged attempted hybrid attack involving an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month.

Germany's foreign and interior ministers said in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the government in Berlin had concluded that Russia was responsible for the failed attack, reinforcing suspicions that arose as soon as the news broke in August.
Kallas says incident has 'all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism'

"We are discussing the Leipzig attacks, and also it is clear that it has all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism," Kallas said ahead of an informal gathering of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.
"The question is, what do we do about this? We have already summoned the Russian ambassador," she said.

The former Estonian prime minister also said that the EU was continuing its work on its next package of some 1,600 sanctions listings related to Russia's war in Ukraine and said "maybe there is more to be added."
France takes similar step, summoning charge d'affaires
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot also told reporters in Dublin that Paris was summoning a Russian ambassador in response.
"I have summoned the Russian charge d'affaires in Paris to protest, Barrot said, adding that sanctions should be taken at a European level, notably against Russia's so-called shadow fleet of ships.
What has Germany said about its investigations?

Foreign Minsiter Johann Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt announced in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the federal government in Berlin held Russia responsible for the failed attack.

"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiate Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," Dobrindt said on Tuesday, without going into specifics.
Wadephul said that the "means used — drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems — are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine."
Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig
Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, have rejected the allegations and accused Germany of fabricating its version of events.

Leipzig/Halle Airport is a key freight hub. Ukrainian airline and aircraft manufacturer Antonov uses the airport as a base of operations, frequently transiting material to Ukraine via the the eastern German city.

articles.title: What really helps Europe deal with drought
articles.summary: Fix leaks or ban pools: As European countries prepare for hotter, drier years to come, here's what the data says about how to really save water

image.caption: Image: Ina Fassbender/AFP

blocks.text: Europe is in drought. As the burning of fossil fuels pushes up temperatures that are making summers hotter and drier, the continent's soils, lakes and rivers are struggling to recover. Southern and Western European countries are particularly affected. But they're not the only ones.

"We've seen drought risks expanding northward during the last decade", says Gisela Elsner, Climate and Sustainability Policy Officer at the German Konrad Adenauer Foundation, who has followed EU water management efforts for years.
"Central and Western Europe, but also southeastern European countries, are increasingly vulnerable due to climate change."
For the month of August this year, satellite data shows areas as far north as Denmark and Sweden experiencing extremely dry conditions more often seen in regions such as the Sub-Saharan Sahel.

The impact is palpable. Some of the continent's longest rivers like the Rhine or the Danube have reached historic lows, disrupting inland shipping routes. Farmers from Germany to Ukraine are reporting below-average harvests, and areas from the United Kingdom to Switzerland to Germany have announced restrictions on household water use.
German municipalities impose water restrictions

To make matters worse, this year's El Niño event — a climate cycle that weakens trade winds and warms tropical Pacific surface temperatures — is set to be one of the strongest on record. Experts predict that 2027 will be even hotter and drier as a result.
Europe will have to adapt to this reality, says Gisela Elsner. "It is not yet a matter of not having water in our taps anymore. But we need to prioritize and use our water resources efficiently."
So, how can countries across the continent set about doing this? DW analyzed water usage in European nations and reviewed the evidence to find out which measures have the most impact.
Which European countries use the most water?

Private households in Europe account for a relatively small share of water usage. Depending on the country, they consume a daily per capita average of between 50 and 300 liters, which equates to less than 20% of all use.
Two thirds of water withdrawn continent-wide is for agriculture — mostly for irrigation — as well as electricity cooling for nuclear and fossil fuel power plants.
In already drought-prone countries like Greece, Turkey and Spain, agriculture accounts for most of the near 2000 liters of water withdrawn per person each day.

Electricity cooling is the biggest factor in Eastern European countries like Bulgaria or Hungary, but also in the Netherlands or Estonia, which use between 1000 and 2000 liters per capita daily in total.
Where Europe can save the most water
"There is no single solution that is sufficient to solve this challenge," says Gisela Elsner. "It has to be a combined bundle of measures."
And they exist. A recent report published by the European Environmental Agency (EEA) found that EU countries could save between 10 and 40% of water annually by implementing targeted strategies.

For states in Western and Eastern Europe, shifting to clean energy would make a big difference. While nuclear, and planet-heating oil, gas and coal need huge amounts of water for cooling, wind and solar do not.
Electricity cooling: renewables to the rescue

So besides becoming the cheapest forms of energy, the renewables that are increasingly replacing fossil fuels are also helping countries to save water. Over the past two decades, Europe has reduced its water usage by around a quarter — mostly because of more efficient electrical cooling.

Even with nuclear plants still requiring water in countries like France, Spain or Sweden, the potential savings are massive. The EEA estimates that EU countries could make significant further savings of between 45 and 95% — equal to hundreds of liters per person each day — by expanding renewables and improving cooling systems.
Better irrigation can help in agriculture

In Southern Europe, agriculture is the big-ticket item. The EEA report recommends, for instance, replacing open water transport channels with closed pipes to avoid evaporation during heatwaves, switching from surface irrigation to sprinklers or drip irrigation, and opting for less water-intensive crops whereever possible.
Public water supply: leaky pipes lose lots of water

In EU countries, around one in four liters of drinkable water from the public supply is lost to leaky pipes and evaporation before it ever reaches its destination — according to estimates by the European association of water providers EurEau.
In Romania and Italy, the share is more than 40%. According to the EEA report, avoiding these losses would account for most of the potential savings in the EU's public water supply.

Once drinking water reaches households and businesses, individual behavior has an impact as well. The EEA report lists extensive recommendations for savings in daily life, from low-flow toilets and efficient washing machines and dishwashers, to harvesting rainwater. Yet even if every citizen in Europe did all they could, it would only reduce the daily per person household water use by between 10 and 40%.

Citizens could also contribute through more responsible consumer decisions, such as considering the water footprint of the products they buy or support, says Alexander Psomas, water resources expert at the Greek consultancy Brilliant Solutions, who co-authored the EEA report.
"Citizens can also push our governments to be more accountable on their energy policy and the impact it has on water."
What Europe can learn

Drought and heat waves are not just a European problem. Many parts in the world are even more severely affected by the climate crisis. And data from the United Nations shows regions in Northern Africa, the Middle East and Asia have been dealing with much higher levels of water stress for a long time.

This also means that Europe can collaborate with, and learn from, the rest of the world on how to adapt to water scarcity. "The UN World Food Program and the FAO are all working on similar questions in the Global South," said Giriraj Armanath, Research Group Leader at the International Water Management Institute.
What one of the world's driest cities teaches us about water
Gisela Elsner recounts, for instance, chip manufacturers in the German state of Saxony recently looking to expertise from Singapore on how to reuse wastewater to cool their factories.
"We can definitely learn from those countries which already have all the knowledge and the technologies that can be used in our context as well," she said.
Public and politics are paying more attention to water use
Both Gisela Elsner and Alexander Psomas say they have noticed both politics and the public becoming more aware in recent years.

"The water scarcity and droughts topic did not have a relevant EU working group until 2022", Psomas told DW. "Today, it's one of the working groups with the highest participation. There is a growing interest and concern on this issue."
What he would like to see more of, he says, is public debates about water strategies, especially during election periods.

"If a country runs low on water, it affects everyone," he says. "I would like to see politicians discuss what kind of solutions they're offering for making their countries more water resilient in 10, 20 years from now."
Edited by Tamsin Walker and Gianna Grün
