Teodoro C. Mendoza is a retired professor at the Institute of Crop Science, University of the Philippines Los Baños.

articles.title: Nepal steps up diplomatic push for support after floods
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — The Nepal government is adopting a multi-pronged strategy to engage with the international community following the deadly Bhotekoshi river flooding of August 26. “From the prime…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — The Nepal government is adopting a multi-pronged strategy to engage with the international community following the deadly Bhotekoshi river flooding of August 26.

“From the prime minister to the foreign minister to Nepali missions abroad, we have activated all our political and diplomatic machinery,” Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said on Tuesday. “The prime minister is receiving phone calls from different heads of government, and I am personally receiving calls from my counterparts on a daily basis. We are gathering solidarity and support from the international community.”

On Tuesday, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called Prime Minister Balendra Shah and requested the Nepal government’s ‘fullest cooperation’ in rescuing five Japanese nationals missing after the flood. In response, Shah said that the government was making every possible effort to address the situation, Takaichi wrote on X.

She also conveyed that Japan would provide emergency relief supplies, including tents and blankets, to support those affected by the disaster. She assured further assistance, including support through international organisations and the dispatch of a Japanese disaster relief team.
Foreign Minister Khanal said more countries have given assurances of support.

“Our divisions in the Foreign Ministry are in touch with Kathmandu-based diplomatic and donor communities in coordination with the Finance Ministry,” said Khanal. “We have also activated our embassies and asked them to brief their host governments on the flood aftermath, our requirements and non-food items and technical support we need, like tunnel rescue experts, Bailey bridges, DNA and forensic experts, among other support.”
Besides providing updates and briefings on the situation, Nepali embassies and missions are also engaging with countries to secure funds required for resettlement and reconstruction, said Khanal.

The government has already made an urgent request to the board of the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), a global climate finance mechanism, for financial assistance following the deadly floods. The mechanism was established at COP27 in 2022 and operationalised at COP28.
The letter co-signed by Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and Forests and Agriculture Minister Geeta Chaudhary, a copy of which has been seen by the Post, requests an immediate response.
“We write to draw your urgent attention to the catastrophic flash flood that struck the

Bhotekosi river basin on August 26, causing widespread loss of life, displacement, destruction of homes and critical infrastructure, and severe disruption to essential services, livelihoods, markets, and connectivity across downstream communities,” reads the letter.

Echoing Nepal’s call, a bloc of 44 countries has expressed solidarity with Nepal and called for stronger adaptation efforts and loss and damage support amid the rising climate crisis. The Least Developed Countries (LDC) Group, in a statement issued on Tuesday, expressed deep condolences and solidarity with Nepal following the devastating floods and landslides.

“We also recognise the courage and dedication of emergency responders, authorities, humanitarian organisations, and community members working tirelessly to save lives and provide relief,” said the letter signed by LDC chair Adão Soares Barbosa.

The LDC Group said the tragedy demonstrates how vulnerable mountain communities and developing countries are increasingly exposed to interconnected environmental and climate risks. It stressed that reducing greenhouse gas emissions and strengthening climate resilience must be treated as an urgent global priority.

Meanwhile, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Poudel Chhetri said Nepal continues to coordinate closely with our immediate neighbours and the wider international community to identify and mobilise specific expertise, equipment and resources required for the ongoing rescue and relief operations.

“Specialised tunnel rescue teams from India (24 personnel in two teams) and China (9 personnel) are mobilised at the affected hydropower sites. A team from the Republic of Korea is also here,” he said.

According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the government has also received specialised equipment for the management and preservation of mortal remains. A 19-member forensic team from India specialising in DNA analysis has been working with Nepali authorities since August 29. A four-member forensic team is arriving from China on Tuesday evening.

“Coordination is also underway to mobilise a Disaster Victim Identification team from Singapore. We have also requested LiDAR, Bailey bridges, freezers, DNA testing kits, load carriers, body bags, high-capacity drones, and gene sequencers, among other things,” said Chhetri.

Authorities are assessing the damage to homes, roads, bridges, hydropower projects, and other critical infrastructure and A more comprehensive assessment, including through the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA), will provide a clearer picture of the overall damage, losses and recovery needs, said Chhetri, adding, more information will become available as these assessments progress.
A total of 1,066 people have been confirmed dead and about 4,606 remain missing, according to figures issued by police at 5 pm Tuesday. /dl

articles.title: Nepal’s disaster response: Drones deliver food, carry bodies
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — On Monday, an unusual scene unfolded in the skies over Benighat, Dhading, one of the areas devastated by last week’s floods. An unmanned aircraft flew overhead carrying a human…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — On Monday, an unusual scene unfolded in the skies over Benighat, Dhading, one of the areas devastated by last week’s floods.
An unmanned aircraft flew overhead carrying a human body.

The drone had been deployed to retrieve a body from an area that rescuers found difficult and dangerous to navigate. Seven bodies were eventually airlifted by drones from Benighat-3 to Benighat-5 under the supervision of security personnel.
It was an extraordinary use of a technology that, barely a decade ago, was largely associated with international search-and-rescue teams responding to disasters in Nepal.

When a 7.8-magnitude earthquake struck Nepal in 2015, killing thousands and destroying large parts of Kathmandu Valley and other areas, international agencies brought drones to help search for survivors, assess damage and support recovery.
Since then, advances in local technology and the growing interest of Nepali youths have helped create a homegrown drone expertise.
The technology is now finding use far beyond aerial photography and mapping.
This spring, drones helped transport heavy loads between Everest Base Camp and Camp I in the Khumbu Icefall in just six to seven minutes—a journey that can take humans up to seven hours.
They carried emergency oxygen tanks, medicines, ropes and ladders to precarious locations, reducing the need for Sherpas to repeatedly undertake one of the most dangerous jobs on the mountain.
The Khumbu Icefall is notorious for shifting ice blocks, deep crevasses and avalanches. A bad day can mean being buried under tonnes of snow and ice.
Drones have also been used to scout shifting crevasses and map ice walls, allowing Sherpa guides to identify dangerous areas before entering them.

With 3D mapping capabilities, drones can remotely scan icy landscapes such as the Khumbu Icefall and measure the length and depth of crevasses. Such information allows climbers and guides to better assess hazards, including the possibility of avalanches and collapsing ice slabs.
Now, the technology is proving its value downstream—in communities hit by floods and landslides.
In Devighat-3 of Nuwakot, one of the worst-hit areas, villagers on Sunday experienced a different kind of disaster relief.
A loudspeaker announcement suddenly came from above.
An AI-enabled drone was flying over the village, following a person before reaching a group of residents. Its speaker switched on and began asking questions.
Do you have water? Raise your hand.
Do you have food? Raise your hand.
Do you have medicine? Raise your hand.
“Based on the villagers’ response, we make an assessment for what they require and send the delivery through drones,” said Milan Pandey, director of Airlift Technology and a drone pilot.
The drone also asked villagers to provide a contact number or address, which could be written on a placard or even in the mud.
Drone operators receive the signals and process the needs of the stranded people.
The approach is particularly useful in areas where roads and bridges have been destroyed and people on opposite sides of a river can no longer reach each other.
“We supplied at least 1.5 tonnes of emergency supplies, including food, to the affected areas in three days,” Pandey said.

On Monday, the team dropped food and other logistics on the top of a four-story school building in Devighat. The ward chairman was informed and later collected the cargo for distribution among villagers.

Drone operators say their role in disaster response remains limited by payload capacity, range and weather conditions. But where conventional transport is impossible, the impact can be disproportionate to their size.
“It’s the cheapest mode of transporting supplies compared to choppers,” operators say.
And in Benighat on Monday, drones took on perhaps their most unusual role yet: carrying the dead.
“We airlifted seven bodies from Benighat-3 to Benighat-5 under the supervision of the security forces, from a place where people can hardly navigate,” said Pandey.

The eight-member drone team, led by Hami Nepal, includes personnel from GarudX, Nepal Police, Nepal Army and the Armed Police Force. Hami Nepal was previously led by the current home minister, Sudan Gurung, during the Gen Z protests in September last year.
The team has been using the DJI FlyCart 100, a heavy-lift industrial cargo drone capable of carrying logistics weighing up to 85 kilograms and operating over a range of up to four kilometers.

Other drones have been deployed to inspect rivers and their banks in the search for missing people. Thermal drones can detect signs of living people, potentially allowing rescuers to locate survivors in areas that are inaccessible or too dangerous to enter.
The technology has also been taken underground.
Drone operators have used unmanned aircraft inside the tunnel of the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, where scores of workers are believed to have been trapped following the floods.
“We reached platform 1 of the project and saw the tunnel filled with water and rocks,” said Adarsha Bhusal, one of the drone operators. “It’s risky and challenging to get inside.”
The drone found no trace of life inside the tunnel during the operation, he said.

Around 900 workers have been reported missing at various hydropower projects along the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi rivers, according to the Independent Power Producers’ Association of Nepal, the umbrella organization of private power producers.
The expanding use of drones in Nepal’s disaster response reflects how quickly the technology has evolved from a niche tool into a potential emergency-response system.

Also known as unmanned aerial vehicles, drones can produce orthophotos and topographical maps with a level of detail that can exceed conventional satellite imagery, according to the World Bank assessment report. Because they can be deployed quickly, they can provide real-time information to emergency teams assessing rapidly changing conditions.

“Specialised sensors can also detect minute changes in topography. Such data could help authorities identify areas at risk of landslides and floods and potentially provide early warning before disasters strike,” the multilateral funding agency said.
For Nepal, this technology is becoming increasingly important.

Nepal, located in the central part of the Himalayan range, is experiencing rapid environmental and climatic changes that are increasing its exposure to floods, landslides, glacier-related hazards and other disasters.

The World Bank argues that Nepal needs to become more resilient to an unpredictable and changing climate through greater use of disruptive technologies, including drones, satellite technology and geospatial analytics.
The country’s drone ecosystem began taking root after the 2015 earthquake, when international agencies introduced and deployed the technology during recovery operations.
A decade later, much of that capability is being developed and operated locally.
Nepal’s experience could eventually become relevant beyond its borders, according to the World Bank.

The country’s private sector has already provided drone-based services to Bhutan for multi-hazard risk assessment, demonstrating how Nepal’s growing expertise could be exported to other countries facing similar climate-related risks.
From the summit of Everest to flooded villages in the valleys below, drones are increasingly filling gaps where people cannot safely go.
They are delivering food and medicine, mapping hazards, searching for survivors, inspecting flooded tunnels and, now, transporting bodies.

“For a country repeatedly exposed to earthquakes, floods, landslides and mountain hazards, the rise of locally developed drone technology could mark a significant shift in how Nepal responds to disasters—putting eyes, cargo and rescue capability into places where human access is simply too dangerous,” said Pandey.
Airlift Technology, led by Pandey, assembles drones in Kathmandu by importing their parts.
“We just need an appropriate policy to promote such a life-saving machine,” he said. /dl

blocks.caption: LIVE UPDATES: Sara Duterte impeachment trial | Sept. 2, 2026

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense counsel and former Department of Education (DepEd) chief of staff Michael Poa is set to take the witness stand on Wednesday, Sept. 2, as the House prosecution panel continues presenting evidence in the impeachment trial.

items: Poa will be called by the prosecution to testify on the DepEd’s use of confidential funds during Duterte’s tenure as education secretary from 2022 to 2024.

His testimony is expected to focus on the department’s disbursement of P112.5 million in confidential funds, including P15 million reportedly used to help fund Armed Forces of the Philippines Youth Leadership Summits.
Poa cannot yet be formally designated as a hostile witness. Such a designation may come only after he has been formally presented by the prosecution and takes the stand before the impeachment court.

articles.title: How the service industry sees AI as a double-edged sword
articles.summary: The AI boom has awakened the Philippine service industry to the need to move toward higher-value work. But what will it take to get there? Service work, including BPO, is knowledge work. It spans…

blocks.text: The AI boom has awakened the Philippine service industry to the need to move toward higher-value work. But what will it take to get there?

Service work, including BPO, is knowledge work. It spans call center agents, accountants, doctors, lawyers, bankers and engineers. Like manufacturing, it ranges from low-value execution to highly specialized design, engineering and coordination.
Lower value work

Today, the Philippines remains concentrated in relatively lower-value knowledge work. Much of the highest-value knowledge work stays in the West, where companies research, design and coordinate complex products. Lower-value execution is outsourced to countries like the Philippines.

This encouraged the local service economy to specialize in work that clients had already decided was not worth deeply investing in. These functions were often cost centers, removed from strategic decision-making and given weak incentives for automation. The industry was neither equipped nor motivated to transform them.

The same problem exists within Philippine companies. Because labor is relatively inexpensive, companies often rely on growing headcount instead of standardized processes and software. Manual work accumulates until it becomes operational debt. By the time systems begin breaking under scale, the problem is expensive and difficult to untangle.
So what will enable the Philippine BPO industry to move up the value chain?
The answer is institutional knowledge.
What AI cannot replace

High-value knowledge work emerges when companies develop a deep understanding of a problem, together with the processes, culture and organization needed to solve it repeatedly. That knowledge is built through execution, coordination and iteration.

Our outsourced industries struggle to develop it because few local companies have created environments where it can accumulate. Repetitive manual work persists, while management often substitutes inexpensive headcount for process discipline, automation and enterprise investment.
AI, particularly large language models, is both a threat and a possible antidote to this incentive structure.

As repetitive execution becomes automated, demand and margins for low-value work will fall. At the same time, coding agents are making software faster and cheaper to build. Local companies can increasingly adapt battle-tested, often open source software already widely used in more mature markets.

This can create a healthier cycle. Companies will be pushed toward software, standardization and automation. Work that was once tedious and error-prone will become routine because the solution has been implemented, documented, and improved. These systems will generate institutional knowledge that compounds over time, raising labor productivity and justifying further investment.
This is why focusing only on English proficiency, AI literacy, or critical thinking is insufficient. It treats workers as better raw inputs that can be plugged into higher-value companies.
But LLMs are rapidly commoditizing many of these capabilities.

The hardest problems in implementing AI are context, coordination and accountability. These are precisely the capabilities the Philippine service industry can develop. These come from deep experience in specific industries, not generic classroom training. The correct answer is often knowable only through the high-resolution context of real work.
Moving up the value chain will be difficult, risky and slow. But building institutional knowledge through automation, standardization and repeated execution is the most realistic path forward.

articles.title: Relief as five Australians missing in Nepal-Tibet flood disaster found alive
articles.summary: Several missing Australians have been found since Tuesday morning, bringing the total citizens unaccounted for to 38

blocks.text: A total of five Australians missing after devastating floods ravaged the Nepal-Tibet border last week have been found.
Of the five Australians confirmed safe, one was found in Nepal, one in Tibet, and three outside the crisis-hit area. The total number still missing is 38.
These Australians had not spoken to families and next of kin since the disaster struck seven days ago.
There were “grave concerns” for the dozens of citizens still missing in the disaster, the minister for multicultural affairs, Anne Aly, told the ABC on Wednesday morning.
“There are real logistic issues, including communications to find out where people are,” she said.

“For those families that are still waiting, those 38 individuals unaccounted for, we understand that it’s a really concerning time, and we’ll continue to do what we can to try and locate those people.”
Earlier, the minister for the Pacific, Pat Conroy, told Radio National the government was “focused on establishing their whereabouts and supporting their families”.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat) has received nearly 800 calls in relation to the floods, with 18 Australian personnel having travelled to Nepal to join staff on the ground.
More humanitarian and disaster relief from Australia was due to arrive in Nepal on Wednesday afternoon.
Another Australian, 25-year-old Cara Severino, was safely located last week.
After an Australian in Tibet made contact with family and Dfat yesterday, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said the government was “incredibly thankful”.
“It’s hard to imagine the sense of relief their loved ones must be feeling after what will have been an incredibly harrowing few days.”
The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet.
More than 4,400 people are missing.
Wong said the government needed to “remain realistic” about the days ahead.
“Communications remain difficult, infrastructure has been destroyed and many areas are still difficult to reach,” she said.
“As each day passes, our grave concerns for those still unaccounted for inevitably grow.
“Our thoughts remain firmly with all those waiting for news of family and friends, and with the search and rescue teams working in extraordinarily difficult circumstances.”
Australia has sent a $8m assistance package for affected communities on the border between Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet.
Nepal has deployed nearly 20,000 security personnel to support search and rescue, and Chinese state media has reported that 2,141 emergency personnel have been deployed.

articles.title: Alex Eala's fans descend on US Open, bearing Filipino flags, lots of love
articles.summary: NEW YORK — The Alex Eala fans came bearing Filipino flags, and wearing hats telling her to fight on (“Laban Alex”). They cheered her sizzling groundstrokes, documented her volleys and…

blocks.text: NEW YORK — The Alex Eala fans came bearing Filipino flags, and wearing hats telling her to fight on (“Laban Alex”). They cheered her sizzling groundstrokes, documented her volleys and serves in photos and video, and in some cases FaceTimed with friends or family.
And this was only at the practice courts.

It was about four hours before Eala was to take the court for her first-round U.S. Open match Monday night, and every seat at the practice court was filled. Many of Eala’s fans didn’t have tickets for the evening session. But they’d come to see their idol hit some tennis balls.

It was hardly surprising, given the enormous, ardent, ever-growing fan base that now surrounds the charismatic 21-year-old. This summer has seen Eala beat Iga Swiatek at Wimbledon and win her first tour singles title, at Washington. She’s at a career-best 18th in the world, and many think she’ll continue her ascent.

One of the fans watching on a rainy afternoon was Andrea Belen, at 21 the same age as Eala. Belen, a premed student at New York University, explained that she hadn’t been a big tennis fan until Eala came along — someone who looked just like her.

Belen’s father back home in Cleveland (the family’s originally from Laguna in the Philippines) also became a tennis fan out of pure admiration for Eala. “It’s his new obsession,” Belen said. “It’s become the family hobby.”
She and her friend, Sarah Frederick, had arrived at the practice court long before Eala was to appear, surmising correctly that the seats would fill quickly.

Belen explained that in the Philippines, basketball and boxing reign supreme, and the sports heroes are men. “It’s just really nice to see a woman out there,” Belen said. “Also, she speaks in our native language, Tagalog.”
As Belen chatted and Eala pounded her groundstrokes, a voice from the row behind Belen called out: “Yay, Alex!”

Ellene Santos had come to the tournament from Orlando, Florida. Like Belen and Frederick, she did not have tickets for the evening match. But Santos, 67, was thrilled to get her Eala fix, just the same. “I’m happy now,” she smiled.
With practice over, four retired nurses, all friends, headed for the exit. They were wearing bright blue hats emblazoned with the phrase, “Laban Alex,” an exhortation to “fight.”

“I love how Alex shows she is so proud to be from the Philippines,” said Joy Rodriguez, 65, explaining her ardent fandom. Her friend, Maria Espiritu, 67, said this was the first tennis tournament she’d ever attended.

Nearby, Frances Arespacochaga, 77, was taking photos with fellow attendees. Arespacochaga lives in Manila, and was in the United States visiting her sister in Massachusetts. Together they drove down to see Eala at the U.S. Open — bearing flags.
“She’s very intelligent, very articulate,” Arespacochaga said of Eala. “In her interviews you can see her values.”

Belen, who FaceTimed with her father during the practice session so he could see Eala, spoke of a special Filipino pride in the achievements of countrymen. Like gymnast Carlos Yulo, who won two gold medals at the Paris Olympics in 2024.
“Everyone went crazy,” she said. “We’re not that big of a country so those golds meant so much.”
She added: “We’re very loud when it comes to supporting our people.”
Should Eala stick around a while at the U.S. Open, it’s bound to get a lot louder.

articles.title: Peso hits 62.5:$1 anew amid Middle East tensions
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine peso weakened below the 62.5-per-dollar level on Wednesday to hit another record low, extending its slide as a stronger greenback and rising oil prices fueled…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine peso weakened below the 62.5-per-dollar level on Wednesday to hit another record low, extending its slide as a stronger greenback and rising oil prices fueled inflation concerns.
The local currency opened at 62.4 per dollar before widening its losses to an intraday low of 62.58 during morning trading, according to data from the Bankers Association of the Philippines.

The move came as renewed hostilities in the Middle East pushed oil prices higher and boosted demand for the dollar as a haven. Brent crude rose almost 1 percent on Wednesday, while the dollar held firm against major currencies.
On Tuesday, the peso closed at a record-low 62.40 as higher oil prices, geopolitical risks, and a stronger dollar weighed on the currency.
Earlier, MUFG Bank Ltd. said the Philippine peso remains Asia’s “weakest link,” despite the central bank’s recent rate hike, as policymakers balance inflation control with weak economic growth. /pai

articles.title: How to turn your smartphone into a gaming console
articles.summary: Let’s be honest: even the most die-hard gamers eventually hit that “What should we play next?” moment. You know the feeling. You’ve played your usual favorites, beaten the same levels, and settled…

blocks.text: Let’s be honest: even the most die-hard gamers eventually hit that “What should we play next?” moment.
You know the feeling. You’ve played your usual favorites, beaten the same levels, and settled the same friendly rivalries with your Katropa more times than you can count.
Sometimes, all you need is a fresh game to make gaming exciting again.
That’s where TNT and Blacknut come in.

The value mobile brand has teamed up with Blacknut to give TNT subscribers access to more than 1,000 premium video games streamed directly from the cloud without the hassle of downloading massive game files or investing in a gaming console.
And because the games are streamed from the cloud, all you need is a TNT-powered smartphone and a reliable connection to jump into a new gaming adventure.
The shift to console-like gaming on mobile
KaTropas nationwide can sign up for the Blacknut Cloud Gaming service at Blacknut Smart for as low as P145 per week, charged directly to their prepaid load.
There’s no credit card required. After a quick OTP verification, subscribers can start playing through their mobile browser.
No console. No high-end gaming rig. No waiting around for huge game downloads.
Just pick a game and play.
And with more than 1,000 titles in the library, finding something new to play with your Katropa suddenly becomes a lot easier.
Something for everyone
The best part? There’s something for practically every kind of gamer.

If your barkada thrives on chaos, Overcooked! & Overcooked! 2 is practically a recipe for disaster and in the best possible way. Players have to prepare, cook, and serve meals while racing against the clock. Between chopping ingredients, washing dishes, and trying not to burn everything, communication with your teammates is key. Expect plenty of laughter, shouting, and the occasional blame game.

Basketball fans can take the rivalry to the virtual court with NBA 2K23. Build your dream team, recreate iconic basketball moments, or challenge your tropa to a one-on-one showdown. With NBA stars and legends in the lineup, it’s an easy choice for settling those “Sino ang mas magaling?” debates.

For a healthy dose of nostalgia, Nickelodeon All-Star Brawl brings familiar cartoon favorites into one fast-paced fighting game. Whether it’s a free-for-all or a team battle, the game offers a fun way to revisit characters many grew up watching except this time, with everyone throwing punches.

Meanwhile, fans of old-school arcade action can revisit the legendary Double Dragon franchise with Double Dragon Gaiden: Rise of the Dragons. The modern take combines classic beat-’em-up action with tag-team gameplay and roguelite mechanics, giving players plenty of enemies to take down and combos to master.
Solo play is highlighted
Not every gaming session has to be about beating the highest score.

For those who prefer getting lost in a good story, Assassin’s Creed Unity takes players to revolutionary Paris, where up to four players can team up for co-op missions and heists while exploring the city and uncovering its secrets.

And if post-apocalyptic survival is more your thing, Far Cry New Dawn puts players in a world trying to rebuild after a global catastrophe. Once co-op mode is unlocked, friends can join forces and take on the campaign together because surviving the end of the world is arguably more fun with the whole tropa.
Connected with cloud, great data packages
TNT is also giving subscribers more ways to stay connected while gaming with SAYA All 109, which comes with 7GB of open-access data plus 10GB of 5G data.

For gamers, a good connection can make all the difference. TNT subscribers can tap into Smart’s network, which has recently been recognized by Ookla® for Best Mobile Latency and Best Mobile Video Experience.
With cloud gaming eliminating the need for massive downloads and TNT making access to data and gaming more affordable, trying something new no longer has to mean spending big.
So the next time the tropa starts complaining that “wala nang bagong game,” you already know what to do.
Grab your phone, pick a title, and let the gaming begin.

articles.title: Williams sisters Serena and Venus start US Open doubles bid
articles.summary: NEW YORK — Serena Williams is getting back on the court against Maya Joint — this time with sister Venus by her side. The Williams sisters were drawn Tuesday to face the team of Hao-Ching Chan and…

blocks.text: Serena Williams, left, first bumps Venus Williams, right, both of the United States, during a women’s doubles match against Marta Kostyuk, of Ukraine, and Peyton Stearns, also of the United States, at the Cincinnati Open tennis tournament, Monday, Aug. 17, 2026, in Mason, Ohio. (AP Photo/Kareem Elgazzar)
NEW YORK — Serena Williams is getting back on the court against Maya Joint — this time with sister Venus by her side.
The Williams sisters were drawn Tuesday to face the team of Hao-Ching Chan and Joint, who beat Serena at Wimbledon this summer, in their opening women’s doubles match at the US Open.
Serena Williams, 44, returned this year after four years out of action and lost to Joint, a 20-year-old from Australia, 6-3, 6-7 (6), 6-3.
She injured her knee in the match and had to pull out of her planned doubles match at the All England Club with Venus, 46.
But they are set to compete at the US Open, where the Williams sisters won the title in 1999 and 2009 and are 27-7 in their nine appearances.
They last played in 2022, losing in the first round in what was expected to be Serena’s final match in Flushing Meadows.
Joint and Chan are the No. 14-seeded team.
The first round of the women’s doubles tournament begins Thursday.

articles.title: Nepal’s disaster response: Drones deliver food, carry bodies
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — On Monday, an unusual scene unfolded in the skies over Benighat, Dhading, one of the areas devastated by last week’s floods. An unmanned aircraft flew overhead carrying a human…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — On Monday, an unusual scene unfolded in the skies over Benighat, Dhading, one of the areas devastated by last week’s floods.
An unmanned aircraft flew overhead carrying a human body.

The drone had been deployed to retrieve a body from an area that rescuers found difficult and dangerous to navigate. Seven bodies were eventually airlifted by drones from Benighat-3 to Benighat-5 under the supervision of security personnel.
It was an extraordinary use of a technology that, barely a decade ago, was largely associated with international search-and-rescue teams responding to disasters in Nepal.

When a 7.8-magnitude earthquake struck Nepal in 2015, killing thousands and destroying large parts of Kathmandu Valley and other areas, international agencies brought drones to help search for survivors, assess damage and support recovery.
Since then, advances in local technology and the growing interest of Nepali youths have helped create a homegrown drone expertise.
The technology is now finding use far beyond aerial photography and mapping.
This spring, drones helped transport heavy loads between Everest Base Camp and Camp I in the Khumbu Icefall in just six to seven minutes—a journey that can take humans up to seven hours.
They carried emergency oxygen tanks, medicines, ropes and ladders to precarious locations, reducing the need for Sherpas to repeatedly undertake one of the most dangerous jobs on the mountain.
The Khumbu Icefall is notorious for shifting ice blocks, deep crevasses and avalanches. A bad day can mean being buried under tonnes of snow and ice.
Drones have also been used to scout shifting crevasses and map ice walls, allowing Sherpa guides to identify dangerous areas before entering them.

With 3D mapping capabilities, drones can remotely scan icy landscapes such as the Khumbu Icefall and measure the length and depth of crevasses. Such information allows climbers and guides to better assess hazards, including the possibility of avalanches and collapsing ice slabs.
Now, the technology is proving its value downstream—in communities hit by floods and landslides.
In Devighat-3 of Nuwakot, one of the worst-hit areas, villagers on Sunday experienced a different kind of disaster relief.
A loudspeaker announcement suddenly came from above.
An AI-enabled drone was flying over the village, following a person before reaching a group of residents. Its speaker switched on and began asking questions.
Do you have water? Raise your hand.
Do you have food? Raise your hand.
Do you have medicine? Raise your hand.
“Based on the villagers’ response, we make an assessment for what they require and send the delivery through drones,” said Milan Pandey, director of Airlift Technology and a drone pilot.
The drone also asked villagers to provide a contact number or address, which could be written on a placard or even in the mud.
Drone operators receive the signals and process the needs of the stranded people.
The approach is particularly useful in areas where roads and bridges have been destroyed and people on opposite sides of a river can no longer reach each other.
“We supplied at least 1.5 tonnes of emergency supplies, including food, to the affected areas in three days,” Pandey said.

On Monday, the team dropped food and other logistics on the top of a four-story school building in Devighat. The ward chairman was informed and later collected the cargo for distribution among villagers.

Drone operators say their role in disaster response remains limited by payload capacity, range and weather conditions. But where conventional transport is impossible, the impact can be disproportionate to their size.
“It’s the cheapest mode of transporting supplies compared to choppers,” operators say.
And in Benighat on Monday, drones took on perhaps their most unusual role yet: carrying the dead.
“We airlifted seven bodies from Benighat-3 to Benighat-5 under the supervision of the security forces, from a place where people can hardly navigate,” said Pandey.

The eight-member drone team, led by Hami Nepal, includes personnel from GarudX, Nepal Police, Nepal Army and the Armed Police Force. Hami Nepal was previously led by the current home minister, Sudan Gurung, during the Gen Z protests in September last year.
The team has been using the DJI FlyCart 100, a heavy-lift industrial cargo drone capable of carrying logistics weighing up to 85 kilograms and operating over a range of up to four kilometers.

Other drones have been deployed to inspect rivers and their banks in the search for missing people. Thermal drones can detect signs of living people, potentially allowing rescuers to locate survivors in areas that are inaccessible or too dangerous to enter.
The technology has also been taken underground.
Drone operators have used unmanned aircraft inside the tunnel of the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, where scores of workers are believed to have been trapped following the floods.
“We reached platform 1 of the project and saw the tunnel filled with water and rocks,” said Adarsha Bhusal, one of the drone operators. “It’s risky and challenging to get inside.”
The drone found no trace of life inside the tunnel during the operation, he said.

Around 900 workers have been reported missing at various hydropower projects along the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi rivers, according to the Independent Power Producers’ Association of Nepal, the umbrella organization of private power producers.
The expanding use of drones in Nepal’s disaster response reflects how quickly the technology has evolved from a niche tool into a potential emergency-response system.

Also known as unmanned aerial vehicles, drones can produce orthophotos and topographical maps with a level of detail that can exceed conventional satellite imagery, according to the World Bank assessment report. Because they can be deployed quickly, they can provide real-time information to emergency teams assessing rapidly changing conditions.

“Specialised sensors can also detect minute changes in topography. Such data could help authorities identify areas at risk of landslides and floods and potentially provide early warning before disasters strike,” the multilateral funding agency said.
For Nepal, this technology is becoming increasingly important.

Nepal, located in the central part of the Himalayan range, is experiencing rapid environmental and climatic changes that are increasing its exposure to floods, landslides, glacier-related hazards and other disasters.

The World Bank argues that Nepal needs to become more resilient to an unpredictable and changing climate through greater use of disruptive technologies, including drones, satellite technology and geospatial analytics.
The country’s drone ecosystem began taking root after the 2015 earthquake, when international agencies introduced and deployed the technology during recovery operations.
A decade later, much of that capability is being developed and operated locally.
Nepal’s experience could eventually become relevant beyond its borders, according to the World Bank.

The country’s private sector has already provided drone-based services to Bhutan for multi-hazard risk assessment, demonstrating how Nepal’s growing expertise could be exported to other countries facing similar climate-related risks.
From the summit of Everest to flooded villages in the valleys below, drones are increasingly filling gaps where people cannot safely go.
They are delivering food and medicine, mapping hazards, searching for survivors, inspecting flooded tunnels and, now, transporting bodies.

“For a country repeatedly exposed to earthquakes, floods, landslides and mountain hazards, the rise of locally developed drone technology could mark a significant shift in how Nepal responds to disasters—putting eyes, cargo and rescue capability into places where human access is simply too dangerous,” said Pandey.
Airlift Technology, led by Pandey, assembles drones in Kathmandu by importing their parts.
“We just need an appropriate policy to promote such a life-saving machine,” he said. /dl

articles.title: Zamboanga del Sur highway crash death toll climbs to 7, 13 hurt
articles.summary: PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur – The fatalities in the highway tragedy in Dumalinao, Zamboanga del Sur, involving a speeding van that allegedly lost its brakes on Tuesday noon, have climbed to…

blocks.text: PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur – The fatalities in the highway tragedy in Dumalinao, Zamboanga del Sur, involving a speeding van that allegedly lost its brakes on Tuesday noon, have climbed to seven, and 13 others were injured, the local government unit (LGU) said.
Initial reports Tuesday afternoon confirmed only six individuals dead, five of them on the spot.

The Dumalinao government expressed its sympathies to the victims of the road disaster, urging the public to refrain from sharing unverified information, photos, or the victims’ identities, and to respect the privacy of affected families.
“To everyone affected by this tragedy, you are in our thoughts and prayers,” the LGU said in a statement issued Tuesday evening.
The LGU also acknowledged the different responders who immediately rushed to the crash site at the national highway in Barangay Paglaum.

The immediate responders included the Dumalinao Municipal Police Station, Municipal Fire Station, Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MDRRMO), Rural Health Unit (RHU), traffic enforcers, and concerned community members.

Dumalinao Mayor Raul Famor said additional support arrived later from the Zamboanga del Sur Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (PDRRMO), the Pagadian City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (CDRRMO), and the Regional, Provincial, and City Bureau of Fire Protection Special Rescue Force (SRF).
“They joined in the difficult rescue and recovery efforts,” he said.
Responders worked together to retrieve trapped victims, administer first aid and triage, and transport the injured to medical facilities in Pagadian City.
The clearing operation was completed at around 4:15 p.m. with the assistance of municipal motor pool personnel, who used the local government’s boom truck to remove the vehicles involved.
An initial police report said the crash occurred when a speeding silver metallic passenger van allegedly lost its brakes, hit a motorcycle, and rammed into a parked wing van.
The van was bound for Pagadian City from Ipil, Zamboanga Sibugay.
Authorities said an investigation is still ongoing to determine the circumstances behind the accident./coa

articles.title: Dalaguete: Man nabbed after hacking, wounding elderly neighbor
articles.summary: CEBU CITY, Philippines — A 39-year-old man was arrested after he hacked a senior citizen using a bolo in Sitio Camintong, Barangay Malones, Dalaguete town, on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, at around…

blocks.text: CEBU CITY, Philippines — A 39-year-old man was arrested after he hacked a senior citizen using a bolo in Sitio Camintong, Barangay Malones, Dalaguete town, on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, at around 6:10 p.m.
The victim was identified as Jose Villahermosa, 60 years old, a resident of the area.
Meanwhile, the suspect was identified by authorities as Greg Selada, 39, a laborer and neighbor of the victim.
Earlier, the Dalaguete Municipal Police Station received a call from a concerned citizen reporting the hacking incident.
The police immediately responded and went to the area.
Based on their initial investigation, the suspect and the victim had a previous misunderstanding which resulted in a fistfight.
Later, a witness told police, that the suspect waited for the victim to pass by near the latter’s house.
When the suspect saw the senior citizen, he suddenly hacked the latter using a bolo, hitting the elderly man on the right forearm.
The victim was immediately brought to Isidro Kintanar Memorial Hospital for medical treatment.
Meanwhile, the suspect was immediately arrested by the responding police.
The suspect was detained at the Dalaguete Police Station pending the filing of physical injury charges.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Consumers in the Visayas may face power interruptions on Wednesday as some large coal plants remain offline.
In an advisory, the National Grid Corp. of the Philippines said a red alert would be up over the Visayas from 3 p.m. to 4 p.m., and 5 p.m. to 9 p.m.
The grid operator said the yellow alert will be from 1 p.m. to 3 p.m., from 4 p.m. to 5 p.m., and from 9 p.m. to 10 p.m.
Mindanao, with portions of Visayas’ power supply also comes from this region, is also seeing a thin supply. The grid will be under a yellow alert from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m., and 5 p.m. to 8 p.m.

A yellow alert indicates that available power reserves are thinning, meaning any unexpected plant outage could trigger service interruptions. A red alert indicates that the supply cannot meet the demand, raising the risk of rotational brownouts unless we manage consumption effectively. /pai

articles.title: NLEx asked to explain flooding that caused heavy traffic in Pampanga
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) Corporation has been directed by the Toll Regulatory Board (TRB) to explain the flooding that occurred at Tulaoc Bridge near San Simon town in…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) Corporation has been directed by the Toll Regulatory Board (TRB) to explain the flooding that occurred at Tulaoc Bridge near San Simon town in Pampanga that caused heavy traffic in the past few days.

In a letter shared by the Department of Transportation (DOTr) on Wednesday, the TRB wrote to NLEx Corporation on August 31 directing the firm to submit within three days a detailed explanation for the flooding situation, as well as its proposed measures to mitigate the flooding in San Simon and Tulaoc, Pampanga “to further avoid its recurrence.”

Due to the heavy rainfall brought by the southwest monsoon last weekend, motorists were stuck along that portion of the expressway. Many of them spent longer hours on the road than their usual travel time.

In a separate letter, the TRB instructed NLEx Corporation to consider reimbursing the toll fees of Class 1 vehicles that were “compelled to make a U-turn due to the flooding incidents in the affected area.”

The TRB also said it expects the corporation to alert motorists three hours before the expected rainfall through Variable Message Signs (VMS), portable VMS, and other messaging platforms that the San Simon-Pulillan Segment of NLEx will be closed to traffic if the water level reaches critical level due to heavy rainfall.

“During such circumstances, NLEX Corporation is likewise directed to closely coordinate with the Department of Transportation (DOTr) and TRB, to jointly ensure the timely implementation of appropriate flood mitigation measures and other necessary interventions, with the primary objective of ensuring the safety of the motoring public and minimizing traffic disruption,” the TRB wrote.

Last Monday, the Metro Pacific Tollways Corporation, the operator of NLEx, apologized to motorists for inconveniences due to flooding and vowed to install concrete barriers in affected areas along the expressway. /jpv

articles.title: ‘Cherish the Earth’: Pope Leo condemns harm to environment
articles.summary: CASTEL GANDOLFO — Pope Leo XIV on Tuesday held a special mass for the environment, urging people to listen to the “melodious voice” of nature and condemning the destruction caused…

blocks.text: CASTEL GANDOLFO — Pope Leo XIV on Tuesday held a special mass for the environment, urging people to listen to the “melodious voice” of nature and condemning the destruction caused by wars.
The mass was held in the gardens of the papal summer residence in Castel Gandolfo near Rome.
“Let us place in silent mode the many noises generated by human activity so that we may hear the melodious voice of creation,” the pope said in his homily.
He said he hoped this would encourage awareness “of the responsibility that we bear both personally and collectively for preserving the original harmony”.
In a written message, the pope also urged followers to “cherish the Earth” and spoke of the “vicious cycle” between armed conflicts and environmental degradation.
“These phenomena are not unrelated; they are a single plea for healing and peace arising from a wounded world,” he wrote.
Pope Leo has repeatedly emphasized the need to protect the natural world.
In November last year, he urged “concrete actions” on climate change and complained that some leaders lacked the will to act.

He has followed in the footsteps of his predecessor Francis, whose 2015 encyclical “Laudato Si” denounced mankind’s ruthless exploitation of the environment and was hailed by experts for its scientific grounding. /dl

articles.title: Thousands pay homage to Bosnian Serb war criminal Mladic
articles.summary: SARAJEVO — Several thousand Bosnian Serbs paid tribute on Tuesday to former military commander and convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, who died while serving a life sentence for genocide.…

blocks.text: SARAJEVO — Several thousand Bosnian Serbs paid tribute on Tuesday to former military commander and convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, who died while serving a life sentence for genocide.

Mladic died on Thursday at the age of 84 in The Hague, where he was convicted of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity during the Bosnian war, including for his role in the Srebrenica massacre, Europe’s worst act of bloodshed since World War II.

Television images showed people gathered at the main square in central Banja Luka, the capital of Bosnia’s Serb entity, and them marching on the city’s principal boulevard holding up a banner proclaiming: “Commander, thank you for everything.”
Some lit smoke flares and waved flags of the Serb entity and then lit candles at a monument dedicated to Serb soldiers killed during the war and lined up to write messages in a condolence book.
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos on Monday criticised Serbia’s plans to bury Mladic with state honours.
Mladic’s conviction for wartime killings as the former Yugoslavia descended into carnage after the fall of communism led the international press to dub him the “Butcher of Bosnia”.
The 1992-1995 war left around 100,000 people dead and 2.2 million displaced.
Mladic was the military face of a brutal trio, led on the political side by ex-Yugoslav president Slobodan Milosevic and former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic. /dl

articles.title: Zelensky warns airlines Russian skies not safe due to Ukraine drones
articles.summary: KYIV — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday warned airlines and passengers that Russian airspace would be “completely unsafe” and filled with Ukrainian drones for the…

blocks.text: KYIV — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday warned airlines and passengers that Russian airspace would be “completely unsafe” and filled with Ukrainian drones for the duration of the war.

“Today, we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” he said in his nightly address.
“Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such — not a single civilian aircraft. There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” he said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin responded by branding Zelensky’s comments “a declaration of state terrorism”.
“They are asking us to resume negotiations… but you don’t negotiate with terrorists,” Putin said in a televised news conference.
More than four years after the start of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, both Moscow and Kyiv have intensified their deadly strikes.
At least 12 people were killed on Tuesday in Kyiv and the surrounding region during fresh massive overnight Russian strikes.
Air traffic at Russian airports is also regularly disrupted by the approach of Ukrainian drones, the number of which has increased in recent months.
“We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That is why we are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” Zelensky said.
“Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation,” he added. “The sky over Russia is currently for drones… as long as the war continues.”

He said Ukraine would, however, clear its drones from Russian skies when its partners requested it, “for the sake of diplomacy, for the sake of negotiations… for specific periods of time and in specific destinations”.
Diplomatic efforts under US mediation to end the conflict have stalled since the outbreak of war in the Middle East in February. /dl

articles.title: Iran strikes back against latest US attacks
articles.summary: TEHRAN — Iran launched strikes on Wednesday targeting American interests in Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan after vowing “severe punishment” in response to US attacks, including one that…

blocks.text: TEHRAN — Iran launched strikes on Wednesday targeting American interests in Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan after vowing “severe punishment” in response to US attacks, including one that the Iranian Red Crescent said left four people dead at a wedding celebration.
US Marine Corps base Camp Titin in Jordan was targeted for an “intense ballistic missile attack”, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said early Wednesday, according to Iranian news outlet Tasnim.

The Jordanian army said it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired from Iran, and did not confirm any injuries or hits on the US training camp located on the Gulf of Aqaba, near the borders with Israel and Saudi Arabia. Three other missiles landed in remote areas, it said.

Missile and drone attacks were also reported in Kuwait, where the army said they were responding to Iranian hostilities, and AFP reporters in Bahrain heard alert sirens for airborne attacks go off early Wednesday.

The latest round of conflict began when Washington hit Iranian targets on Sunday, the first known strikes in several weeks, after which Tehran’s forces targeted US troops in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, and projectiles struck two oil tankers in unclaimed attacks.

More US strikes came on Tuesday, with Iranian state television reporting that explosions were heard in the country’s south along the strategic Strait of Hormuz waterway and on an island in the Gulf, and that US forces hit an airport in the southern province of Kerman.

The Iranian Red Crescent said shrapnel from a US missile attack hit a home where a wedding celebration was taking place in the city of Kuhestak, killing four people, including a child, and wounding more than 50.
And the official IRNA news agency said that “four projectiles hit areas within the counties of Chabahar and Konarak,” without specifying whether there was any damage.

Asked if the US military had received any credible reports of civilian casualties from the Tuesday strikes, US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesperson, Captain Tim Hawkins, said “the US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC,” referring to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards.

CENTCOM had earlier said on X that the strikes followed “recent attempted attacks by (the Revolutionary Guards) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region”.

US President Donald Trump said the “large and powerful” strikes were “in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait” and “the Iranians shooting eight missiles, all successfully knocked down, at our Military Base in Jordan”.
Earlier, Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi warned on X that Washington “will regret its new attacks”, saying that “severe punishment awaits the aggressors”.
Tankers attacked
After six months of war, the foes remain at an impasse, with Iran keeping the Strait of Hormuz closed and the United States persisting with a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Washington said its forces attacked Iranian rocket launchers on the island of Larak on Sunday to prevent Tehran from planting mines in the strait’s key shipping lanes.
The Middle East war began in late February with the US and Israeli attacks on Iran that killed its supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
A fragile ceasefire between the United States and Iran collapsed after attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies flowed before the war.
Greek maritime risk management firm Marisks said Tuesday that two crude tankers were hit by “unknown projectiles” late the previous day.
One of the incidents had been publicised earlier by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency, which added that no casualties or environmental effects had been reported.
Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian meanwhile vowed Tuesday to match any US move to return to a deal aimed at ending the war.
He also warned that a return by the United States to “a policy of pressure and threats could derail the path of diplomacy”. /dl

articles.title: Will self-flying planes transform the skies?
articles.summary: Autonomous crop-spraying aircraft are leading the way in pilot-free flying.

blocks.text: Over an alfalfa field in California's San Joaquin Valley, a small crop-spraying plane is flying scarily low to the ground. There's little risk to humans though, as the plane is pilot-free.
"We can actually go lower than a human pilot can," says Russ Marotzke, as the aircraft skims over the crop.
Flying lower means less spray drift and therefore less chemicals are needed than in conventional manned crop-dusting, he says.
The pilotless plane belongs to Pyka, where Marotzke works as a flight test engineer.
Based in a converted Second World War hangar overlooking San Francisco Bay, the start-up makes self-flying aircraft without cockpits, designed either to spray crops or deliver cargo.
It is among a small group of companies racing to bring autonomous fixed-wing aircraft into commercial service.
Flying urban air taxis, so called electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft, have captured much of the attention around autonomous aviation.
But a quieter race is also under way to deploy self-flying planes, first for jobs like crop spraying and cargo delivery – and eventually, many of their makers hope, carrying passengers too.

"A fully scaled, ubiquitous passenger operation is the holy grail," says Michael Norcia, Pyka's co-founder and CEO, who envisions a large fleet of minibus-capacity Pyka planes ferrying passengers up and down the US east and west coasts.
"There's a decent chance we'll get to that point before the eVTOL industry."
I've come to one of Pyka's crop-sprayer test sites, about 80km (50 miles) east of the company's factory and reached by a bumpy dirt road.
Today, Marotzke and a colleague are trying out a software update on a demonstration aircraft.
About a dozen Pyka aircraft are already in Brazil where they are used to spray crops such as cotton and soybeans, work previously carried out by human pilots.
The crop-spraying plane is fully electric, with its battery in the nose. It can fly for about 35 minutes and carries up to 300L of spray in a tank in its middle.
Pyka's planes are sometimes called large drones, but it seems an understatement: they all have 11.5m wingspans.

Inside a shipping container beside the field, the engineers highlight on a computer the area they want the aircraft to spray. The software then plans the route, taking account of obstacles such as nearby power lines that have already been mapped.

The take-off, down a runway beside the field, is seamless. About 15 minutes later, after sensing that it is running low on spray – water for today's purposes – the aircraft lands itself for a manual refill and demonstration battery swap. It then takes to the air again to resume spraying precisely where it left off.
Autonomous flight is different from autopilot.
Autopilot assists, much like cruise control and lane-keeping functions in a car.
Autonomous systems aim to handle the entire flight, including take-off and landing, with little or no human intervention, using algorithms to process sensor data and control the aircraft.
Self-flying planes have been slower to emerge than self-driving cars, despite operating in what is generally considered a more structured and predictable environment.
That is partly because big tech companies "doubled down" on cars, pouring vast sums into the technology, says Mykel Kochenderfer, an expert in safe aviation autonomy at Stanford University.
But it is also because aircraft are held to stricter safety standards than cars, creating a much higher bar for deployment.
"The consequences for air accidents can just be so severe," says Kochenderfer.

Military interest has been helping propel the technology. Many of the companies have defence contracts to demonstrate and trial their systems, often with fewer regulatory hurdles than on the civilian side, and some are even already supplying military customers, external.
In the US, the largest autonomous fixed-wing aircraft approved for commercial civilian use so far is Pyka's crop sprayer, which won authorization last year.

Though operations are limited to a tightly defined agricultural setting and require a ground operator and visual observer. It earlier secured similar approval in Brazil, where rules are more permissive.
Pyka aims to scale up production from around two dozen planes a year currently to 1000 by 2030. Each sells for $550,000, with customers trained to operate them.

The UK has yet to approve any such longer-term operations, though British firm Windracers is seeking permission to launch an autonomous cargo service in Shetland and Orkney. Its aircraft, designed to carry goods to remote areas, are also flying missions in Ukraine.
"It would be the first heavy-lift air cargo service by drone certainly in the UK and probably anywhere," says Stephen Wright, Windracers founder and chairman.

Supporters say autonomous aircraft could address pilot shortages, remove people from dangerous work such as crop spraying, improve efficiency – for example, by allowing aircraft to carry more cargo – and cut costs if one operator can oversee many planes.
They also argue automation could make flying safer, pointing to past declines in accidents as more automated systems have been introduced.
Pilots' groups remain wary.
The US Air Line Pilots Association (ALPA) calls removing pilots "a serious gamble with safety and a step too far".

The US National Agricultural Aviation Association, which represents crop dusting pilots, says small uncrewed aircraft can be hard for its aviators to see. Piloted planes, it adds, can spray a much larger area faster.
Pyka and Windracers are building aircraft from scratch, arguing this allows autonomy to be designed in from the outset and the aircraft tailored to the job.
Others are retrofitting existing larger planes.

Backed by Boeing's investment arm, US-based Reliable Robotics is currently testing its system on the Cessna 208B Grand Caravan, a single-pilot cargo plane that can carry about 1360kg of payload over hundreds of kilometers.

Retrofitting on certified aircraft lets the company focus exclusively on proving the autonomous system's safety rather than also having to seek approval for a new aircraft, says Robert Rose, its co-founder and CEO.

Merlin Labs, also US-based, has been working its way up through progressively larger military aircraft and is now applying its system to the two-pilot Lockheed Martin C-130J military transport plane, with commercial multi-crew cargo planes next.
"It is a common autonomy brain that can transition between different aircraft," explains Matt George, Merlin's founder and CEO.
The companies also differ in their approach to AI.
Reliable is avoiding it altogether, arguing it would complicate certification.
Merlin, meanwhile, is taking a far more AI-centric approach.
The divide is evident in so-called detect and avoid systems.
One of autonomous flight's biggest challenges is replicating a pilot's ability to spot and maneuver safely around other aircraft and obstacles, and there is virtually no margin for error.
With no perfect solution yet, companies are adding different sensor systems as well as duplicating those that already come as standard to provide extra back-up.
Reliable has added forward-looking air-to-air radar to detect other aircraft more than eight kilometers ahead, with software that follows fixed rules to decide how the plane should respond.
It is "better than a pilot's eyeballs" says Rose.
Merlin, meanwhile, is using AI-powered cameras to detect and classify objects.
Pyka has used lidar from the outset to detect trees, vehicles, large birds and terrain. But it's short range, so the company also plans to add AI-powered cameras, its first real use of AI onboard.
"For a lot of things there's no need to use AI…but for figuring out that six pixels in the distance are an airplane versus some other smudge, it is perfect territory," says Norcia.
The AI dilemma also extends to communicating with air traffic control.
In shared airspace, aircraft must be able to receive, interpret and respond to radio instructions, typically from air traffic control.
Reliable's solution is to have a remote pilot on the ground, initially fully trained, to handle communications and make safety-critical decisions.
Merlin plans to use generative AI, trained on thousands of hours of recorded exchanges, to interpret instructions and respond itself.
"Our problem is harder… but we want to move beyond remote piloting," says George.
Merlin plans to reduce pilots in stages, from two to one and eventually none.
Pyka, says Norcia, is content to let others "blaze the trail" in finding the best way to operate in shared airspace.
Meanwhile, even if fully autonomous passenger flight remains elusive, many expect the technology being pioneered will inch into commercial aviation, potentially making piloted flying safer.
That, notes ALPA, the US pilots' association, would be a welcome development.

articles.title: Could the man who murdered a Christian missionary and his sons walk free in India?
articles.summary: Dara Singh is serving a life sentence for burning alive Graham Staines and his two sons in Odisha in 1999.

blocks.text: Warning: This article contains details of violent death that some readers may find distressing
One of India's most shocking incidents of anti-Christian violence is back in the news more than a quarter of a century after it drew condemnation from around the world.

On Wednesday, the Supreme Court is due to take a call on a petition seeking release from prison by a man, who is convicted of killing Australian Christian missionary Graham Staines and his two young sons in 1999.

Dara Singh - whose real name is Rabindra Kumar Pal - has been in jail since his arrest in 2000, serving a life sentence for burning alive the Australian missionary and his six and 10-year-old sons in a village in the eastern state of Odisha (formerly Orissa).

Staines had spent 30 years working with leprosy patients, but Singh and his associates from Hindu hardline groups had accused him of forcibly converting poor Hindus from disadvantaged castes and tribals to Christianity.

The viciousness of the crime sent shockwaves through India's minority Christian community and caused global outrage. Now reports that Singh may be set free have brought alive memories of the heinous crime.
Staines lived in Baripada in Mayurbhanj district, where he worked among the local tribal community.

On the night of their murder on 22 January 1999, Staines and his sons had attended a Christian gathering in Manoharpur, a remote village in the neighbouring district of Keonjhar. They were sleeping in their jeep when a mob of 60 to 70 people led by Singh surrounded their vehicle, set fire to it and prevented them from escaping.

As Singh went on the run after the crime, police put up posters all over the state, offering an 800,000-rupee (approximately $18,000 then) reward for information leading to his capture. Reports at the time said he was helped by villagers and tribals who eulogised him as "a modern-day Tarzan who plays with elephants and rides tigers". He was arrested a year later during an overnight raid on a jungle hideout.

In a sensational interview, external with the India Today magazine's Ruben Banerjee from prison a few months later, he denied killing Staines and his children but said he "did not like Graham Staines" and had "spearheaded the movement against missionaries".

"Missionaries have been targeting our religion. They have been converting Hindus by deceit and inducements. Our religion is under siege. As a true Hindu, it was my responsibility to oppose them," he said. "Since I was possibly the most famous name in the region, the police implicated me in the killings."
Singh added that he was "prepared to be a martyr for the cause of Hindus" but believed that he would never get convicted.

His optimism was misplaced - in 2003, a trial court sentenced Singh to death and 12 others to life imprisonment. Two years later, the high court commuted his death sentence. It confirmed the life term of his accomplice Mahendra Hembram but freed 11 others, saying there was not enough evidence to support their convictions.
In January 2011, the Supreme Court upheld Singh's life sentence, refusing the prosecutors' plea to reinstate the death penalty.

The Staines murder was not the only crime Singh was guilty of. In 2007, he was convicted for two other heinous crimes he committed against religious minorities in 1999 - the same year he murdered the Australian missionary and his children.

He received life sentences, external for leading a mob that set fire to a church and killed Catholic priest Arul Das with an arrow as he tried to flee the burning building and, in the second instance, for beating and burning to death a Muslim garment trader Shaikh Rahaman.

Police had registered 10 cases accusing Singh of involvement in hijacking trucks of Muslim traders transporting cows - an animal many Hindus consider sacred - and setting them free. In his interview, Singh denied being "involved personally", saying "my supporters might have done it". But he admitted that he was "actively involved in the movement against illegal trade in cows and cowslaughter" which "had to be stopped at any cost".

Church leaders had alleged the attacks were carried out at the behest of hardline Hindu organisation Bajrang Dal but Singh denied he was a member and an enquiry commission, led by retired top court judge DP Wadhwa, later ruled that he had worked alone.

Graham Staines' widow, Gladys, who stayed on in India with her daughter Esther until July 2004, said she had "forgiven" Dara Singh in the Christian spirit. "Forgiveness opens up the path of healing," she said.

In July 2024, Singh filed a plea for remission in the top court, saying he was entitled to be released because he had spent more than 25 years in prison. He said his conduct had been good in jail and expressed remorse for his actions.
The 62-year-old blamed the crime on "the fervour of youth" in his petition, external seeking early release.
"The petitioner acknowledges and deeply regrets the transgressions committed more than two decades ago.

"In the fervour of youth, fuelled by impassioned reactions to the brutal history of India, the petitioner's psyche momentarily lost restraint and it is imperative for the court to scrutinise not merely the actions but the underlying intent, noting that there was no personal animosity harboured towards any victim," he wrote.
Last year, the top court asked the state government to take a call on his plea, but the authorities have so far not told the court what they intend to do.
At the last hearing on 19 August, authorities told the court that the Sentence Review Board (SRB), which is examining Singh's plea, was waiting for some more paperwork and sought an adjournment.

The two-judge bench of Justices Manoj Misra and Vijay Bishnoi expressed their annoyance at the several adjournments the state had sought in the case and said if the SRB failed to decide Singh's plea by 2 September, the court would. "You take a decision, whichever way you want. If you do not take a decision, then we will."

Reports that Singh may walk free if the state government or the court accept his remission petition have led to some disquiet in India's 30-million Christian community - some of it because of unease over his earlier statements.

In his 2000 India Today interview, he said he had "no regrets" and "will never regret" killing Staines' children. "When Hindus die, others don't cry. Why should we weep when others die? Whatever has happened is right. Whatever will happen will also be right."
If released from prison, he said, he would "go back to what I have been doing - oppose cow slaughter and conversions".
"The government must stop them. If they are not stopped, more people might get killed. Anything can happen," he added.

In an article on the Union of Catholic News (UCN) website, human rights and Christian political activist John Dayal wrote recently that remission after decades in jail is "not unusual" in India and "the principle behind it - that punishment should allow for reform and eventual return to society - is humane".

But the anxiety among religious minorities in Odisha "is not abstract given the state's history of anti-Christian violence", Dayal points out, citing the Kandhamal riots of 2008, in which dozens were killed and tens of thousands were displaced.

"The Staines murders were not an ordinary homicide but a public, theatrical act of terror, intended to be seen and understood as a warning. The killings of Father Arul Doss and Sheikh Rehman extended that same message," he writes.

"What remains to be seen is not whether Singh will eventually walk free, but how the government conducts itself around that decision...and whether minority communities are given any reassurance," Dayal adds.

articles.title: Cup noodles made with cold water? BBC tries Japan's viral snack
articles.summary: The BBC's Tokyo correspondent Kurumi Mori tries Japan's latest food trend, instant noodles made using cold water.

blocks.text: The BBC's Tokyo correspondent Kurumi Mori tries Japan's latest food trend, instant noodles made with cold water. The product has sold out in the country after going viral online.
Unlike regular cup noodles, this version is designed to be a cooling summer snack, but does it really do the job? The BBC puts them to the taste test.

articles.title: Ariana Grande ends tour and steps back from public life
articles.summary: The star makes an emotional farewell as she wraps up a tour she's described as her "last hurrah".

blocks.text: Ariana Grande made an emotional exit on Tuesday night, as she wrapped up her Eternal Sunshine tour, and prepared to step back from public life.
The singer was occasionally close to tears - most notably during One Last Time, the song that took on extra meaning as an anthem for survivors of the 2017 Manchester terror attack.
"London, I'm going to need you to help me on this one," she said, kneeling down to be near the audience throughout the performance.
Last month, Grande announced a break from all future public-facing appearances following months of intense speculation about her health and appearance.
The step-back includes Grande's withdrawal from a production of Stephen Sondheim's Sunday in the Park with George at London's Barbican next summer.
She was due to appear alongside her Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey. He also pulled out of the production on Tuesday.
On stage in London, Grande showed no signs of fragility or poor health - other than a foot injury that required her to swap her trademark stilettos for a succession of knee-high platform boots.
Nonetheless, she sprang across the stage in sync with her dancers, often on tip-toe to compensate for the lost height of her high heels.
But her composure slipped during the song Nowhere, Nobody, as she sang the line: "Hard to believe in a perfect ending."
The blip was short-lived, though. Professional to the core, Grande was never less than magnetic on stage.

Even before that announcement, Grande had described the Eternal Sunshine tour - which started in the US in June - as "one last hurrah", saying she wanted to take more acting roles after her Oscar-nominated performance in Wicked.
That meant her 10 show residency at London's O2 Arena represented many fans' last chance to see her in concert.
They flew in from all over the world - from China and Australia and cities all across Europe - with 200,000 people attending the London dates alone.
On the second night, Grande surprised the audience by bringing out her Wicked co-star Cynthia Erivo for a rendition of their movie duet For Good.
Across the board, reviews were positive.

"There's no question about it - Ariana Grande is one of the best singers of her generation," wrote Rolling Stone magazine, external, noting that "there were no signs" of the singer "struggling or not wanting to be there".
The Telegraph called the show "flawless", external, praising its "Hollywood-indebted" staging, and Grande's "genuine affection for Britain".
The BBC's review highlighted quieter songs like Imperfect For You, describing them as "delicate and gorgeous and strangely intimate in a room of 20,000 people".

But Guardian writer Kate Solomon said she was "gripped by genuine concern", external for Grande, even when she was enjoying the show, adding: "I really hope this tour does not go down in history for the wrong reasons".
The NME, by contrast, was left breathless by the star's physical prowess.
"Throughout the show," marvelled Nick Levine, external, "she skips across the stage in skyscraper heels that most drag performers would baulk at."
That wasn't the case on the final night, however, due to what Grande described as a "deep cut" on her foot.
Writing on Instagram, she assured fans the injury wasn't serious, insisting she was "on the mend" and would complete her final shows "even if I am a few inches shorter than usual".
She did so with a huge smile spread across her face, leaning into the big notes of Dangerous Woman, and sprinting across the stage during Break Free - one of many up-tempo highlights.
She ended the show as she always does - attached to a harness, ascending into the rafters of the O2 and disappearing.
Fans were left wondering when, if ever, they'd see her perform again.

articles.title: DOT eyes more visa-free gateways for Chinese tourists
