articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Spurred by a surge in Chinese tourist arrivals following relaxed visa rules, the Department of Tourism (DOT) is pushing to expand the 14-day visa-free scheme beyond the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Spurred by a surge in Chinese tourist arrivals following relaxed visa rules, the Department of Tourism (DOT) is pushing to expand the 14-day visa-free scheme beyond the country’s main gateways to draw more visitors to secondary destinations.

Tourism Secretary Dita Angara-Mathay said that aside from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (Naia) in Metro Manila and Mactan-Cebu International Airport in Cebu, the DOT wants the visa-free arrangement extended to other gateways serving major tourist destinations, including Clark, Caticlan, Palawan and Bohol, among others.

“If we’re going to get all the other agencies to sign up on this, then we can expect a lot more charter flights from China and a lot more arrivals,” Angara-Mathay said on the sidelines of the DOT’s partnership renewal with online booking platform Klook on Tuesday.

According to her, the DOT has prepared a position paper laying out the economic case for the expansion, backed by statistical analysis showing what she described as the “profound effect” of easier visa access on Philippine tourism.
Booming Chinese arrivals

Based on preliminary eTravel registrations, China recorded the biggest jump in tourist arrivals from January to August, with 310,088 visitors so far this year, up 69.15 percent year-on-year—an increase that the DOT chief said strengthens the case for expanding the visa-free arrangement.
“Can you imagine if you expand to cover more areas?” Angara-Mathay said.
That made China the country’s fourth-largest source of foreign visitors behind the United States, South Korea and Japan.

Overall, the Philippines recorded about 4.11 million arrivals as of Aug. 31 based on eTravel data. The DOT is targeting between 6.4 million and 6.8 million arrivals this year, although Angara-Mathay said reaching 7 million remains possible.
“It looks like, and we might just be sure to hit this target. And even more, especially if we’re able to get more tourist arrivals from target markets,” she said.
Secondary cities push
Apart from expanding visa-free entry, the DOT is pushing for more air links between secondary cities in the Philippines and key overseas markets, according to Tourism Assistant Secretary Ren Sapitan.
Tourism Undersecretary Stanley Ng, a former Philippine Airlines president, has been leading talks with carriers on potential new services, particularly involving China and South Korea.

Rather than concentrating connectivity on major hubs such as Seoul, the DOT wants airlines to explore secondary cities abroad and link them through charter flights to Philippine destinations such as Bohol and Caticlan. /cb

articles.title: ‘Foreign malign influence’ going ‘street level’ – AFP
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — “Foreign malign influence (FMI)” operations targeting the Philippines are adopting a more “street-level” approach, using the Filipino language to integrate themselves into…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — “Foreign malign influence (FMI)” operations targeting the Philippines are adopting a more “street-level” approach, using the Filipino language to integrate themselves into divisive domestic issues and thus becoming harder to detect, a military official said on Tuesday.

Reservist Rear Adm. Roy Vincent Trinidad, the Armed Forces of the Philippines spokesperson on the West Philippine Sea (WPS), said the shift became apparent in the “first quarter” of the year, as the WPS maritime issue became linked to other local controversies.

The intended discourse “used to be clearly identifiable as pro-Davao [when it comes to] West Philippine Sea issues,” Trinidad said in a press briefing. But “today, the formalized influence approach is they meddle with local issues.”

He cited the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, the flood control scandal, and criticism against President Marcos and Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro Jr. among the issues the AFP is monitoring for possible FMIs.
Raid on Chinese-run firm
One local issue which, he said, has been exploited by foreign propaganda is the May 15 raid on Chinese-run Philippine Sanjia Steel Corp.

The raid at an ecozone in Misamis Oriental led to the arrest of 69 Chinese nationals and the discovery of radioactive materials in the Sanjia plant. The Chinese Embassy at the time filed a diplomatic protest over the arrests.
Trinidad said “It is now more difficult to detect [foreign influence] because it is already mixing with local issues.”
He also said the language “now is [more] prevalent in Tagalog,” whereas “before, it was mostly in English.”
“Attacks on the SND (secretary of national defense), attacks on [Rear Adm.] Jay Tarriela are now in Tagalog,” Trinidad noted. Tarriela serves as Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson on WPS issues.
He also noted a shift in language among officials of the Chinese Embassy.
“When it’s the deputy spokesperson of the Chinese Embassy, they use Tagalog and street-level [phrasing]. When it’s the spokesman of the Chinese Embassy, his tone is diplomatic,” Trinidad said.
This shift to a more informal messaging may be part of efforts to make social-media content harder to identify as foreign and more acceptable to Filipinos, Trinidad said.
“Definitely, this is part of their approach. They are adjusting to make it more acceptable to our fellow countrymen, so they can conceal it better,” he said.
In an advice to netizens encountering such content, he said: “Before ‘liking,’ before forwarding, before clicking, make sure carefully if what you are reading is true.” /cb

articles.title: Remarkable US oil deal puzzles analysts - and angers many Venezuelans
articles.summary: Amounting to 65 billion barrels of crude, the deal is labelled by one ex-envoy as a colonialist "fever dream".

blocks.text: From the moment elite US troops swooped into Nicolás Maduro's compound in Caracas to forcibly remove him from power in January, President Donald Trump made clear that securing control over Venezuela's oil resources was a key goal of his administration.
The United States would "run" Venezuela, he said at the time, and manage the sale of Venezuelan oil for the foreseeable future.

The signing of a huge US-Venezuela oil deal in Caracas on Wednesday marks the fruition of that plan. The agreement grants a US-led company 100-year concessions over 17 oilfields in Venezuela, amounting to a staggering 65 billion barrels of crude. That equates to more than a fifth of the country's proven oil reserves.
Beyond the eye-watering numbers, both sides heralded the deal as good for their respective nations.

President Trump called it "the biggest oil deal in world history", while the interim Venezuelan President, Delcy Rodríguez, said the agreement was "historic", and would generate $100bn (£74bn) in investment and more than $200bn in tax revenue.
Others profoundly disagreed.

"This is a terrible deal. [Rodríguez] has given away 20% of the national patrimony for nothing," said Trump's former special representative on Venezuela and Iran, Elliott Abrams. "I think she is simply complying with the demands she's getting from Washington."

On Tuesday, the White House released a fact sheet which set out some details of the deal's framework. The US government will work alongside a private business in Venezuela called North American Blue Energy Partners (Nabep), the second largest private oil producer in Venezuela after Chevron.

One extraordinary detail of how the Trump administration will work with Nabep is that the US government will have "veto power over the appointment of any member of the board of directors, and a majority of Nabep's board of directors must be US citizens".
With the ongoing US war with Iran increasing prices at the petrol pumps, a boost in oil production outside of the Middle East could affect consumers.

Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum told Fox Business the pact was "shifting the geopolitical centre of the global energy markets" away from what he called the "choke points in the Middle East" and back to the Western Hemisphere.

There is a logic to the US-Venezuela partnership, Elliott Abrams argued, while Gulf oil supplies are currently so unreliable. But he said the terms are so one-sided they are a "kind of fever dream of what colonialism looks like".

The White House has spoken of the deal having "re-established the Monroe Doctrine", an 18th Century principle exerting US power across South America - "purging foreign malign influence from our backyard and ensuring American dominance in our hemisphere is never again questioned".
Despite the insistence from both governments that the plan will benefit both Venezuelans and Americans, it is not without pitfalls and clear unanswered questions.

The proposed timeframe alone is problematic. Trump has said the agreement will generate profit within two or three years. Energy experts, however, warn the dire state of the Venezuelan oil sector means a decade is more realistic.

Luis Pacheco, of the Baker Institute at Rice University in Houston, told BBC Mundo that Venezuela needs to invest about $100bn over eight years in order to return to its oil production levels of 30 years ago.
"It's important to know who will manage those resources and for what purpose," Pacheco said.

"Are they going to put the same people in charge of managing that money who already squandered the biggest oil boom of the century?" he asked, referring to past mismanagement of the country's oil wealth.
The Venezuelan opposition is concerned the deal deepens President Trump's relationship with Delcy Rodríguez, whom they accuse of heading the same regime as Maduro.
The Trump administration not only decried Maduro's government as a corrupt drug cartel, but surrounded Venezuela with the biggest armada of the modern era.
The ease and speed with which Washington has now pivoted to working with Maduro's former vice-president infuriates the opposition.

The Nobel Peace Prize winner and presidential hopeful, María Corina Machado, may choose not to publicly criticise President Trump, whose support she needs if she hopes to come to power. Others, though, have been more forthcoming.

"You chose to use the power of the United States not to liberate Venezuelans, but to ally yourself with our oppressors," said Venezuelan economist, Ricardo Hausmann, on social media, directing his comments at the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"You opted to push through an asset seizure, an unconstitutional agreement with an illegitimate and oppressive government, instead of using the leadership of the United States to first restore constitutional order and democracy," he said.
The lack of an imminent election in Venezuela – or, indeed, any clear plan towards one – strikes many opponents as a betrayal.

There is betrayal felt at the other end of the ideological spectrum, too. Although the governing socialist party, PSUV, has backed Rodríguez over the US deal, many Venezuelan socialists see it as capitulation.
After almost three decades opposing Washington's influence in the region, they feel she has gifted the country's most valuable asset to the old enemy.

The deal "hands over [the oil] and opens the doors to a new colonialism of the United States," said Rafael Ramírez, who served as the head of the state-run energy firm, PDVSA, and as the oil minister under former President Hugo Chávez.
In early 2008, Chávez presented his Sunday television programme, Aló Presidente, from former ExxonMobil oilfields in the Orinoco River Belt.
Having expropriated some of the oil company's assets in the region, he was in a defiant mood.

"We have the reins in our hands and we won't ever let them go again," he said of the state-run oil company's ownership of oilfields, and denounced how previous Washington-friendly governments had turned Venezuela into "a nation of gringos".
"It was a theft of our nation but the Bolivarian Revolution has put a stop to it," he thundered to applause from PDVSA employees.
Yet it was one of his disciples – his handpicked successor's successor – who has now signed this opaque deal with Washington and praised it as a victory for Venezuela.

articles.title: Thieves steal $70,000 worth of beer
articles.summary: MONTCLAIR, California — Thieves made off with tens of thousands of cans of Pabst beer in two separate heists from a Southern California warehouse on the same day, police said. Pabst Blue Ribbon has…

blocks.text: MONTCLAIR, California — Thieves made off with tens of thousands of cans of Pabst beer in two separate heists from a Southern California warehouse on the same day, police said.

Pabst Blue Ribbon has turned the thefts—valued by police at $70,000—into a light-hearted social media promotion. But police in Montclair said on Friday that investigators are trying to determine whether they were part of a single operation.
In the first heist, about $45,000 worth of beer headed to Tucson, Arizona, was picked up but never delivered, according to police.

An hour later, a “purported subcontracting company” submitted fake documents to pick up another $25,000 worth of beer, Montclair police said in a news release. Both thefts occurred on Aug. 17 at an Anheuser-Busch distribution center about 65 kilometers east of Los Angeles.
Roughly 34,000 cans of Pabst Blue Ribbon and non-alcoholic Old Milwaukee beer—more than 1,500 cases—were stolen, according to a police report obtained by the Los Angeles Times.
In Instagram posts, Pabst put the weight of the stolen cargo at 18,145 kilograms and started a countdown seeking its return.

“To the thief: we don’t fault you for wanting to brag to your friends how much PBR you have, we just wish you obtained it the honorable way,” the company wrote. It added, “P.s. this is real and we are deadly serious.” /cb

articles.title: Briton among 119 more people rescued in Nepal after flash floods
articles.summary:
More than 1,000 people confirmed dead and more than 4,000 still missing in disaster triggered by glacial collapse

A British national was among 119 people rescued in Nepal on Tuesday, an…

blocks.text: A British national was among 119 people rescued in Nepal on Tuesday, an official said almost a week after deadly flash floods on the country’s border with Tibet.
An army spokesperson told reporters at a press conference that Tuesday’s rescue efforts had saved 118 Nepali nationals – 44 women and 74 men.
“We have also rescued one British male during this search and rescue operation, and the search and rescue operation is continuing,” he said.
The British man is yet to be identified. The UK Foreign Office was contacted for comment.
The rescues mark a rare breakthrough in a devastating week for Himalayan communities on both sides of the Nepal-Tibet border.
At least 1,050 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal since Wednesday’s flash floods, while Chinese state media said 66 people had been killed in Tibet. More than 4,000 people are still missing.
Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region. This included 330 foreign nationals, the Nepalese tourist board said in an update on Tuesday.
Preliminary analysis of satellite imagery suggests the collapse of a glacier high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the disaster.

The collapse – so large it was initially recorded as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake – triggered a deadly torrent of water, mud and ice that tore along the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on Wednesday.
Crews have faced dangerous and difficult conditions while searching unstable terrain and flood debris.
Search efforts are now focused on attempts to reach about 600 workers believed to be trapped inside tunnels at several hydropower stations in the region.
“Massive work has been going on in the tunnel, all the tunnels,” the army spokesperson said on Tuesday.
Thirty-six British nationals are missing, the Foreign Office minister, Stewart Wood, told the House of Lords on Tuesday. The figure had previously been put at 33.

A rapid deployment rescue team from the UK arrived in Nepal on Saturday to provide support for Britons and their families as part of the government’s £5m commitment to support relief and recovery efforts.
The Red Cross estimates that 93,000 people have been directly affected by the disaster.
Scientists have said such disasters are more likely as the climate crisis affects mountainous and polar regions.
The UN’s top scientific advisory body said in 2023 that previously ice-bound landmasses – such as permafrost tundra and mountain glaciers – would become increasingly unstable as temperatures rose.
Officials from Nepal, China and Tibet met in May to discuss strengthening their joint response to floods, weather and glacier-related hazards, Reuters reported on Tuesday.

articles.title: Ed Miliband promises ‘comprehensive reset’ of UK policy toward Israel
articles.summary:
Foreign secretary tells MPs he will try to stop illegal settlements carving up the West Bank

Ed Miliband has promised to “reset” Britain’s policy on Israel, saying he will try to stop…

blocks.text: Ed Miliband has promised to “reset” Britain’s policy on Israel, saying he will try to stop British companies helping build settlements in the West Bank.

Speaking to the Commons for the first time as foreign secretary, Miliband said he would set out measures to prevent UK involvement in projects such as the illegal E1 plan, which critics say would split the West Bank in half.
Tuesday’s comments came after Israel issued tenders for around a third of the 3,400 homes planned for the project. Miliband called the settlement “the crossing of a red line”.

He said: “It cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable. This government will not acquiesce in the destruction of the two-state solution. We will act, and I will set out a comprehensive set of measures in the coming weeks.
“I want a comprehensive reset of our approach on these issues because it is necessary, it is high time.”
Ministers have been under pressure for weeks to place tighter sanctions on Israel, specifically in relation to the E1 plan.
Last month, Israel invited companies to bid for contracts to build 1,200 homes for the project between East Jerusalem and the settlement of Ma’ale Adumim.

blocks.caption: Ma’ale Adumim in the E1 area of the occupied West Bank, where the Israeli government plans to build thousands of homes. Photograph: Debbie Hill/UPI/Shutterstock

blocks.text: A group of former British diplomats called on the government in May to threaten action against any companies bidding to build any illegal settlement “designed to divide the West Bank in two and destroy Palestine’s viability”. They warned that E1 was part of Israel’s “systemic West Bank annexation”.
Other governments have condemned the project. The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz – usually one of Israel’s staunchest defenders – called it a “big mistake”.
The UK joined a group of 20 other countries, including France, Germany and Italy, as well as the European Union, to issue a joint statement calling E1 “unacceptable”.

The statement said: “The E1 settlement will undermine the prospect of the two-state solution by driving a wedge through the West Bank and harming the territorial contiguity of the Palestinian territories.”
Miliband said: “We need to look, and we are looking indeed, at our wider economic relationship with the occupied territories and the different tools we have to tackle it.
after newsletter promotion

“I want to be very clear: we do not want British companies financing, constructing, or advertising new settlements. The work we are now undertaking is how we can stop that. And as I say, I’ll have more to say soon.”
Ministers are under pressure to go further and ban trade in goods and services with people or organisations linked to illegal settlements.

James Naish, the Labour MP for Rushcliffe in Nottinghamshire, said: “Does the foreign secretary accept that this pace of expansion shows that current UK measures are failing to change Israeli government behaviour, and that a trade ban is now the necessary next step?”

Stephen Doughty, a Foreign Office minister, indicated this could be included in the government’s measures. He said: “We have absolutely condemned the settler violence, the settler terrorism that we have seen, absolutely our condemnation of the proposals for E1 and all illegal settlements, and indeed we have joined other countries around the world in condemning this proposal and been very, very clear with the government of Israel that this must stop.

“The prime minister has been very clear that we need to do more, including looking at further sanctions, both those involved in the violence in Gaza, but also looking at measures to ban trade in goods with illegal settlements.”

The Israeli embassy to London responded by referring to previous comments by Gideon Sa’ar, Israel’s foreign minister, who said: “If Britain acts against the state of Israel, the state of Israel will act against Britain. We have the tools. The period is over when people act against the state of Israel and the state of Israel doesn’t respond.”

articles.title: US launches new airstrikes on Iranian targets as hostilities flare
articles.summary: Move from Washington quashes hopes that exchange of fire last weekend might not presage ⁠wider renewal of hostilities

blocks.text: The US launched new airstrikes on Iranian targets on Tuesday, quashing hopes that an exchange of fire last ⁠weekend might not presage a ⁠wider renewal of hostilities.

Oil prices had ​already risen after that first exchange of direct attacks since July and after reports of two tankers being hit leaving the strait of Hormuz, the global oil supply waterway that Iran has effectively closed to shipping.

Tehran remained defiant, warning ⁠that it would prevent oil being exported from the Gulf, despite a threat by Donald Trump to hit Iran “hard” in response to the renewed Iranian strikes, and a warning from Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, that Washington was about to ⁠impose new sanctions.

“Today at 12 p.m. ET (1600 GMT), U.S. forces began striking Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran,” US Central Command posted on X. “The strikes follow ​recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of ‌Hormuz and against American service members deployed to ‌the region.”
Iran’s state broadcaster said there had been reports of explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island, on the northern side of the strait.
The state-linked news agency Nour ‌News said there had been reports of explosions in the port city of Bandar Abbas and in Chabahar, a port on the southern coast.

The six-month conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before the weekend strikes, in which US forces attacked Iran’s Larak Island on Sunday and Iran responded by launching missiles at two US airbases in Jordan.

Although he warned of a US response to the Iranian strikes, the US president also told reporters on Monday that they did not signal a return to full-scale war, and a senior Iranian source told Reuters they were a “limited ‌and contained confrontation”.

However, Trump made dire threats against Tehran on social media. He warned that if Iran retaliates against the US’s latest strikes, “they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran”.

The ominous last part of Trump’s message was starkly reminiscent of threats the US president has made in the past that could amount to war crimes if carried out, including threatening to destroy critical civilian infrastructure such as power plants and bridges, threatening to bomb Iran “back to the Stone Ages”, and an April threat that “a whole civilization will die tonight” if a peace deal wasn’t reached.
In Iran, the Fars news agency quoted an IRGC spokesperson as saying the US “will regret its new attacks”.

More recently pledges by both sides to respond to further attacks have highlighted how quickly a conflict that has increasingly been fought through sanctions, blockades and economic pressure could spill back into military action.

Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, had said early on Tuesday ​that Tehran would reciprocate immediately if Washington honoured its commitments under a June memorandum of understanding (MOU) that was intended to halt the conflict.

The MOU declared an end to fighting that has now killed thousands in Iran and Lebanon since US and Israeli strikes began on 28 February. But it also deferred many of the most difficult issues and paved the way for a broader 60-day negotiation period – which passed without further agreement.

“I am stating clearly that if the US returns to its commitments under the ⁠memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Pezeshkian said in the Kyrgyz capital, Bishkek, at ​a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, which includes Russia ​and China.
But Iranian officials have shown no public ​sign of bowing to pressure.

“If the enemy wants us not to export oil from the Persian Gulf, no one will be ​able to export oil,” Mohammad Baqer QalibafIran’s parliament speaker was ​quoted as saying by Iranian media. If ​the US intensified its “siege”, he said Tehran would respond militarily.
Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, told a press conference in Tehran that Washington was “addicted to making excessive demands and has mistaken negotiations for dictating terms”.

“As long as they act in this manner, they will certainly get no result other than what they have achieved so far,” he added, warning that Tehran would “use all our capabilities, whether on the battlefield or through our diplomatic apparatus”.
Reuters contributed reporting

articles.title: Chinese national nabbed over alleged rogue cell site, phishing scheme
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has arrested a male Chinese national in General Trias, Cavite, for allegedly operating a rogue cellular site supposedly being used to…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has arrested a male Chinese national in General Trias, Cavite, for allegedly operating a rogue cellular site supposedly being used to transmit fraudulent text messages and direct mobile users to a fake banking website.

NBI director Melvin Matibag said Tuesday that the bureau’s Special Action Unit (SAU) conducted an operation following an intelligence report it received on foreign nationals allegedly operating an International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) catcher in parts of southern Metro Manila.
The IMSI catcher can supposedly mimic legitimate cellular towers and interact with nearby mobile phones.
It was allegedly mounted inside a vehicle and moved through densely populated areas.
“Ang may possession nito ay isang foreign national, isang foreigner na umiikot, nakasakay sa sasakyan na ginagamit ito dun sa phishing, sa mga scams,” Matibag explained in an ambush interview.
(We tracked it down and confiscated it from a foreign national. This foreigner was driving around in a vehicle, using the device for phishing and scams.)
The messages deceitfully claimed it came from a legitimate source and directed recipients to a website designed to resemble that of a prominent Philippine bank.

“Kumokopya na parang signal siya ng tower kung saan pumapasok yung mga cellphone, yung signal ng cellphone, na maaaring gamitin ito para kuning mga information, kunin yung data ng credit card ninyo, na ginagamit ito pang scam,” Matibag noted.
(It mimics a cell tower signal that cell phones connect to, which can be used to gather information and steal your credit card data for scamming purposes.)
The agents arrested the suspect inside his residence after conducting physical surveillance and technical monitoring.
A separate rogue cellular site was also found at the location, the NBI said.
The suspect is facing violations of the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012, as well as the Anti-Financial Account Scamming Act.

The NBI emphasized that the case goes beyond financial fraud, noting that the unauthorized use of telecommunications equipment could pose a national security concern by allowing criminal groups to exploit communications infrastructure and reach large numbers of mobile users. — RENDELL IVAN MANUEL, INQUIRER.NET TRAINEE

articles.title: Pistol in a lake gives hope for French cold case
articles.summary: Saad al-Hilli was shot dead with his wife and mother-in-law while holidaying in eastern France in September 2012.

blocks.text: Police investigating the unsolved murder of a British family in France 14 years ago have an unexpected new clue with the discovery of a Luger pistol in the waters of a nearby lake.

One of the few certainties in the killings of Saad al-Hilli with his wife and mother-in-law – as well as a passing cyclist – is that they were shot through the head with a Luger model P06, a type used by the Swiss army until around 1960.
Now France's cold case unit has confirmed the discovery of a Luger in Lake Annecy, not far from the scene of the murders in September 2012.
According to Marianne magazine, which broke the story, it was British tourists on 20 August who found the weapon lying in two metres of water.
At first they thought it was a water pistol, but realised their mistake when they felt its weight.
The discovery was made near the very camping site – Le Solitaire du Lac – where the al-Hillis were staying in their caravan, Marianne reported.
Forensic experts are now examining the weapon, which has been badly damaged by its time under water, to see if it is indeed a P06 model.
It is estimated that around 60,000 Luger P06s were manufactured. But the number of Luger pistols in general that were made is more like three million.

Exhaustive investigations in France and the UK have left police no closer to understanding who carried out the al-Hilli murders and why. Over the years a series of leads have been pursued then dropped.
A British national of Iraqi birth, Saad al-Hilli was holidaying with his family in the picturesque countryside of Lake Annecy in eastern France.

On the afternoon of 5 September, his body with those of his wife and mother-in-law were found in their car, its motor still running, on a forest road near the village of Chevaline. A passing cyclist had – like the other victims – been shot through the head.

Poignantly, the two al-Hilli daughters, aged four and seven, survived. The older girl had been hit on the head with a pistol butt and was badly hurt. The younger, lying in the car under her mother's skirts, was not discovered till forensic experts began examining the scene many hours later.

It was fragments from the pistol butt which enabled police to identify it as a Luger P06. The model is regarded more as a collector's item than a working weapon, which made the theory of a professional hit against the family seem less likely.

Lake Annecy is only 50km from Switzerland, where the Luger P06 will have been familiar to older people from their military service. French police said many examples of the gun have been kept by families on either side of the border.
Among the theories that have been entertained are that the murders were linked to a family row over money; that they were the work of a motiveless crank; and that the main target was the cyclist.
Police were also briefly intrigued by the fact that al-Hilli's wife's first husband – an American – died of a heart attack just hours before the killings in France.

articles.title: Germany terminates lease for Berlin's Russian House
articles.summary: Germany has announced the termination of the lease for the Russian House in the heart of Berlin. Critics have long said it is a hub for propaganda and espionage.

image.caption: The Russian House has been a fixture on Berlin's Friedrichstrasse since 1984Image: Schoening/picture alliance

blocks.text: Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has announced that the contract under which the Russian House is operated will be rescinded. This is one of several measures in retaliation for Russian involvement in the attempted airport drone attack at the Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4.

The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations, it has long been the subject of fierce disagreements and a bone of contention in Berlin.

The massive seven-story building covering an area of almost 30,000 square meters opened in 1984. At that time, back in the days of the East German state, its role was to celebrate friendship with the Soviet Union through concerts, film screenings and book readings. It even had its own small bookstore.
Leipzig drone threat prompts security concerns in Germany
French authorities have previously linked the building to possible activities by Russian intelligence services.

"In light of the measures taken against German cultural institutions and organizations, the federal government is comprehensively and continuously reviewing the legal basis of the Russian House under international treaty law,” said German Foreign Ministry spokesperson Martin Giese at a press conference in Berlin at the beginning of August.

Back then, in response to a question from DW about the organization's future activities, Giese emphasized that the fate of the Russian House is linked to that of the Goethe Institut in Moscow, and that any action taken against one would also have direct consequences for the other.
German tax money for Russian propaganda?

The property on Friedrichstrasse belongs to Germany, yet the building is run by the Russian agency Rossotrudnichestvo, the Federal Agency for the Commonwealth of Independent States, Compatriots Living Abroad and International Humanitarian Cooperation.

Rossotrudnichestvo, whose primary purpose is to promote the Russian language abroad, currently has dozens of similar institutions worldwide. The German Foreign Office has repeatedly stated that the employees of the institute have diplomatic status in Germany.

Since 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the agency has been on the EU sanctions list. At the time, the EU justified this by stating that the agency's goal was to consolidate "a wider public perception of the occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian."

blocks.caption: Symbols of friendship remained on display in Berlin's Russian House in October 2023, more than year after the Russian invasion of UkraineImage: Dmyrto Katkov/DW

blocks.text: Moscow still maintains that the Russian House is a place to celebrate the friendship between the two countries: "The Russian House is Russia's cultural embassy in the heart of Berlin," according to the Russian Embassy's website.
The events that take place there attract 200,000 visitors a year, according to Russian House organizers. Critics label them as propaganda.
Berlin media outlets have repeatedly reported on events at the in-house cinema where, for example, films were shown in which Ukrainian citizens were portrayed as Nazis.
Germany fears closure of Goethe-Institut in Moscow

The Russian House is owned by the Russian Federation, but the Federal Republic of Germany pays the property tax for the building on the basis of its legal obligation under the bilateral German-Russian agreement on property issues relating to cultural institutes.

Moscow and Berlin are also bound by the Intergovernmental Agreement on Cultural Cooperation, which was signed in December 1992 and entered into force in May 1993. It has a term of five years and is automatically extended for the same period unless one of the parties notifies the other at least six months before the expiration of the respective term.

Both agreements — regarding the property of the Russian House and the Goethe-Institut, as well as the cultural cooperation between Russia and Germany — remain in force even in the fifth year of Russia's war against Ukraine.

It is an open secret that the German government has been shying away from conflict over the Russian House because it fears the Russian government could respond by closing the Goethe-Institut in Moscow.
The institute was already forced to significantly scale back its operations in Russia in May 2023, when restrictions were imposed on the number of German officials in Russia.

A few weeks earlier, the Goethe-Institut's bank accounts in Russia were frozen in retaliation after the Berlin Public Prosecutor's Office opened a preliminary investigation against the Russian House for violating sanctions and ordered the freeze of its accounts.

So far, the Goethe-Institut continues to offer digital language courses in Russia. The libraries at its branches in Moscow and St. Petersburg continue to receive the latest German literature despite logistical difficulties, as representatives of the institute assured DW earlier this year.
Direct Russian-German contacts have become virtually impossible
In recent years, several German foundations in Russia have been classified as "undesirable organizations."
This includes the foundations run by Germany's established political parties.
Anyone who cooperates with "undesirable organizations" faces criminal prosecution in Russia. This makes all direct contact provided for in the cultural agreement virtually impossible.
This article was originally written in German and first published in August 2025. It was updated and republished in September 2026 to reflect news developments.

articles.title: Mark Carney tells US to ‘start being serious’ amid escalating trade war
articles.summary: Canadian PM is set to retaliate against tariffs levied by Donald Trump and criticized US officials over insults

blocks.text: Mark Carney has rebuked Donald Trump’s administration and urged officials in Washington to “start being serious” amid escalating trade tensions between the US and Canada.

Days before Canada is due to retaliate against Trump’s sweeping tariffs with its own duties on US goods, the Canadian prime minister criticized US officials for insulting his country. “It is beneath their office,” he said.
“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions” about trade, Carney said.
Trump signed an executive order last week directing the US federal government to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America – a move that has been rejected by Canadians.
The US president’s most senior trade negotiator has meanwhile downplayed the potentially disastrous effects of a US trade war with Canada, declaring the spat to be “more their emergency than ours”.

The US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, argued that Canada was more vulnerable after the breakdown in talks set the stage for sweeping tariffs between the two neighbors, telling Politico: “There are no negotiations happening on trade right now.”
The comment comes just more than a week after US-Canada trade talks imploded. The US levied 50% tariffs on $20bn in Canadian goods.

Canada, the US’s second-largest trading partner, announced it would impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of American goods starting on 8 September. Now, US residents are poised to feel extreme pressure from Trump’s tariffs and Canada’s retaliatory measures, including on day-to-day items.
Greer appeared to blame the escalating trade war on Canadian officials, telling Politico: “It’s not clear Canada wants a deal.
“If Canada believes that prohibiting and banning American goods and services is appropriate, then obviously that’s something that the United States should consider as well.”
Unacceptable asks from Canada included lighter taxes on heavy-duty trucks, according to Greer, who said such requests torpedoed the trade talks.

Canadian officials, on the other hand, attributed the collapsed negotiations to a White House disagreement over who was directing trade talks. Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister, also said that American negotiators saw the French language in Canada as an “irritant”, but added: “In Quebec, these are rights.”

Trump, for his part, has argued in recent weeks that Canada “wants the benefits” of being a US state, without being one – a preoccupation of the US president – as he lashed out at the country’s leaders. “They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs,” claimed Trump. “No more!!!”

Greer suggested that negotiations broke down after a misunderstanding around what was, and wasn’t, on the table. “Was that political? I don’t know,” he told Politico. “Was it economic? … I’m not sure how much economic sense it makes because the choice is not between the current tariffs and … you know, duty-free trade. Like, that is that. Those weren’t the options.”

articles.title: 'Tapusin na yan!': Prosecution to finish confidential funds article next week, says Chua
articles.summary: Saying they don't want an overly lengthy impeachment trial, members of the House prosecution panel intend to conclude its presentation on the confidential funds misuse article against Vice President…

blocks.text: Saying they don't want an overly lengthy impeachment trial, members of the House prosecution panel intend to conclude its presentation on the confidential funds misuse article against Vice President Sara Duterte next week.
According to solon-prosecutor Manila 3rd district Rep. Joel Chua, the team is already looking to shift to the two remaining articles of impeachment.

“Masasabi natin, baka by next week ay matapos na, hopefully, ang confidential funds, and we will move on to the next article,” Chua said Tuesday afternoon, Sept. 1 during the prosecution's post-hearing press conference.
(We can say that, hopefully, we could finish the confidential funds article by next week, and we will move on to the next article.)

On Tuesday, Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Colonels Manaros Boransing II and Magtanggol Panopio testified about Army certifications that were used in the Department of Education’s (DepEd) response to state auditors.

In an effort to shorten its witness list, Chua said two other military officers would no longer be presented since their expected testimony would largely repeat the points already placed on the record.
“Iisa lang naman iyong sasabihin nila. To shorten—ayaw naman natin ng protracted hearing. Gusto natin matapos na rin ito.”
(They would only be saying the same thing. To shorten [the proceedings]—we don’t want a protracted hearing. We also want this to be finished.)
Chua said prosecutors already covered the central points involving the Youth Leadership Summits (YLS) and the military certifications.

Respondent Duterte is being accused--among other things--of misuing a total of P612.5 million worth of confidential funds released to the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and Department of Education (DepEd).
On Wednesday, Sept. 2, the prosecution expects to present former DepEd undersecretary and chief-of-staff Michael Wesley Poa, as well as a representative of the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA)

Poa, currently Duterte’s defense lawyer, is expected to address the chain behind the military certifications, while the PSA witness will cover its checks of names appearing in confidential-fund records.

After those witnesses, the Manila solon said the remaining article I lineup would be short. “Ang natitira na lamang si Mr. Edward Fajarda, and probably isa—or at most, dalawa,” he said, referring to DepEd’s former special disbursing officer (SDO).
“The only one remaining is Mr. Edward Fajarda, and probably one—or at most, two [more witnesses].”
He said the prosecution will make its final lineup decision after Wednesday’s hearing. The panel previously finished its presentation of evidence on article IV, or the death threats article.
Defense's turn next
Chua reminded impeachment trial watchers that once the prosecution finishes all four articles of impeachment, the defense must present its own case.
“May target kasi tayo. We have to understand, after us mayroon pang defense; sila naman ang magpe-present. Siyempre ayaw naman natin na umabot pa ito by next year,” he said.
(We have a target. We have to understand that after us, there is still the defense; they will be the ones to present [their case]. Of course, we don’t want this to extend into next year.)

"Sana, hopefully, by November tapos na lahat (Hopefully, everything will be finished by November), so by December we can have the decision of the impeachment court whether or not to convict the Vice President," Chua said.

articles.title: Germany says Russia behind attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport
articles.summary: Investigators believe an explosives-laden drone was deliberately targeting a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport in early August.

image.caption: The airport is ​a cargo and military logistics hub used by NATO and Ukraine's Antonov Airlines for military suppliesImage: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The German government on Tuesday said Russia was "responsible" for an attempted drone attack at the Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4.

"The federal government concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack in Leipzig," said Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt at a press conference in Berlin on Tuesday afternoon, adding that the attack fitted the pattern of a "long series of destabilization operations" against Europe.
Leipzig airport attack: What has Germany said?

"The means used — such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems — are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine," added Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul.

Authorities discovered a drone fitted with explosives and a detonation mechanism on the evening of August 4 in the security area of Leipzig/Halle Airport between Ukrainian cargo aircraft and believe a second drone may have collided with a DHL aircraft nearby.
Last week, German media reported a third drone, also loaded with explosives, had also been discovered at the airport.
German federal prosecutors described the incident as a "serious attack on Germany's transport and logistics infrastructure."
"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiate Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," said Dobrindt.

Over the weekend, German chancellor Friedrich Merz had promised that a formal response to the incident would be made public in the coming days. He did not go into further detail but said that Germany's European Union and NATO allies would "not be surprised."

Earlier on Tuesday, Foreign Minister Wadephul vowed a measured response to the discovery of the drone, but stopped short of holding Russia directly responsible for the incident until his press conference with Interior Minister Dobrindt.
EU top diplomat points finger at Russia

The European Union's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said earlier on Tuesday that it was "clear" that Russia was involved in the drone incident, but declined to comment further until Germany had identified those it believes were responsible,
Kallas said Russia was becoming increasingly provocative, raising the question of what could be done to deter Moscow from escalating tensions any further.
Third drone found in suspected Leipzig hybrid attack
This is a developing story. Please refresh for updates.

articles.title: Norway's Haakon takes oath as mourners pay respects to late King
articles.summary: Norway's new King takes the first major step of his reign as his father, the late King Harald V, lies in state at the Royal Palace.

blocks.text: Norway's Haakon VIII has sworn an oath before parliament in Oslo in the first major step of his reign as King.
During Tuesday's ceremony, parliament also held a minute's silence for Haakon's father, the late King Harald V, who died on Friday.
Haakon's wife, Queen Mette-Marit, was absent from the formalities as she continues to recover from a lung transplant.
Following the ceremony, mourners began paying their respects at the late King's coffin, which is lying in state at the Royal Palace until 8 September.

articles.title: As glaciers melt, can communities be protected?
articles.summary: Rising temperatures are increasing the risk of floods and avalanches in mountain regions. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet shows the urgent need for solutions, and the tools that could help save lives.

image.caption: Thousands are still missing following last month's devastating floods in Nepal and TibetImage: Sunil Sharma/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: High mountain glaciers formed in the ice age are retreating and becoming unstable as the burning of fossil fuels heats the climate and leads to a decline in snowfall.
The instability creates the conditions for large glacial sections to collapse, triggering ice and rock avalanches that can dam river valleys before tidal waves of water are released.

Following the glacier collapse that triggered what is know as a mountain tsunami in Nepal and Tibet on August 26, thousands are still missing and feared dead. Unlike the 2025 glacier avalanche that destroyed the town of Batten in Switzerland — where nearly all inhabitants were evacuated — a lack of early warning systems in the Himalayas left locals and tourists at the mercy of flash floods.
How much is climate change to blame?
The causes of glacier collapse are part of a complex web of interrelated changes to high mountain landscapes due in part to rising global temperatures, say scientists.

Levan Tielidze, research fellow in Glacial Geomorphology at Australia's Monash University, says the Himalayas are not, as is often imagined, a "frozen and relatively stable environment," but "dynamic systems in which glaciers, snow, permafrost, rock slopes, rivers and monsoon processes interact."

"As the climate warms, these components are changing simultaneously, meaning hazards can cascade from one process into another," he told DW. When rock, ice and water interact in more unpredictable ways on the world's highest peaks, the resulting debris flows "can transform into a catastrophic flood far downstream," Tielidze added.

Almost 25 years ago, in what was then the biggest glacial collapse in history, one glacier crashed onto another in the Caucases Mountains of North Ossetia in the Russian Federation. The event caused avalanches of ice and debris that slid more than 24km (15 miles) and killed around 125 people.
"The Kolka Glacier disaster was one of the early warnings of the increasing occurrence and potential severity of such glacier-related hazards," Tielidze told DW.
Meanwhile the UN says glaciers in Nepalese mountains have declined by one-third in 30 years, which has added to their instability.

Some research suggests that even if emissions from burning fossil fuels were low enough to prevent the planet from heating by more than 2 degrees Celsius (36 degrees Fahrenheit) compared to pre-industrial times, the wider Hindu Kush Himalayan region could lose up to half its glacier cover — compared to 2020 levels — by the end of the century.

For Dipesh Chapagain, senior scientist at the United Nations University Institute for Environment and Human Security, there is "ample scientific evidence linking greenhouse gas emissions to global climate change, which in turn is driving glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and ice avalanches."
"These changes are increasing both the frequency and intensity of climate-related disasters in mountain regions," he added.

Chapagain has studied hundreds of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region — caused when meltwater from glaciers and snow creates a lake that eventually bursts and sends extreme flash floods downstream. The number of these events per decade has increased fivefold since the 1950s.
Pakistani villagers face climate change, melting glaciers

The glacier collapse in Nepal and Tibet shares similarities to a GLOF event; however the former was very different as it skipped the "intermediate lake-formation stage entirely … and directly triggered the flash flood," said Chapagain.

The avalanche also generated seismic activity equivalent to about magnitude 5.2 before the momentum of the water-rich debris flow that entered the river system saw it travel roughly 100 kilometres, noted Tielidze.
"These hazards are becoming so difficult to classify," he added, in reference to the way mountain rock, ice and water are interacting in more unpredictable ways due to climate change.

blocks.caption: Riverside communities in Nepal were destroyed by the unprecedented flash flood and mudslide  Image: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP

blocks.text: Is it possible to adapt to more extreme glacier collapse impacts?

The 2025 glacial collapse in the Swiss Alps that destroyed the entire village of Blattan resulted in one fatality. Detailed surveillance of glacier deformation and the surrounding terrain allowed authorities to evacuate the population before the catastrophic collapse.
But this is less possible in the Hindu Kush Himalaya, which contains more than 63,700 glaciers, notes Tielidze.
"In the Himalayas, we need to move beyond monitoring only individual dangerous lakes," he said.
"We need integrated systems combining satellite observations, seismic detection, glacier and slope monitoring, river gauges, weather forecasts and automated warnings."
For rapidly evolving events such as the Nepal disaster, detecting seismic movement could give downstream communities "precious minutes of warning," he added.

blocks.caption: The destroyed village in Blatten, Switzerland, was in the path of an avalanche of rock, ice, and debris triggered by the collapse of the Birch GlacierImage: Laurent Gillieron/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

blocks.text: Chapagain says the transboundary nature of glacial hazards in the Himalayas makes "cross-border and regional cooperation on disaster preparedness" just as urgent as early-warning systems.
However, currently available adaptation technology and capacity may be insufficient to "respond to a disaster on the scale we've just witnessed on the Bhotekoshi River in Nepal," he added.

"What we have learned from this is we can adapt to climate change but not to climate apocalypse," said Shreya K.C., the Kathmandu-based advocacy working group co-coordinator of the Loss and Damage Youth Coalition, in a statement.
A rapid reduction in planet-heating emissions that are at driving glacial melt and instability will need to accompany any adaptation measures.

"We cannot engineer our way out of unlimited warming," said Tielidze. "Some mountain hazards will remain unpredictable and some changes will eventually exceed the capacity of communities and infrastructure to adapt."

articles.title: Will impeachment trial prosecutors resign? Not anymore, says Chua
articles.summary: The House prosecution team's core of 11 solon-prosecutors will remain intact in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial. Thus, said prosecutor Manila 3rd district Rep. Joel Chua, with the…

blocks.text: The House prosecution team's core of 11 solon-prosecutors will remain intact in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial.
Thus, said prosecutor Manila 3rd district Rep. Joel Chua, with the revelation shelving a proposal for some of them to resign from the panel so they could speak publicly about the merits of the case.
“We have decided, wala na lang munang mag-resign,” Chua said Tuesday, Sept. 1 following day 20 of the high-stakes proceedings.
The panel considered a reshuffle after the Senate impeachment court reiterated the sub judice rule, or the limits on public comments about matters being tried.

One option was for selected House prosecutors to leave the panel and serve only as spokespersons. “Noong una, isa iyon sa mga naging discussion kung ganoon ang mangyayari. Kasi iyon ang talagang unang option,” Chua said.
(At first, that was one of the discussions, if that was what would happen. Because that was really the first option.)
The idea drew support from lawyers working with the team. “May mga suggestion ang ibang private prosecutor at public prosecutor na may ilan mag-resign para maging spokesperson."
(Some private prosecutors and public prosecutors suggested that some members resign so they could serve as spokespersons.)
But Chua said the prosecution members ultimately chose continuity. He noted that changing the structure of the team at this stage would require finding replacements.
“After considering everything, total isang buwan na lang kung masusunod iyong ating target...Too late na kung magbabawas tayo at magdadagdag pa,” Chua said.
(After considering everything, there’s only about a month left if we follow our target...It’s too late if we start removing and adding members.)
As such, the team will keep public briefings focused on schedules, witness sequencing, and other procedural updates.
More importantly, Chua said the prosectors "will just try to explain things in a way that does not touch on the merits [of the case]".

That was also why Chua, a public prosecutor, appeared at Tuesday’s briefing. He said reporters could still ask about what comes next without forcing prosecutors into a public discussion of the evidence.
“Baka may magtanong tungkol sa procedural aspect outside the merits of the case, so I can answer that,” said the veteran lawmaker from Manila.
(Someone might ask about the procedural aspects outside the merits of the case, so I can answer that.)
The approach allows the public to receive practical updates while the same prosecutors continue their work inside the impeachment court, Chua said.
It also preserves the team’s current assignments as the prosecution tries to finish article I on confidential funds and move to the remaining articles of impeachment against Duterte.
Fifteen private prosecutors are helping the solon-prosecutors gain a conviction from the respondent, free of charge.

articles.title: Mladic's death, Bosnia and Serbia's unfinished reckoning
articles.summary: The death of Ratko Mladic did not close a dark chapter of European history; it reopened old wounds. The ideology that created him lives on. The Dayton Peace Agreement ended the war, not the divisions…

image.caption: Former Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic (pictured here in 1994) was convicted of genocide for the Srebrenica massacre and other war crimes by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in 2017Image: Pascal Guyot/AFP

blocks.text: The death of Ratko Mladic should have closed one of the darkest chapters in European history.

Instead, it has reopened old wounds, proving that both the Dayton Peace Agreement that ended the 1992-95 Bosnian War and the three decades of international engagement that followed never came close to addressing the causes that led to the conflict.

When Mladic, the former commander of the Bosnian Serb army, died on August 27, 2026 in a prison hospital in The Hague, his conviction for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes — including the 1995 Srebrenica massacre and the siege of Sarajevo — had been final for nearly a decade.
Former Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic dead

What was never settled, however — and what, it seems, was never even seriously attempted — is the question of how a society lives with a man who remains a convicted criminal in the eyes of an international court but is viewed by some as a hero and symbol of the Serbian people.
For this reason, the reactions that followed Mladic's death came as no surprise.
Mladic openly mourned in Republika Srpska

In Serbia and the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska, one of the two semi-autonomous entities created within Bosnia and Herzegovina by the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, Ratko Mladic's death was mourned as the loss of a national hero, not the end of an era of crimes — a narrative that stands in direct contradiction to the facts established by international courts.

Senior officials in Republika Srpska, which covers around 49% of the territory of the former Yugoslav republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, called on citizens to gather in squares and light candles "for the salvation of the general's soul."

blocks.caption: Senior officials in Republika Srpska called on people to gather in squares and light candles 'for the salvation of the general's soul'Image: Radivoje Pavicic/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Milorad Dodik, still the most powerful political figure in Republika Srpska despite stepping down as its president last year after a six-year ban on holding public office imposed by Bosnia's constitutional court, called his death a "murder," suggesting it was "an organized approach that was meant to lead to a fatal outcome."

That Mladic is not perceived as a man convicted of genocide but as a symbol of "a time and a struggle" was confirmed by Drasko Stanivukovic, mayor of Banja Luka, the de facto capital of Republika Srpska.
Institutional support in Belgrade
In the Serbian capital, Belgrade, this stance received institutional backing.
Serbia's justice minister announced a funeral with the highest state and military honors.
President Aleksandar Vucic accused the Hague tribunal of "uncivilized behavior" for not allowing Mladic to spend his final days outside his prison cell.

Moreover, former interior minister Aleksandar Vulin spoke of Mladic in the same breath as other Serbian national heroes, invoking a narrative that links the First World War to the 1990s, saying, "From Gavrilo Princip to Ratko Mladic, the best Serbs are killed tied up."
A very different response elsewhere in Bosnia

In the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the other main entity in Bosnia, where Bosniaks and Croats form the majority, news of Mladic's death was met with unanimous condemnation of the deceased, given that Mladic was finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, a town in eastern Bosnia where around 8,000 men and boys were killed in July 1995.

Bosnia's foreign minister, Elmedin Konakovic, framed the official Serbian response as Serbia's conscious choice: "No one is forcing Serbia to treat Mladic as a hero, nor to attribute his crimes to it. Serbia is choosing this itself," he said.
Representatives of victims and survivors pointed out that any public glorification is a direct insult to the families of those killed.

The European Commission, responding to questions about the announced state funeral, said that "glorifying convicted war criminals is contrary to the most basic European values" and that such practices have no place in either member states or candidate countries.

blocks.caption: 'No one is forcing Serbia to treat Mladic as a hero [...]. Serbia is choosing this itself,' said Bosnia's foreign minister, Elmedin KonakovicImage: Denis Zuberi/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: The European Movement in Serbia warned that a state funeral would amount to "institutional glorification" and a "serious moral, legal and political attack on Serbia" and urged the Serbian government to abandon the plan.
How can this happen?
But how is it possible that a man who has been finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica is still honored as a military commander?
The answer is not simply that he is viewed by some as a national hero. It is structural, and it begins with the Dayton Peace Agreement itself.
The 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement ended the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina by turning existing front lines and territorial control into the constitutional architecture of a new state.
One of the fundamental elements of the agreement was Republika Srpska, which is recognized by all signatories and embedded in the constitutional structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

That division was not an administrative technicality, it reflected the political reality on the ground at the time negotiations were held, including territories under the control of forces commanded by Ratko Mladic.
The compromise was necessary to stop the bloodshed. The problem is that since 1995, it has never been accompanied by a mechanism for dealing with the past that would match the political compromise.

Dayton created a complex constitutional architecture — a state divided into two entities and the Brcko District with a total 14 governments and parliaments at state, entity and cantonal level — for a country of just 3 million people.

It is a system built to prevent war, not a system built to produce common citizenship, and was described by the Council of Europe's Venice Commission as long ago as 2005 as "neither rational nor efficient."
In such a system, where ethnic identity is built into the very logic of power, denial or relativization of crimes is not a marginal phenomenon, it is a political resource.
In other words, each side sees itself as a victim, which makes joint recognition of committed evil as a precondition for reconciliation impossible.
The price of missed responsibility
Bosnia and Herzegovina has state-level legislation that criminalizes the public denial, gross minimization or justification of genocide and the glorification of persons convicted of such acts.
The Dayton Peace Agreement 30 years on
In reality, however, enforcement of this legislation remains uneven.
Serbia has no such law, and its public authorities, instead of distancing themselves from Mladic's legacy, openly embrace it.
This is not just a symbolic difference, it is the difference between treating the wartime legacy as something shameful to be overcome or as a resource to be politically exploited.
The role of the international community
The international community, which stopped the war in 1995 through force and diplomacy, subsequently retreated into the role of administrator of the status quo.

The Office of the High Representative, the international envoy empowered to impose laws and remove obstructive politicians under the Dayton Agreement, did indeed impose laws and remove obstructive politicians for decades, but in doing so only stabilized the system without dismantling its causes.
The result is twofold: a deeply divided society that has not moved forward in the 30 years since the end of the war and the fact that an ideology that gave rise to that war is still very much alive.

articles.title: Philippines prepares for unprecedented 5-million tons rice imports
articles.summary: The Philippines will import a record-high five million metric tons (MT) this year, as it turns to foreign supplies to offset a projected shortfall in domestic production caused by El Niño, according…

blocks.text: The Philippines will import a record-high five million metric tons (MT) this year, as it turns to foreign supplies to offset a projected shortfall in domestic production caused by El Niño, according to the Department of Agriculture (DA).

“As we are facing El Niño, we are projecting that we might need to import up to five million MT for this year,” said Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel during his agency’s budget hearing on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
The projected import volume this year is nearly four percent higher than the current record of 4.81 million MT set in 2024.
Total rice imports as of Aug. 13 reached 3.46 million MT, already higher than the 3.39 million MT recorded last year, according to the Bureau of Plant Industry (BPI).
Tiu Laurel said the additional rice supply will serve as a buffer as the country’s rice production losses are estimated to reach 900,000 MT within the year.
He said the decline represents the “worst-case scenario” of a strong El Niño in the fourth quarter of the year, which is projected to damage several hectares of rice farms.
“What we are all doing this year is precautionary. It is better to be prepared and have enough supply rather than risk having a shortage,” said Tiu Laurel.
Tiu Laurel noted that increased rice imports for the year will also serve as a supply cushion for the first quarter of next year in order to get ahead of a potentially weaker harvest season.
Considering this, the import volume for 2027 may go down to the normal range of between 3.8 million MT and four million MT.
While the country relies on foreign supplies to meet domestic demand, Tiu Laurel said the main objective of the government continues to be increasing local output.
He told lawmakers that the DA is focused on rolling out mechanization measures, expanding irrigation, and developing new rice seeds to further boost productivity.
The agency is also preparing to implement a program requiring traders to first invest in rice mills and processing facilities before they allowed to purchase rice from abroad.
It is estimated that around 80 percent of rice importers in the country are engaged solely in importing and have yet to commit investments in the local rice sector.
“That is one of the plans to make the industry self-sustaining and competitive in the international market,” said Tiu Laurel.
Based on BPI data, Vietnam has maintained its position as the country’s top rice supplier with imports reaching 2.56 million MT, or 74 percent of the total volume, as of Aug. 13.
Other top sources of rice include Thailand with 378,404 MT, Myanmar with 286,052 MT, Pakistan with 107,485 MT, and Cambodia with 87,802 MT.
The DA’s proposed budget for next year is ₱198.45 billion, down eight percent from the allocation of ₱215.69 billion for this year.

Under this budget, the agency wants to prioritize programs that raise farm and fishery productivity, improve infrastructure, reduce post-harvest losses, strengthen logistics and market access, and expand the use of technology.

articles.title: Thailand shortens visa-free stays for dozens of nations from Sept. 15
articles.summary: BANGKOK, Thailand — Thailand will halve the length of visa-free stays for tourists from more than 60 countries and territories to 30 days, effective September 15, the foreign ministry said Tuesday.…

blocks.text: BANGKOK, Thailand — Thailand will halve the length of visa-free stays for tourists from more than 60 countries and territories to 30 days, effective September 15, the foreign ministry said Tuesday.
Tourism is vital to the Southeast Asian nation’s economy, but officials say the move is part of an effort to curb crime involving foreign nationals.
A string of recent arrests has included foreigners accused of drug offences, sex trafficking and operating businesses such as hotels and schools without proper permits.

Under Thailand’s current tourism scheme, travellers from more than 90 countries — including Europe’s 29-nation Schengen area, China, India, the United States and several South American countries — are eligible to visit for up to 60 days without a visa.

The reduction to 30 days visa-free applies to over 60 countries and territories, including China, the United States and 27 EU countries, the Thai foreign ministry’s consular affairs department said on Tuesday.
The visa-free status for around 20 other countries was unclear, with a foreign ministry official declining to comment on Tuesday.
Visitors from Peru, Brazil and South Korea will be granted 90-day visa-free stays, up from 60 previously.
Tourists will be able to extend their stays once, at the discretion of an immigration officer, a government spokeswoman told AFP in May when the cabinet approved the measure.
Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said that month that the plan to trim visa-free visits was part of a crackdown on individuals abusing the visa system by committing crimes in the country.
Thailand has attracted 20.9 million foreign tourists since the beginning of the year, down three percent on the same period in 2025, according to the latest official figures.

articles.title: Creamline stays unscathed; EST Cola sweeps Farm Fresh
articles.summary: Creamline routed Ho Chih Minh City, 25-18, 25-16, 25-6, to remain unscathed, while EST Cola swept Farm Fresh, 25-21, 25-16, 25-22, to barge into the win column in the PVL Invitational at the Smart…

blocks.text: Creamline routed Ho Chih Minh City, 25-18, 25-16, 25-6, to remain unscathed, while EST Cola swept Farm Fresh, 25-21, 25-16, 25-22, to barge into the win column in the PVL Invitational at the Smart Araneta Coliseumon Tuesday, Sept. 1.
The Cool Smashers exposed the Vietnamese’s lethargic plays, needing 61 minutes to dominate the guest team for their second straight win in as many outings.
Tots Carlos, Jema Galanza and Jaja Santiago-Minowa paced Creamline with 12 points apiece, including combined 21 kills from Carlos and Galanza, and three blocks from Santiago-Minowa.
So dominant were the Cool Smashers that they overpowered the Vietnamese spikers on attacks, 49-19; blocks, 11-4; and aces, 5-3.
None from Ho Chi Minh City scored in twin figures with skipper Dang Thi Kim Thanh and Le Thi My Xuyen pacing only eight and six points, respectively, as they absorbed their second straight loss.
Earlier, EST Cola made its title bid to improve its record to 1-1 behind the efforts of Papatchaya Phontham.
Phontham blasted 17 points built on 13 kills, three aces and one block to shackle Farm Fresh, which struggled despite the 15-point effort of Trisha Tubu.

articles.title: Yamsuan bent on helping CHEd once travel tax windfall stops
articles.summary: A solon who holds a key position in the House 2027 national budget process has vowed to help find alternative funding for the Commission on Higher Education (CHEd) should the measure abolishing the…

blocks.text: A solon who holds a key position in the House 2027 national budget process has vowed to help find alternative funding for the Commission on Higher Education (CHEd) should the measure abolishing the travel tax becomes a law this year.

Parañaque City 2nd district Rep. Brian Raymund Yamsuan has noted that CHEd, which regulates higher education and administers the government’s financial aid programs for tertiary-level students, gets part of its funding from 40 percent of the total gross collections from the travel tax.

Yamsuan, a member of the House Budget Amendments and Review Subcommittee (BARSc) pointed out that under Malacañang’s National Expenditure Program for Fiscal Year 2027, a portion of the allocation for the CHEd’s Higher Education Development Fund (HEDF) would still be sourced from the travel tax collections of the Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (TIEZA).

“Kami po ay magtatrabaho sa Kongreso para hanapan kayo ng alternative sources of funding once mangyari po ang pagsasabatas ng abolition ng travel tax,” Yamsuan told CHEd Chairperson Shirley Agrupis during the House Committee on Appropriations’ recent budget deliberations on the agency’s proposed 2027 budget.
(We will work in Congress to look for alternative sources of funding once the travel tax measure is enacted into law.)

Formed during last year's budget cycle as a pro-transparency measure, the BARSc effectively replaced the so-called "small committee", which incorporates individual ammendments to the General Appropriations Bill (GAB) or proposed national budget.

If the bill abolishing the travel tax is passed into law, Agrupis told the House Committee on Tourism last March that without a substitute funding source, the CHEd would lose 85.6 percent of the funding for the HEDF.
She calls this prospect “a structural loss that directly affects scholarships, research and institutional upgrading, and tourism education programs".

The House of Representatives approved on March 16 the measure seeking to abolish the travel tax. Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian earlier said the Senate version of the measure is included in the chamber’s priority list of bills and will be passed this year.

“Kami bilang member ng BARSc, sisiguraduhin ko po na sa susunod na pagpupulong with (Committee on Appropriations) Chair Mika (Suansing) ay gagawa po kami ng paraan upang maibalik ang pondo para hindi maantala ang magagandang programa ng CHEd,” Yamsuan added.

(As member of the BARSc, I would make sure that in the next meeting with Committee on Appropriations Chairperson Mikaela Angela Suansing, we would find ways to restore CHEd’s funding so as not to delay the implementation of CHEd’s good programs)

During the hearing, the Parañaque solon also thanked the CHEd for its efficient implementation of the government’s higher education initiatives and financial assistance to tertiary-level students, particularly the Tulong Dunong Program (TDP).
The TDP provides a financial grant of up to P7,500 per semester or a total of P15,000 per school year to help cover the tuition and other daily expenses of qualified college students.
Yamsuan urged the CHEd to conduct more consultations with Local Universities and Colleges (LUC) to help them institute reforms that would allow them to take part in the TDP.
Out of 170 LUCs, only 116 are CHEd-recognized institutions qualified to accept TDP grants from its enrollees.

articles.title: ICC prosecution submits witness list, evidence vs Duterte
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecution has submitted the list of witnesses and evidence in the crimes against humanity case of former President Rodrigo Duterte, the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecution has submitted the list of witnesses and evidence in the crimes against humanity case of former President Rodrigo Duterte, the Office of the Prosecutor revealed on Tuesday.
In a three-page document, confidential files containing the prosecutors’ list of witnesses and evidence were submitted to Trial Chamber III, pursuant to the chamber’s order.
Under Regulation 23bis(1) of the Regulations of the Court, the files were filed confidentially because “both include sensitive witness information” relating to the witnesses.

Duterte is facing three counts of crimes against humanity over the war on illegal drugs during his presidency, which killed at least 6,000 people based on government records, and more than 30,000, according to a human rights group’s records.
His trial will begin in November.
The prosecution previously disclosed that at least 6,909 pieces of evidence from Jan. 7 to July 31 were turned over to the defense. /mcm

articles.title: On the borderline
articles.summary: With these three novels, we use borderline in both a physical sense and in a metaphorical manner, as the trio of books explores what ‘the other side’ can mean. "Sublimation" by Isabel J. Kim Think of…

blocks.text: With these three novels, we use borderline in both a physical sense and in a metaphorical manner, as the trio of books explores what ‘the other side’ can mean.
"Sublimation" by Isabel J. Kim

Think of the immigrant experience, but now seen through a SciFi lens, and you have an idea of what this novel bravely explores. Kim has written short stories that have won Nebula, Locus, and Shirley Jackson Awards, and this is her debut novel. Soyoung Rose Kang is the protagonist here, and at the age of 10, she left Korea with her mother to emigrate to the USA. She left an ‘instance’ in Korea, who would continue to interact with her family and grandfather. And now, with the death of the grandfather, Soyoung (the instance in Korea) gets in touch with Rose (the instance in the USA), to let her know it was their grandfather’s wish that she come to Seoul for the funeral. What Rose isn’t aware of is that Soyoung harbors the desire to reintegrate.
