articles.title: NLEX operator MPTC steps up anti-flood measures; find out what
articles.summary: Metro Pacific Tollways Corporation (MPTC), owner and operator of the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) said on Tuesday, Sept. 1 that it will continue to work with national and local agencies to speed up…

blocks.text: Metro Pacific Tollways Corporation (MPTC), owner and operator of the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) said on Tuesday, Sept. 1 that it will continue to work with national and local agencies to speed up flood-prevention measures and restore reliable travel through the affected expressway corridor.
This, as MPTC told motorists that it recognized their difficulties as far as the recent episodes of floods were concerned.

In a statement, the company also said it is closely coordinating with the Department of Transportation (DOTr), Toll Regulatory Board (TRB) and other government agencies to assess immediate measures to support motorists affected by days of "Habagat" rains and rising water levels in the Pampanga River, while speeding up necessary flood-prevention measures.

As part of a permanent solution to recurring flooding in the San Simon segment of NLEX, MPTC said it will raise the northbound and southbound pavements in Tulaoc, San Simon, Pampanga once the Tulaoc Bridge elevation is completed.

Earlier, Pampanga Governor Lilia Pineda said the flooding reflects a broader drainage problem across the province, with water backing up because downstream areas like Macabebe and Masantol are already full and floodwater cannot readily discharge toward Manila Bay.
MPTC also shared observations by Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Secretary Vince Dizon that the sheer volume of water dumped by the southwest monsoon overwhelmed the system.
In a media interview, the DPWH chief acknowledged that pumping alone would not solve the problem as the water would simply flow back.
Heavy flooding disrupted traffic along NLEX, especially in San Simon, Pampanga, where water from the overflowing Pampanga River submerged lanes and caused hours-long gridlock.
Motorists faced diversions and road closures, while government agencies and NLEX management tried to mitigate the situation by deploying barriers, pumps, and emergency crews.

articles.title: Free NLEX toll amid flood? Palace says it's up to management
articles.summary: Waiving the toll fees for motorists affected by heavy traffic at the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) due to severe flooding is up to its management, Malacañang said. Palace Press Officer and…

blocks.text: Waiving the toll fees for motorists affected by heavy traffic at the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) due to severe flooding is up to its management, Malacañang said.
Palace Press Officer and Communications Undersecretary Claire Castro said the directive should come from the expressway's management.
President Marcos could only give a recommendation, but stressed that the management knows what actions should it take.

"Siguro, bago po magmungkahi ang Pangulo, alam naman po ng NLEX kung ano ang nangyari dito. At ano ang kanilang responsibilidad, dapat sa kanila manggaling ang kautusan na ito (Perhaps, before the President makes a recommendation, NLEX already knows what happened here and what their responsibilities are. The directive should have come from them in the first place)," Castro said in a Palace briefing on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
'Avoid NLEX'
The Palace official also advised motorists to avoid NLEX instead, arguing that waiving the toll fee would only further decongest the expressway.

"Iyong stranded doon? Libre? Bakit ka pa papasok kung trapik na. Huwag na muna kayong dumaan doon, kasi kung hindi naman siya makakalusot, so ano ang purpose ng libre (Those who are stranded there? Toll free? Why would you still enter if there is already heavy traffic? For now, avoid passing through that area, because if you won’t be able to get through anyway, then what’s the point of making it free)?" Castro questioned.

"Magandang adhikain iyong libre. Pero kung ililibre natin, ‘di ba mas maraming sasakyan ang papasok. So kapag maraming papasok na sasakyan, mas lalong magkakaroon ng trapik. So dapat nga iwasan na muna nila itong NLEX (Free toll is a good initiative. But if we make it free, won’t more vehicles enter? And when more vehicles enter, it will only make the traffic worse. So, for now, they should really avoid using NLEX)," she stressed.
'Imposing sanction, not a priority'

Asked whether the President would instruct the Toll Regulatory Board to impose sanctions on the management of North Luzon Expressway for hours-long traffic caused by floods, Castro said it is not the President's priority at present.

"Kahapon ay napag-usapan ang problemang iyan, pero hindi napag-usapan kung anumang sanction. Ang nasa proposal po ng Pangulo ay paano po matutulungan iyong mga naipit nating mga kababayan sa NLEX (Yesterday, that problem was discussed, but no sanctions were discussed. The President’s proposal focuses on how we can help our fellow citizens who are stranded on NLEX)," Castro said.

"Most probably, kapag nakausap ko ang Pangulo ay itatanong ko po iyan, dahil hindi po sa ngayon ang pag-sanction ang inuuna ng Pangulo, kung hindi ang kaginhawaan ng ating mga motorista (Most probably, when I speak with the President, I will ask him about that. For now, the President’s priority is not imposing sanctions, but ensuring the convenience and welfare of our motorists)," Castro added.

articles.title: Putin-Modi meeting at SCO: Can Russia-India ties hold?
articles.summary: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin are set to meet in Kyrgyzstan’s capital, Bishkek, on Monday on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization…

blocks.text: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin are set to meet in Kyrgyzstan’s capital, Bishkek, on Monday on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit — a bloc often seen as a counterweight to US influence.
The meeting comes against the backdrop of the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted global energy markets, and Russia’s war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year.
India has remained engaged with the SCO while resisting efforts to turn it into an anti-Western bloc. Its position reflects a broader effort to maintain relationships with competing powers.

That approach is under greater pressure. Russia remains under Western sanctions over the war in Ukraine. Meanwhile, India has faced US pressure over its purchases of Russian oil, alongside wider trade tensions.
A former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, told DW that India’s relationship with Russia should not be seen as directed against the US.
“India has a long-standing strategic relationship with Russia. This is not directed against any country but intended to help India meet its national goals,” said Shankar.
Energy ties deepen between India, Russia
Energy has become the most visible change in the India-Russia relationship.

Before 2022, when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it supplied only a small share of India’s crude imports. Discounted Russian oil rapidly changed that, making Moscow one of India’s biggest suppliers.

It has also become the most contentious part of India’s relationship with the US, which has pressed New Delhi to reduce its purchases from Russia. India maintains that securing affordable and reliable energy is a national interest.

The disruption to traditional energy supplies has made that calculation more complicated. This year’s US-Israel war on Iran and disruption of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz have affected India’s purchases from the Gulf and pushed up prices.
Shankar said India is responding by diversifying its sources of supply, including both Russia and the US.
“In the long run, a transition to a non-fossil fuel economy would strengthen India’s energy independence. But this will not happen overnight,” she added.
Until then, Shankar said, India will take steps it considers necessary to stabilize supplies and protect its people.
Future of India-Russia defense cooperation
Defense remains the other major pillar, but here the direction of travel is clearer: India’s dependence on Russian equipment has been declining.
The Ukraine war has raised questions over Russia’s production capacity, delivery schedules and ability to supply spare parts after decades as a major supplier of India’s military hardware.

“India remains one of Russia’s oldest and largest arms buyers, and perhaps the last major one,” Aravind Yelery, an associate professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University in the Indian capital, New Delhi, told DW.

“New Delhi is increasingly reluctant to commit to Russia’s fifth-generation fighter program and has little appetite for new Russian hardware unless it can be incorporated into India’s indigenous production plans,” he added.
While India has diversified its purchases, that does not mean the defense relationship is disappearing.
However, the terms are changing, with India looking for a relationship that contributes to its own defense production, so that it can move away from simply buying finished systems.
The China question
Russia’s growing dependence on China has also become an unavoidable part of the India-Russia equation.

Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began in early 2022, China has become indispensable to Russia as a market, supplier and economic partner. That has reduced Moscow’s ability to serve as a counterweight to Beijing.
Yelery sees an important distinction in the two relationships.
“Strategically, Russia’s relationship with China remains structurally transactional, a dependence it can ill afford to compromise, whereas its relationship with India rests on partnership,” he said.
India still has reasons to keep Moscow close: energy, defense, access to the Russian market and a longstanding political relationship across Eurasia. But the strategic calculation has changed.
India’s ‘America plus’ strategy
Strategic affairs expert C Raja Mohan said that Russia’s growing dependence on China has changed its strategic value for India.
“Russia is no longer in a position to help India balance China,” Mohan, a professor of American studies at Jindal Global University, told DW.
This changes India’s expectations from the relationship with Russia.

The emphasis is increasingly on specific interests — energy security, defense supplies, trade and access to technology — while India’s larger strategic weight increasingly rests on relationships with the US and its allies.
India has expanded defense and technology cooperation with Washington, while deepening ties with partners such as France and Israel.
Mohan describes this approach as an “America plus” strategy, whereby India maintains its partnership with the US while widening its engagement with other major powers.
“India is trying to reduce its exposure to American volatility, but it still recognizes that Washington is its most important partner,” he said.
What do Modi and Putin want?
Rajan Kumar, a professor of Russian studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, said Putin wants reassurance that India will remain engaged with Moscow despite pressure from Washington.
“President Putin needs an assurance from Prime Minister Modi that India will not ditch Russia when the latter is facing the worst possible crisis after the 1990s,” Kumar told DW.
He expects continuity rather than a dramatic reset. “I think it is more about continuation of existing ties amid US pressure,” he added.

Energy trade and payment mechanisms, ways to increase Indian exports to Russia, defense cooperation and the two countries’ assessments of the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran are likely to remain important.
The bigger test will come in Delhi in September, when Putin is expected to return for the BRICS summit.
The Bishkek meeting can keep the political relationship on track, but the Delhi talks will show whether that political continuity can produce progress on trade, energy, defense and technology.

The relationship is no longer what it was before the Ukraine war. Energy has become far more important, India’s defense dependence is being recalibrated, and Russia’s closeness to China has altered the strategic equation.

“The relationship has a value that goes beyond individual deals. Putin appears well aware that India carries an independent strategic weight that China’s structural leverage cannot substitute,” said Yelery. /dl

articles.title: The floods keep coming. Nepal keeps starting over
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — When the flash flood tore through the Bhotekoshi corridor on August 26, it hit a road that had already been taken once. The stretch connecting Syaphrubesi to the Rasuwagadhi border…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — When the flash flood tore through the Bhotekoshi corridor on August 26, it hit a road that had already been taken once. The stretch connecting Syaphrubesi to the Rasuwagadhi border crossing was rebuilt and reopened about a month after the July 2025 flood that destroyed the “friendship bridge” linking Nepal to China and killed at least eight people. That repair was the fast part. The rest of the valley’s reconstruction was still unfinished 13 months later when the water came back, this time carrying ice and debris from a collapse high on Langtang Lirung.

“People were starting to forget the pain of last year’s flood,” Kaisang Nurpu Tamang, chairperson of Gosaikunda Rural Municipality, told the Kathmandu Post. “Everything was becoming normal.” Tamang’s own municipal building, thirteen kilometres up the valley in Timure, is gone now too, swept away along with the rest.

The 2026 flood has killed more than 900 people in Nepal, with over 4,200 still missing. Forty-one bridges and 42 kilometres of road were gone in a single morning. Swarnim Wagle, the country’s finance minister, told Reuters the preliminary estimate to rebuild could be anywhere between $4 billion and $5 billion. Binod Chaudhary, Nepal’s only billionaire, told Bloomberg Television days earlier that rebuilding could cost $5 billion.

Both estimates are less than what the 2015 earthquake reconstruction took. It is a fair comparison, except that Nepal was still working through pieces of that earthquake recovery when the floods of 2024 arrived, killing 300 more people across the eastern lowlands. Then came Rasuwagadhi in 2025. Last week’s was the latest.

For anyone paying attention — which most Nepalis are — three consecutive years of disaster have been described in strikingly similar language. Officials called last week’s Bhotekoshi flood unprecedented. The 2025 flood was described the same way. The 2024 floods were the worst rainfall the region had recorded since 1970. At some point, one has to ask: when the same word is used every year for the same kind of event, does it still describe the event, or has it started describing our relationship to it?

I asked Nepal’s foreign minister, Shishir Khanal, whether the government sees a pattern here or is still treating each flood as its own emergency. “We should anticipate such disasters are likely to be more frequent occurrences than in the past, and be prepared for them,” he said.

blocks.caption: The 2026 flood has killed more than 900 people in Nepal, with close to 4,250 still missing.  Angad Dhakal/TKP

blocks.text: There is a useful contrast next door. Bangladesh used to be cyclone country the way Nepal is flood country now — a place where a single storm could kill on a scale that defied comprehension. The 1970 Bhola cyclone is estimated to have killed between 300,000 and 500,000 people, among the deadliest disasters of the twentieth century. Bangladesh did not stop having cyclones after that. It has been hit by dozens since, but Bangladeshis now have a system that works. They have built a national network of concrete shelters, trained tens of thousands of volunteer evacuators village by village, and tied a warning system so tightly to that structure that a storm of comparable strength now kills in the dozens.

There’s a caveat in the comparison, of course. A cyclone is a meteorological event that announces itself days out, and the people at risk live in a flat, densely settled area where they can be moved to a shelter. A glacial collapse, like the one last week, forms in a high-altitude terrain, sometimes across an international border, and arrives down a narrow valley in minutes.

Nepal’s own mountain research body has been saying something similar about the ground itself. Five months before last week’s flood, the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) published findings that ice loss across the Hindu Kush Himalaya had doubled since 2000. Of 38 glaciers it monitors, only seven meet global monitoring standards; large parts of the range, it said, remain unmonitored altogether.

“We are trying to navigate a rapidly changing future with an incomplete map,” Mohd Farooq Azam, a cryosphere specialist at ICIMOD, said at the time. “Accelerated changes in water flows and cryosphere risks could remain undetected until the impacts are severe.” ICIMOD’s director general put it even more matter-of-factly. “These aren’t blind spots becoming surprises anymore,” he said. “They are our new reality.”

Nepal’s pattern over the last three years runs the other way from Bangladesh’s. Each flood over the past few years has been met with an improvised response built largely from scratch: army units are mobilised after the fact and drone surveys are ordered once the water level has receded.

“Our primary challenge is that our initial hydrological station was swept away on the first day,” Dharmaraj Upreti, chief executive of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, told the Post on Sunday. Replacing it, he said, requires the consent of both Nepal and China — a diplomatic step now unfolding in the middle of a disaster.

blocks.caption: Each flood over the past few years has been met with an improvised response built largely from scratch: army units are mobilised after the fact, and drone surveys are ordered once the water level has receded. Photo: Courtesy of Nepali Army

blocks.text: Prime Minister Balendra Shah, five months into office, said the state has been mobilised at full capacity. He visited Nuwakot to assess the damage, which is what his predecessor did after the 2025 flood, standing in front of a different stretch of the same river. Part of what makes the pattern hard to see, let alone address, in a country like Nepal is that each flood resets the political clock. Every natural disaster is an act of geology or weather that no government could have prevented, so the response gets judged only on the speed and visibility of relief.

When the Post asked the head of NDRRMA what it had learned, Upreti had this to say: “We are reviewing helicopter deployment logistics, helipad placements, body management procedures, and the availability of body bags. We have many lessons to implement from this experience.” But these are machinery for responding faster next time, not for catching the next flood before it happens.

Tamang, the Gosaikunda chair whose rural municipality has yet to receive federal coordination since the flood, described the same sequencing problem locally. A geologist needs to survey the area to determine what ground is safe, he said, before any long-term plan can be made. “Right now, we haven’t even been able to think that far,” he said.

Minister Khanal told me that two months before the flood, he had been pressing Chinese counterparts for a bilateral framework on hydrological and meteorological data-sharing across the border. The two sides, he said on Monday, were actively exchanging communications toward a framework agreement. It was not in place as of last week.

“I was told by some scientists who know the region very well that the glacial collapse didn’t even have a name in Nepali,” Khanal said, which probably means that Nepal either didn’t know it existed or didn’t consider it an imminent threat. Since the disaster, he said, Chinese authorities have been sharing real-time information on the new lake that formed upstream — the cooperation the framework was meant to formalize before there was a lake to worry about.

That new lake, high in the mountains in Tibet and formed by the same landslide, is being labelled “extremely concerning” by global scientists. Tamang, cut off from his own municipal building, said he and his community have no idea what’s happening above them. “There’s no electricity here, the telephone network still has no signal,” he said. “So we’re quite confused about what’s happening further up.” /dl

articles.title: Thai resort city Pattaya readies for US carrier’s 5,000 sailors
articles.summary: THAILAND — A US aircraft carrier at the center of a political row over conditions on board was set to arrive in Thailand on Tuesday, the first port call for its 5,000 crew since November. The…

blocks.text: THAILAND — A US aircraft carrier at the center of a political row over conditions on board was set to arrive in Thailand on Tuesday, the first port call for its 5,000 crew since November.

The resort city of Pattaya, a rest-and-recreation destination for US troops since the Vietnam War, has stepped up security as it prepares to welcome the sailors and Marines from the USS Abraham Lincoln.
“About 600 officials will provide security and other necessary assistance,” provincial Governor Narit Niramaiwong told AFP.
The nuclear-powered ship left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago.

Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health on board — including attempted suicides — have made headlines in the United States, provoking criticism of President Donald Trump’s war against Iran.
Pattaya’s mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, said the massive carrier would dock just after midnight (around 1701 GMT on Tuesday) at Laem Chabang port.
Around 40 buses have been laid on to transport the sailors to Pattaya and back in staggered groups until the carrier departs on Sunday.
“They come to relax because it’s been almost 280 days since anyone came ashore,” Poramase said in a Facebook post.

blocks.caption: An aerial photo shows the main beach in Pattaya on June 1, 2020. FILE PHOTO/Agence France-Presse

blocks.text: “Our preparations will focus on safety and ensuring fair pricing, so we don’t take advantage of them.”
No jet skis or cannabis
Once a sleepy fishing village, Pattaya was transformed by the Vietnam War in the 1960s, when US soldiers on leave began coming for rest and recreation (R&R).
The city has since become hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and a nightlife scene that has long drawn scrutiny over sex tourism.
Poramase told AFP there had been a recent crackdown on sex workers but denied it was linked to the US arrivals.
In his Facebook post, the mayor said he was hoping the soldiers could bring in up to 100 million Thai baht ($3 million) during their stay — a boon to the city during low season.

They have been banned from water sports such as jet skis, and from taking advantage of Thailand’s lax cannabis laws, he added, encouraging them to take part in the city’s many other attractions, from malls to religious sites.

“We’re happy to get business from anybody,” Nicko, the French owner of a go-go bar in Pattaya, told AFP. “We’ll have to be careful because as we know, things can get out of hand with alcohol involved.” /dl

articles.title: Nxled thumps PLDT, bounces back from loss
articles.summary: Nxled came out sizzling dumped defending champion PLDT, 25-19, 25-22, 25-20, to barge into the winning column of the PVL Invitational 2026 at the Smart Araneta Coliseum on Tuesday, Sept.1. Still…

blocks.text: Nxled came out sizzling dumped defending champion PLDT, 25-19, 25-22, 25-20, to barge into the winning column of the PVL Invitational 2026 at the Smart Araneta Coliseum on Tuesday, Sept.1.

Still licking their wounds from their four-set loss to the Creamline Cool Smashers less than 24 hours ago, the Chameleons took out their frustrations on the High Speed Hitters to even their win-loss record at 1-1.
MJ Phillips spearheaded the Nxled assault by pumping in eight kills and four aces to finish with 13 points, while skipper Myla Pablo took charge defensively with three blocks to chip in 12 points.
Nxled coach Ettore Guidetti said his stalwarts responded well with the defeat by playing better.
“(Today) simply confirmed we played pretty good volleyball. We’re getting better. Our defense especially worked better compared to (yesterday) and we also served much, much better today,” he said.
So impressive were the Chameleons that they only gave up 12 points on errors throughout the one hour, 30-minute match compared to the High Speed Hitters, who stumbled into 21 unforced errors.

Though PLDT held the edge in attacks, 44-41, Nxled made the most of its net defense with seven blocks. The Chameleons also capitalized on the High Speed Hitters’ shaky first ball, firing six aces to keep PLDT on the back foot.
Lyann De Guzman also paced Nxled by pouring all her 10 points on attacks, while Gel Cayuna distributed the ball well with 15 excellent sets.

Savi Davison was the lone bright spot for PLDT after erupting for 20 points, but couldn’t get the needed support as none from her teammates scored in double figures. Mika Reyes was limited to eight points, while Kianna Dy and Majoy Baron were held to just four and three points, respectively.
The High Speed Hitters fell to a 1-1card, failing to follow up their four-set win over EST Cola on Monday, Aug. 31.

articles.title: Foreign debt service burden climbs to $6.21 billion at end-May on higher principal payments
articles.summary: The Philippines ’ external debt service burden (DSB) increased by 4.8 percent to $6.21 billion in the first five months of 2026 from $5.93 billion in the same period in 2025 on the back of scheduled…

blocks.text: The Philippines ’ external debt service burden (DSB) increased by 4.8 percent to $6.21 billion in the first five months of 2026 from $5.93 billion in the same period in 2025 on the back of scheduled repayments. The latest Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) data showed that the increase in the country’s servicing of its foreign debt was fueled by a rise in principal payments, which offset a marginal decline in interest payments (IPs). An increasing external DSB indicates that a larger portion of the country’s financial resources is being used to pay off foreign obligations. Amortization, or principal payments, rose by 13.6 percent to $3.01 billion during the five-month period from $2.65 billion last year. Meanwhile, IPs edged down by 2.3 percent to $3.2 billion from $3.28 billion a year ago. SM Investment Corp. (SMIC) group economist Robert Dan Roces said the rising debt service largely reflects “scheduled repayments, not financial stress.” “More debt matured during the period, pushing principal payments higher, while IPs declined. With ample reserves and steady foreign currency inflows, the country remains well-positioned to meet its external obligations,” Roces said. As of end-March, the Philippines’ total external debt stood at $147.35 billion, a slight increase from $146.74 billion a year ago. Government debt accounted for approximately $95.66 billion, or nearly two-thirds of total, while the private sector accounted for $51.7 billion. Foreign borrowings were equivalent to 26.1 percent of the country’s annualized gross national income (GNI) as of end-March, down from 27.8 percent a year ago. Meanwhile, the ratio fell to 30 percent of annualized gross domestic product (GDP) as of end-March, compared with 31.5 percent as of end-March 2025. GNI measures the total income generated by a country’s residents, both domestically and abroad, while GDP accounts for local output. As of end-May, the DSB-to-export shipments ratio eased to 21.6 percent from 22.4 percent in the same period of 2025, while the DSB-to-current account receipts ratio remained unchanged at 8.9 percent. Furthermore, gross international reserves (GIR) stood at $103.99 billion by end-May, down from $105.18 billion a year ago. Despite the lower reserves, the annualized GIR-to-DSB ratio rose to 773.6 percent from 616.2 percent a year ago, reflecting a strengthened liquidity buffer relative to the DSB. According to the BSP, the foreign DSB represents principal and IPs. This covers payments on fixed medium- and long-term (MLT) credits, including those from the Washington-based multilateral lender International Monetary Fund (IMF) and new money facilities. It also includes IPs on fixed and revolving short-term liabilities of banks and nonbanks. However, it excludes prepayments on future maturities of foreign loans and principal payments on short-term obligations.

articles.title: 11 Pangasinan towns placed on alert ahead of opening of two San Roque Dam gates
articles.summary: SAN MANUEL, Pangasinan — Residents in San Manuel, San Nicolas, Asingan, Tayug, Sta. Maria, Rosales, Villasis, Sto. Tomas, Alcala, Bautista and Bayambang are being urged to remain alert as the San…

blocks.text: Pangasinan Provincial Mobile Force Company personnel inspect San Roque Dam and monitor water levels as part of disaster preparedness and critical infrastructure security efforts on Tuesday. (Photo courtesy of PMFC via Liezle Inigo)

SAN MANUEL, Pangasinan — Residents in San Manuel, San Nicolas, Asingan, Tayug, Sta. Maria, Rosales, Villasis, Sto. Tomas, Alcala, Bautista and Bayambang are being urged to remain alert as the San Roque Dam prepares to open two gates beginning 8 a.m. on Sept. 2, 2026.
The National Power Corporation (NPC) said the planned gate-opening will release water at a rate of about 300 cubic meters per second (cms), equivalent to a two-meter gate opening.
As of 12 noon on Sept. 1, the dam’s water level was recorded at 283.68 meters above sea level (MASL).
The NPC said the discharge is a precautionary measure to manage the continuing rise in the dam’s water level.
Residents living near riverbanks and downstream areas are advised to closely monitor official advisories from local disaster risk reduction and management offices.

articles.title: Whirlwinds batter 10 Ilocos Sur towns, damage homes, beach huts
articles.summary: VIGAN CITY, Ilocos Sur — Whirlwinds battered at least 10 towns in Ilocos Sur over two consecutive evenings, ripping off roofs, damaging houses and beach huts, and toppling trees as heavy rains and…

blocks.text: VIGAN CITY, Ilocos Sur — Whirlwinds battered at least 10 towns in Ilocos Sur over two consecutive evenings, ripping off roofs, damaging houses and beach huts, and toppling trees as heavy rains and strong winds brought by the enhanced southwest monsoon, or "habagat", continued to lash at the province.

Ilocos Sur Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Officer Rhon Arquelada said that, as of noon Tuesday, September 1, the affected towns were Burgos, Bantay, Narvacan, Cabugao, Sinait, Magsingal, Sto. Domingo, San Vicente, Santa Catalina, and Caoayan.
The first reported whirlwind struck Burgos on Sunday evening, August 30, while the nine other towns were hit on Monday evening, August 31.
“We are still in the process of assessing the damage to houses and huts caused by the whirlwinds in the other towns in the province,” Arquelada said.
Except for Burgos and Bantay, most of the affected areas were in coastal towns.
At least 10 houses were partially damaged after a strong whirlwind swept through Barangays Manaboc and Bangbangar in Burgos at around 6 p.m. Sunday at the height of heavy rains.
The whirlwind ripped through roofs of houses and garages and uprooted trees as powerful winds swept across the two villages.
According to the Burgos Municipal Police Station, barangay officials alerted authorities about the whirlwind while police personnel were conducting situational monitoring through handheld radios.
Police personnel and members of the Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office immediately responded to verify the reports and assess the damage.
Affected residents were assisted and moved to safer areas while clearing operations were conducted in the communities.
In Narvacan, four huts at WOW Sulvec Beach in Barangay Sulvec were heavily damaged after a whirlwind suddenly struck the area.
PLT Reynald Ramos of Narvacan town said some of the huts collapsed while others had their roofs blown off by the powerful winds.
Several trees in the area were also knocked down.
Authorities and concerned agencies immediately conducted clearing operations to remove debris, ensure public safety, and make the affected area passable.
In nearby Cabugao town, another whirlwind struck at around 6:30 p.m., affecting Barangays Quezon, Baclig, and Rizal.
PMajor Pol Areola of the Cabugao Municipal Police Station said authorities were still assessing the damage to houses and other properties.
Several trees were toppled onto roads, while some houses sustained partial damage.
Another whirlwind also swept through Barangay Aging in Sinait town, damaging houses and uprooting trees as strong winds battered the village.
Several houses reportedly had their roofs blown off.
Authorities were continuing damage assessments in all affected areas.
No injuries or casualties were reported in any of the whirlwind incidents.
Arquelada said the Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office remains on heightened alert as heavy rains associated with the Habagat continue to affect Ilocos Sur.
As of noon Tuesday, at least 90 families, or 225 individuals, from 18 towns in the province remained in evacuation centers for safety amid continuing heavy rains.
Meanwhile, a total of 5,026 families, or 17,371 individuals, have been affected by the continuing inclement weather in the province. (Freddie G. Lazaro)

articles.title: Mayon sulfur dioxide emissions surge amid signs of rising volcanic unrest
articles.summary: Mayon Volcano’s sulfur dioxide (SO2) emissions rose on Monday, Sept. 1, reaching the second-highest level recorded since volcanic gas concentrations began declining in July, said the Philippine…

blocks.text: Mayon Volcano’s sulfur dioxide (SO2) emissions rose on Monday, Sept. 1, reaching the second-highest level recorded since volcanic gas concentrations began declining in July, said the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (Phivolcs).
The volcano recorded 7,115 tons of SO2 emissions on Aug. 31 based on averaged measurements from stationary ultraviolet spectrometry.
Since Mayon’s alert status was lowered to Alert Level 2 on Aug. 5, its SO2 emissions had averaged only 3,844 tons per day.
The increase was accompanied by a slight rise in low-frequency volcanic earthquakes (LFVQs), which are attributed to volcanic degassing.
As of Tuesday, the Mayon Volcano Network had recorded 12 LFVQs.
However, Phivolcs said real-time seismic energy release has remained in the background levels.
The agency also noted “a short-term trend of swelling or pressurization” in the northern and eastern sectors of the volcano’s edifice based on readings from electronic tilt deformation stations.
“Elevated volcanic SO2 emissions could forewarn of a potential shift to renewed eruptive activity at the summit crater,” Phivolcs said.
It warned that renewed activity could generate volcanic hazards around Mayon, with the impacts potentially worsened by prevailing poor weather conditions.
Phivolcs reminded the public that Mayon remains at Alert Level 2, or moderate level of unrest, but said there are “new possibilities of eruptive unrest recurring.”

The agency warned that a new phase of eruption could generate life-threatening volcanic hazards, including pyroclastic density currents (PDCs) or uson, rockfall, ballistic fragments that can be thrown from the crater, and extensive ashfall that could severely affect communities downwind of the volcano.

Phivolcs reminded the public to refrain from entering the six-kilometer radius permanent danger zone and urged communities and local government units within predetermined PDC hazard zones to prepare for a possible escalation to Alert Level 3.

It also called for increased vigilance and pre-emptive response actions against lahars and sediment-laden streamflow along channels draining Mayon during sustained heavy or intense rains, especially if an explosive eruption occurs simultaneously.

Civil aviation authorities were also advised to continue telling pilots to avoid flying close to Mayon’s summit, as ash and ballistic fragments from any sudden eruption could pose hazards to aircraft.

blocks.text: September 1, 2026
Russia threatens 'devastating' response amid Baltic tensions
Russia says it will "deliver a devastating response" to any hostile action against it in the Baltic region.

"In the event of a further escalation of the military-political situation in the Baltic region, it must be emphasized once again: Russia's response to the instigators of reckless anti-Russian ventures will be decisive. articles.title: ‘The mountains are changing’: What the floods tell us about the future of India’s Himalayas
articles.summary: As families await news of missing loved ones, the disaster is a stark reminder of how the climate crisis is creating a fast-growing threat. Plus, the town considered India’s ‘Jurassic…

blocks.text: It has been hard not to despair while watching the ruinous floods swallow parts of Nepal, and harder, still knowing that the agony compounds each passing day for dozens of Indian families whose members remain unaccounted for.

Social media is awash with desperate pleas, photos and details of the young and old, men and women, from Mumbai to Kolkata, posted by families searching for traces of life. The disaster unfolded when a melting glacier slammed into the valley below, unleashing a deadly cascade of rock and ice down the Bhote Kashi River, which flows from Tibet into Nepal.

Among the 275 Indians missing at the time of writing are workers of a hydropower project and people undertaking the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Another 128 people of Indian origin, including a large group of Sadhguru’s Isha Foundation spiritual group, are also missing; 149 Indian people have been rescued as of Monday.

For Gauri Joshi, whose five relatives remained unaccounted for over the weekend, the last few days have been a blur of calling their numbers in vain, watching news of rescue operations and trying to reach Indian officials – over and over again. What she has pieced together so far is that her relatives, part of a pilgrim tour group from Maharashtra, cleared immigration at the Gyirong border between Nepal and Tibet and boarded buses shortly before the flood waters destroyed the crossing.
“Chances appear very bleak now. But maybe a miracle will happen,” Joshi said.

The tragedy has reignited the question of how vulnerable the Himalayas are to climate change, and what its implications are for India. To understand the risks of glacier collapse and thawing permafrost leading to sudden floods and debris flows, I spoke to Dr Ashim Sattar, a professor at Indian Institute of Technology Bhubaneswar and an expert on glacial lake outburst floods. The conversation has been edited and condensed.
What are the climate- or glacier-related risks emerging across the Himalayas?

“There are different forms of cryosphere and how they pose a hazard. In a layperson’s terms, the cryosphere is where water exists in solid form, for example a glacier. When it melts, it forms glacial lakes. If they have an outburst, they can cause damage downstream.

Another cryospheric component is glacier ice. This is what we’ve seen in Nepal, where a glacier detachment happened. The frontal part of the glacier detached from the main glacier and eventually led to a debris flow.

The third component is permafrost. They exist widely in the Himalayas, but there has not been much monitoring because it’s very difficult. Everything – these lakes, glaciers and permafrost – are all hazards. Unless they’re triggered, they would not cause damage.

With climate change, these grounds will go above zero degrees and will start to degrade. These would need very little … to mobilise debris. We might expect a higher frequency of debris flows in the future. We won’t know how they are getting conditioned, unless we have some monitoring stations and scientific investigation.

And given the Himalayas are very vast, monitoring every part of it becomes tricky. It can be the mountain ranges within India, or maybe outside India, eventually, which drains into the Indian subcontinent. That needs to be well studied.”

blocks.caption: ‘[Floods] might happen any time’ … a Devighat resident retrieves some of his belongings. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

blocks.text: How big are the downstream risks for India?

“Right now, this is a gap in scientific studies; nothing [is] quantified yet. There is direct evidence of climate impacts, even in the Indian part of the Himalayas. The number of glacial lakes is increasing, the size of glacial lakes is increasing, the volume of glacial lakes is increasing, and glaciers are retreating. The risk exists because it might happen any time.”
Which parts of India are the most vulnerable?

“Everyone in the Himalayas, every Himalayan state has hazards. We can’t deny it. If you look at the eastern side, they have a lot of glacial lakes. They have already reached their maximum extent. Most full-grown lakes are about to reach their limits, like maximum extent. In the western Himalayas or even the central Himalayas, there’s a lot of scope for the lakes because they have not reached their full extent. As the glaciers would retreat, they would keep on growing.

We are still unsure when the status is going to change for any of these states. That’s a very, very difficult question, and I don’t think anyone [can] answer it at this moment without any scientific investigation.”

How would you describe India’s early warning systems and disaster preparedness?“The National Disaster Management Authority is taking proactive steps now with the glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) Risk Mitigation Programme to install early-warning systems.

Maybe an early warning system should be community-based. It should be for the people and by the people. It’s not always the scientist or the policymakers who can actually make this work at its full potential. We need to have local knowledge, involve the communities to make them more effective.”
How long will it take to have these systems in place?

“I have no idea because each of these organisations are working at their own pace. They have their own style of working. I’m sure it is going to happen soon. I can just comment on the areas where I know, and I’ve been in touch.”
Is prevention possible, or can it only minimise the damage?

“Prevention is possible, but it is very expensive: computationally, financially and manpower-wise. Minimising is also possible. It would require a lot of intervention in the high mountains, which is very difficult in those terrains.

We know that the mountains are changing and the hazard levels are increasing, so the only way forward is to minimise the exposure to the risk below. That means how much of the hazard is going to interact with the downstream. If something is in the path, we remove them.”

blocks.caption: ‘Jurassic Park of India’ … a dinosaur museum in Raiyoli. Photograph: Ajit Solanki/AP

blocks.text: Photographer Aashim Tyagi (@aashim), who once documented Art Deco architecture in Gujarat’s Balasinor, suggests a prehistoric side quest: “I was intrigued by the town’s reputation as the ‘Jurassic Park of India’ and a little digging led me to a dinosaur museum in neighbouring Raiyoli. It’s set amid open fields near one of Asia’s largest fossil beds where Rajasaurus narmadensis and a dozen other species once roamed. Much of the museum and the village’s paleontological preservation is owed to Aaliya Babi of Balasinor’s erstwhile royal family, earning her the nickname ‘Dinosaur Princess’. Balasinor and its dinosaur museum are a worthwhile detour from Ahmedabad or Baroda.”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: India ranked 176th out of 177 countries in the 2026 Environmental Performance Index. Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters

blocks.text: India ranked 176th, second from the bottom, in the 2026 Environmental Performance Index, which evaluates countries on environmental health, climate change and ecosystem vitality. The country recorded negative values on air-quality indicators but showed an improvement on the index’s 10-year change metric. In 2022, when India had been ranked last, the central government had dismissed the EPI’s conclusions, saying it used “unscientific methods”.

articles.title: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
articles.summary: As of August, the number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran had reached another million.

blocks.text: Watch: BBC's Lyse Doucet reports on the biggest cross-border movement of people
ByLyse Doucet
Chief international correspondentReporting fromTorkham crossing and Kabul
The elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind.
"It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan.
The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins.

"But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags.
Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran.
They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world.

Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021.

Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt.
The expulsions show no sign of stopping.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Trucks carrying returnees parked along the highway near the border

blocks.text: Image source, AFP
Trucks carrying returnees parked along the highway near the border
The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR.

"In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan.
"We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border.

It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go.
Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all.

"I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry.
"We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says.
"But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Afghan returnees deported from Pakistan arriving at the Torkham crossing

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Afghan returnees deported from Pakistan arriving at the Torkham crossing
Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan.

The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law".
Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden.

The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants".
In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025.

The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel".
The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified".
But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zarina, 40, is among the million Afghan who have returned this year alone

blocks.text: Zarina, 40, is among the million Afghan who have returned this year alone
Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children.
Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university?
Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried."
Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified.
"I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house.
"We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside."

He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work.
"I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country.
Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights.
Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN.
But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zarina says she is worried about the future of the girls who cannot attend school in Taliban-run Afghanistan

blocks.text: Zarina says she is worried about the future of the girls who cannot attend school in Taliban-run Afghanistan
At the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face.
"There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan."
In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide.

The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition.
"No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive.
But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support".
Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girl's education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve.

The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule.
But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states.
As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?"
He answers his own question: "Nothing."
We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense.
All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

articles.summary: The rapper's killing became one of popular culture's great mysteries, with countless theories but no arrests until 2023.

blocks.text: Duane "Keffe D" Davis, a 63-year-old former gang boss, has been found guilty of murdering rapper Tupac Shakur.

The famous rapper was shot multiple times on 7 September 1996 in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas and died several days later. Davis was unexpectedly charged with murder in 2023 and has been standing trial in Las Vegas.
Davis was charged with murder with a deadly weapon. He faces a potential sentence of life in prison without parole.

articles.title: South African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clash
articles.summary:
• Cape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risks

  • Airlink insist flyby conducted according to regulations

A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets…

blocks.text: A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of around 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks.
The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.

Flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41 to 46 feet (12 to 14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.
Allow Instagram content?

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Airlink, a sponsor of the South African rugby union team, said that the flyby was conducted according to safety regulations. The airline said that it was carefully planned and rehearsed, with the aircraft travelling at around 150 knots (172 mph), when they went over the stadium. Each jet had three senior captains on board, Airlink said, operating in the roles of a commander, a co-pilot and a safety officer. The jets were not carrying any passengers.

“Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium,” Airlink said on Sunday. “The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude, at around 150 knots. The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby.”

blocks.caption: The planes fly above the stadium before kick-off. Photograph: Gallo Images/Getty Images

blocks.text: South African rugby union has a tradition of stadium flybys at big games, starting when a Boeing 747 flew over another stadium in Johannesburg before the 1995 World Cup final between the same teams, who are fierce rivals. But this weekend’s flyby was especially low and dramatic, generating global interest after it was shown as part of the pre-game broadcast, and sparking a flurry of videos shot by witnesses.

blocks.caption: The second jet flies through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Some aviation experts questioned whether the margin for error was too small. “Basically, that lead aircraft … was kind of like dodging over the roof and climbing over the one side and dipping below and then climbing over the other side. That was a little bit uncomfortable,” said Chris Martinus, president of Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association South Africa. “[If] something adverse happens, you just don’t have options at that kind of altitude.”
after newsletter promotion

Keith Tonkin, an Australian aviation consultant and former military and commercial pilot, said on Monday that the Embraer passenger jets – which are small-to-medium jets designed for regional flights – were not designed or intended for that kind of low-level operation and warned against the precedent.

“The bigger picture is that a benchmark has been established and others may expect to do something similar, and that’s not going to end well,” Tonkin said. He added that turbulence or a bird strike at such a low altitude could leave the pilots with too little room to manoeuvre without hitting the stadium.
Airlink said that the flight data recorded by both aircraft confirmed that their flights were performed within civil aviation safety limits for speed and altitude.

articles.title: Countries legally obliged to consider slavery reparations, says UN committee
articles.summary:
Guidance says states must implement ‘comprehensive measures’ to address legacy of racial discrimination

A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the…

blocks.text: A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.

Guidance published on Monday by the committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) said the obligations arose from ⁠a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.
The committee described the approach as a “paradigm ⁠shift” away from debates over historical responsibility that have often been used by governments to resist reparations ​claims.
“States parties must implement comprehensive reparatory measures for ‌people of African descent, ‌covering all aspects of remedies,” said the UN document, which may be cited in courtrooms.
At least 12.5 ‌million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries in what CERD called the largest forced displacement in history.

Calls for reparations – ranging from official apologies to financial compensation – have gained momentum internationally, though opponents argue states and institutions should not be held responsible for historical crimes. The EU and Britain abstained from a UN resolution ‌on slavery in March.
Some states have sought to dodge claims for justice in courtrooms by arguing that there were no international laws outlawing the slave trade ​at the time – the so-called intertemporality principle.

But the UN document argues that, regardless of whether slavery and the slave trade were illegal under the laws of the day, countries remain responsible under current international obligations to tackle their continuing effects.

“Irrespective of the legal characterisation of the original historical acts, states parties remain bound ⁠by their present obligations under the convention to address structural inequalities,” the UN document ​says.
Financial compensation alone is ​not sufficient, it adds, urging “transformative” measures including ​opening archives, revising public memorials and establishing independent truth commissions.
after newsletter promotion
Pela Boker Wilson, a committee expert ​from Liberia who helped draft ‌the document, said ​she expected states ​to move beyond broad expressions of regret and review policies and laws.

“We are calling on state parties to take concrete and meaningful action,” she told Reuters. “We want to affirm the dignity of those whose suffering was denied, whose suffering was minimised or forgotten.”

articles.title: Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM
articles.summary:
Pedro Sánchez says two countries are cooperating after mass incursion by 70,000 people into north African enclave

Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has insisted there was no evidence…

blocks.text: Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has insisted there was no evidence to suggest the Moroccan government was behind last month’s massive border crossing into Ceuta.

As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter the Spanish enclave at the end of July. The influx of about 70,000 men, women and children unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions over immigration within the EU.
Although the overwhelming majority of the migrants crossed back into Morocco weeks ago, hundreds of people, including minors, are still on the streets of Ceuta, leading to tensions with residents.

Despite speculation that Rabat may have engineered the mass crossing as a means of showing its displeasure at Spain’s rapprochement with Algeria, Sánchez said there was nothing to indicate the involvement of the Moroccan authorities.
“There’s no information from any intelligence agency that raises doubts over the involvement of Moroccan authorities,” he told Cadena Ser radio on Monday.

“Cooperation with Morocco is frankly positive. I’d like to stress that we need to be aware that this crisis can be resolved only through cooperation – and not through a lack of trust in Morocco, which would only further aggravate the already complex situation we have in Ceuta.”

The prime minister once again pointed the finger at “criminal gangs” who had used disinformation to falsely claim that a ruling by Spain’s supreme court meant that no one who entered Ceuta by swimming could be deported back to Morocco.

He also said fake news had been pumped out on social media accounts “associated with Russia, Israel and the international far right that always use migration to attack not just Spain but also Europe”.
Sánchez said that about 1,500 migrants remained in Ceuta, of whom 1,200 are minors, and there would soon be “sufficient capacity” to accommodate all those still in the enclave.

Their continuing presence has led to clashes between some Ceuta residents and police, while some of the migrants have had their belongings burned while sleeping rough on beaches. On Saturday, four Moroccan migrants were arrested for throwing stones at Spanish soldiers.

Spain’s conservative People’s party has accused the government of failing to protect the people of Ceuta. “It did nothing to avoid the invasion on 30 July and it’s doing nothing to stop the public order crisis that’s getting worse every day,” the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said last week.

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, has described events in Ceuta as “an invasion and an act of war promoted by Morocco and allowed by Sánchez, who is incapable of responding because he is subservient to Morocco”.

articles.title: Republicans back Trump in his trade war with Canada

image.caption: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, centre, arrives to meet with Speaker of the House Mike Johnson and Republican lawmakers at the U.S. Capitol in Washington on Wednesday. (J. Scott Applewhite/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Republican members of Congress are publicly backing U.S. President Donald Trump in his trade war with Canada and blaming Prime Minister Mark Carney's government for walking away from negotiations.
After meeting with U.S. trade rep on Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers defend president's tactics
Dozens of GOP House members gathered on Capitol Hill on Wednesday for a closed-door meeting with Trump's point man on tariffs, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

While some Republicans are quietly concerned that an escalation of costly tariffs could worsen their re-election prospects in the midterms in November, those who spoke with CBC News after meeting Greer generally expressed support for the president's trade strategy.
Trade war a campaign hurdle for some Republicans ahead of U.S. midterms
Texas Republican August Pfluger praised Trump for bringing manufacturing jobs back to the U.S. and pinned blame for the trade war on Ottawa.
"It's a war that is perpetuated by Canada," Pfluger told CBC News. "The Canadians need to get reasonable. They've taken advantage of the United States for a long time."

items: Carney says Trump and his cabinet should stop 'throwing shade' and get serious about a deal

blocks.text: Brian Mast, a five-term Congressman from Florida, also criticized Canada for the breakdown in trade talks.
"They were given the best possible deal, more generous than anybody else across the globe, and it's something that they turned their back on," Mast told CBC News.
When Greer emerged from the meeting, he did not respond to reporters' questions about the state of negotiations with Canada.
Trump criticizes Canada's banking policy
Meanwhile at the White House, Trump gave no sign of shifting his position that Canada has long taken advantage of the U.S. on trade.
Trump told reporters that one of his biggest grievances against Canada is the limits it puts on U.S. bank operations north of the border.

items: Donald Trump mistakes Bank of Canada for retail bank
Canada has leverage in this trade fight, but economists warn it comes with a cost

blocks.text: "They basically don't allow banks of America to be in Canada, that's sort of emblematic of the way they treat us," Trump said in the Oval Office on Wednesday afternoon.
"Canada has all of its major banks here, and we're their biggest source of income, far bigger than they are in Canada," he said.
How Trump mastered the art of the distraction
On Capitol Hill, the sole Republican who raised concerns about the impact of the trade war on voters was Ralph Norman, who represents a South Carolina district.
"What I hear in South Carolina is affordability," said Norman. "It all goes into affordability, whether it's this [trade war with Canada], whether it's tariffs, whether it's housing, gas."
He says Greer expressed willingness to address how tariffs are affecting each state.
"The concerns, they were real," Norman said. "I think the White House will be listening."

items: Can the U.S.-Canada trade war change course if Democrats win the midterm elections?
Iran war hits 6-month milestone with Trump's attention largely elsewhere

blocks.text: Although polling suggests Trump's tariffs are deeply unpopular, other Congressional Republicans lined up to defend the president's trade war with Canada, in some cases repeating his arguments almost word-for-word.
Missouri Congressman Eric Burlison said it would not be a smart move for Canada to levy counter-tariffs on U.S. exports, as Carney has threatened to do next week.
"We're the economic powerhouse obviously compared to [Canada]," Burlison said. "I think Canada needs the United States more than we need them."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Mike Crawley is a correspondent for CBC News, based in Washington. He began his career as a newspaper reporter in B.C., spent six years as a freelance journalist in various parts of Africa, then joined the CBC in 2005. Mike reported on Ontario politics for 15 years. He was born and raised in Saint John, N.B.

articles.title: Pentagon makes testosterone screening mandatory for U.S. service members effective immediately

image.caption: The Pentagon released new guidance Wednesday for mandatory testosterone screening following a July directive from U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

The ​U.S. Pentagon issued detailed guidance on Wednesday for a new, mandatory testosterone deficiency screening policy for active-duty and reserve service members age 30 and older, ‌a follow-up to a July announcement from U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.
People aged 30 and up will be subjected to screening for hormone levels or disrupted menstrual cycles

The guidance, which is effective immediately, establishes standardized screening and treatment pathways for men and women that ​the Pentagon says are aimed at ​improving military readiness by identifying and managing hormonal and energy-availability issues.

Hegseth, who has promoted the use of ​testosterone, announced the mandate last month, raising questions ⁠among experts about whether ⁠there was a ‌scientific basis for such a policy. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration plans to hold a meeting of experts to discuss medical use of testosterone in ⁠mid-September.

items: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth unveils plan to test troops for low testosterone
Canada's top soldier expresses pride in 'who we are' after Hegseth targets cadets in post

blocks.text: According to the guidance, men age 30 and older will receive mandatory testosterone blood tests, while younger men will be tested ‌only on request or if clinicians identify warning signs.

For women, the guidance does not mandate routine testosterone blood tests, but it calls for screening for ​fatigue and disrupted menstrual cycles that can be associated with hormonal dysregulation and ⁠conditions called low-energy availability and relative energy deficiency in sport.
The ⁠document lays out guidelines for when it is appropriate to ⁠prescribe ⁠off-label testosterone in ​women, namely for postmenopausal women with unusually low sexual desire.

Doctors have ​raised concerns ⁠that broad testosterone testing could lead to unnecessary, or potentially harmful, treatment, saying there is little evidence that universal screening for low testosterone among military personnel would improve U.S. combat readiness.
